topics.formula: I am / he, she, it is / we, you, they are — short forms: I'm, he's / she's / it's, we're / you're / they're.
topics.key_idea: The verb 'be' always needs a subject in front of it, and its form changes depending on who or what you're talking about. It's one of the most-used verbs in English — for saying who someone is, their age or job, how they feel, what the weather's like, prices, time, and general descriptions.
examples: Bekzod is an engineer. Nadia's a nurse.
Carlos is from Mexico. They're my neighbours.
It's chilly this evening. It's half past two.
common_mistakes: Dropping the subject: saying 'Is cold today' instead of 'It's cold today' — English always needs the subject, even when it seems obvious.
Using a short form in a positive short answer: 'Yes, she's' instead of the full 'Yes, she is.' Short forms are fine in negative answers ('No, she isn't'), just not positive ones.

topics.formula: this (singular, near) / these (plural, near) — that (singular, far) / those (plural, far).
topics.key_idea: Pick the word based on two things at once: is it one thing or more than one, and is it close to you or further away. They can go in front of a noun ('this bag') or stand on their own ('this is mine'). 'This is...' has a special job too — it's how English introduces people and answers the phone.
examples: This is my new laptop.
These are my cousins.
That building over there is enormous.
Those boots are too expensive.
Hi, this is Marcus.
common_mistakes: Mismatching number: saying 'this books' or 'that shoes' instead of 'these books' or 'those shoes' — the word has to match singular or plural, not just near or far.
Using 'that' instead of 'this' when introducing someone standing right there, or answering the phone — it's 'This is Marcus,' not 'That is Marcus,' since the person is 'here,' not 'there.'

topics.formula: my, your, his, her, its, our, their + noun. Possessive adjectives never change form — not even before a plural noun.
topics.key_idea: Subject pronoun + verb is one pattern ('I love...'), possessive adjective + noun is a different one ('my friend'). For people, use his/her; for things, use its; but in the plural, they/their covers both people and things. Its and it's look alike but aren't related: it's always means 'it is,' and its (no apostrophe) is the possessive.
examples: I love my brother.
The dog wagged its tail.
They found their keys.
It's freezing outside, and its wind chill makes it worse.
common_mistakes: Adding a plural ending to the possessive: 'these are theirs suitcases' instead of 'these are their suitcases' — the word stays the same no matter how many things follow it.
Mixing up its and it's — 'it's' always means 'it is' ('it's beautiful'), while 'its' with no apostrophe is the possessive ('I like its color').

topics.formula: a + consonant sound / an + vowel sound — before a singular, countable noun only. Never before a plural.
topics.key_idea: The choice between a and an is about sound, not spelling — that's the part that trips people up. A silent 'h' still counts as a vowel sound ('an hour'), and a 'u' pronounced like 'you' still counts as a consonant sound ('a university'), even though both look like they should go the other way.
examples: It's an apple.
Give me an hour to finish.
I want to buy a hat.
Is there a European embassy nearby?
common_mistakes: Using a/an with a plural noun: 'these are a tables' instead of just 'these are tables.'
Choosing a/an by spelling instead of sound: saying 'a hour' instead of 'an hour,' or 'an university' instead of 'a university.'

topics.formula: most nouns: + -s. Endings in -s, -x, -ch, -sh, -o: + -es. Consonant + y → change y to i, + -es. Some -f/-fe endings → change to -ves. A number of common nouns are irregular.
topics.key_idea: Regular plurals mostly just add -s, but the sound at the end of the word decides whether you need a small spelling change first. A handful of very common nouns break the pattern completely and just have to be learned as irregular.
examples: one desk → two desks
one box → two boxes
one baby → two babies
one tooth → two teeth
common_mistakes: Adding -s to everything: 'citys' instead of 'cities,' or 'boxs' instead of 'boxes.'
Adding -s to an irregular noun instead of using its special form: 'childs' or 'mans' instead of 'children' or 'men.'

topics.formula: adjective + noun (before the noun) — or after be / feel / look / smell / sound / taste, with no noun needed. Adjectives never change form for plural.
topics.key_idea: In English, adjectives always come before the noun they describe — unlike many other languages, which is exactly why this trips learners up. Adjectives also stay in their singular form no matter how many things they describe, and a small group of sense verbs (feel, look, smell, sound, taste) can take an adjective directly, the same way be does.
examples: It's a spacious apartment.
This apartment is spacious.
You seem worried.
These are my newest shoes.
common_mistakes: Putting the adjective after the noun: 'a guitar expensive' instead of 'an expensive guitar' — common if your first language usually places descriptions after the noun.
Adding -s to an adjective to match a plural noun: 'favourites shoes' or 'blues eyes' instead of 'favourite shoes' or 'blue eyes.'

topics.formula: I / you / we / they + base verb — he / she / it + verb+s (spelling changes to -es or -ies in some cases). Questions: do / does + subject + base verb. Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb.
topics.key_idea: Present simple is for things that are true in general, not just happening right now — habits you repeat, and facts or situations that stay the same. The one tricky part of the form is he/she/it, which needs an extra -s and switches do to does.
examples: I clean my room every day.
He works in a hospital.
Ice melts at 0 degrees.
Does she like tea? She doesn't drink it.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the -s on he/she/it: 'she work in a bank' instead of 'she works in a bank.'
Keeping the -s on the main verb after does: 'does he works' instead of 'does he work' — once do/does shows up, the main verb goes back to its base form.

topics.formula: (Question word) + auxiliary + subject + base verb. Auxiliary is am/is/are for the verb 'be', or do/does for every other verb. Yes/no questions just drop the question word.
topics.key_idea: Every present simple question needs an auxiliary right before the subject. If the main verb is 'be', that auxiliary IS the verb (am/is/are). For every other verb, do/does gets borrowed just to build the question, and the real verb stays in its base form the whole time — even with he/she/it.
examples: Where do they study?
What does he do?
Do you understand Spanish?
Is she busy?
common_mistakes: Keeping the -s on the main verb after does: 'What does she does?' instead of 'What does she do?' — the verb goes back to its base form once does is there.
Adding do/does to a question that already uses be: 'Does she is tired?' instead of 'Is she tired?'

topics.formula: what + noun (what time, what colour, what size...) / how + adjective or adverb (how old, how tall, how often...)
topics.key_idea: 'What' and 'how' regularly pair up with a noun or an adjective/adverb right after them to ask about something specific — and that pairing changes the question a lot. 'How' alone isn't the same question as 'how often' or 'how tall.'
examples: What size is your jacket?
What time do you want?
How tall is your building?
How often do you cook?
common_mistakes: Dropping the noun and leaving the question too vague: asking 'What is your jacket?' when the real question is 'What colour is your jacket?'
Mixing up the pairings: saying 'what tall' instead of 'how tall' — 'what' pairs with nouns, 'how' pairs with adjectives and adverbs.

topics.formula: subject + be + adverb, or adverb + other verb — after the subject in questions, after don't/doesn't in negatives. Longer expressions (once a week, every day) go at the end of the sentence instead.
topics.key_idea: Short frequency adverbs like always, often, and never sit in the middle of the sentence — right after 'be', but right before any other verb. Never and hardly ever already carry a negative meaning on their own, so the verb next to them has to stay positive, not negative. Longer frequency phrases (twice a week, every day) skip this rule entirely and go at the very end.
examples: She is usually early.
We don't often stay up late.
He is never rude.
I check my email twice a day.
common_mistakes: Double-negating with never or hardly ever: 'He isn't never late' or 'They don't hardly ever go' instead of 'He is never late' / 'They hardly ever go' — the verb has to stay positive.
Putting a short adverb at the end of the sentence instead of before the verb: 'I go always to school' instead of 'I always go to school.'

topics.formula: Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) go before the verb. Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) go after the verb, or after a preposition.
topics.key_idea: Most pronouns change form depending on whether they're doing the action (subject, before the verb) or receiving it (object, after the verb or a preposition) — I becomes me, he becomes him, and so on. You and it are the only two that stay exactly the same either way, which can hide the pattern at first.
examples: I like your bag.
Can you call me later?
She doesn't trust him.
Give it to her.
common_mistakes: Using a subject pronoun where an object pronoun belongs: 'Give it to he' instead of 'Give it to him,' especially after a preposition.
Reversing the pair in a two-person phrase: 'Me and him went' instead of 'He and I went' — subject pronouns are still needed when they're doing the action, even in a pair.

topics.formula: singular noun + 's (Anna's) — plural noun ending in -s + apostrophe only (the students') — irregular plural + 's (the children's). For things, not people, use 'of X' instead.
topics.key_idea: 's shows that something belongs to a person or pet, or describes a relationship — it's for people and pets, not things. Things use 'of' instead ('the end of the street,' not 'the street's end'). Where exactly the apostrophe goes depends on whether the noun is singular, a regular plural already ending in -s, or an irregular plural.
examples: This is Diana's mother.
The teachers' office is on the second floor.
The children's shoes are by the door.
The entrance of the building is on the left.
common_mistakes: Using 's with a thing instead of 'of': 'the street's end' instead of 'the end of the street.'
Putting the apostrophe in the wrong place for a regular plural: 'the student's books' when talking about many students, instead of 'the students' books.'

topics.formula: whose + noun, or whose alone ('Whose car is this?' / 'Whose is this?'). Answers use 's + noun, or 's alone ('It's John's car.' / 'It's John's.')
topics.key_idea: Whose asks who something belongs to, and it works both with a noun right after it and completely on its own. It's easy to mix up with who's, but the two are unrelated — whose is about possession, while who's is just the short form of 'who is,' the same kind of trap as its and it's.
examples: Whose bike is this?
Whose is this bike?
It's Diana's.
Who's that woman in the hallway?
common_mistakes: Confusing whose and who's: 'Who's car is this?' instead of 'Whose car is this?' — whose is possession, who's is short for 'who is.'
Assuming whose always needs a noun right after it, and missing that 'Whose is this?' is correct on its own.

topics.formula: at + specific times (at 3 o'clock, at night) — in + months / seasons / years / long periods (in May, in 1990) — on + days / dates (on Sunday, on 25 December). No preposition at all with last / next / every / this (last June, next Tuesday).
topics.key_idea: Think of it as zooming in: 'in' covers the biggest chunks of time (months, years, seasons), 'on' covers a specific day or date, and 'at' covers an exact point in time or a handful of fixed expressions. The one exception worth memorizing on its own is 'at night' — the other parts of the day use 'in' (in the morning/afternoon/evening). And whenever last, next, every, or this is already in front of a time expression, no preposition is added at all.
examples: I'll meet you at 5 o'clock.
My exam is in July.
The party is on Friday.
I visit my parents every Sunday.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition after last/next/every/this: 'in last June' or 'on next Tuesday' instead of just 'last June' or 'next Tuesday.'
Using 'in' for night instead of 'at': 'in the night' instead of 'at night,' even though the other parts of the day do use 'in.'

topics.formula: at + a point or specific spot (at the door, at school, at work) — in + an enclosed or bounded space (in the bag, in France, in the car) — on + a surface, or a set of transport/media expressions (on the table, on the bus, on TV).
topics.key_idea: Picture the three as different kinds of space: 'at' treats a place as just a point — you're 'at' it, not really inside or on top of it — 'in' means genuinely inside something with boundaries (a room, a box, a country), and 'on' means resting on top of a surface. A handful of common expressions (on the bus, on TV, at work) don't perfectly follow that logic and just have to be learned as set phrases.
examples: Who's that woman at the counter?
The keys are in the drawer.
The plate is on the shelf.
I heard it on the radio, and now I'm at the office.
common_mistakes: Using 'at' for something enclosed instead of 'in': 'at the classroom' instead of 'in the classroom.'
Forgetting the fixed expressions that skip the general logic: 'in the bus' or 'in work' instead of 'on the bus' or 'at work.'

topics.formula: can / can't + base verb — no 'to', no -s ever (even with he/she/it), no do/don't in questions or negatives. Can already works as its own auxiliary.
topics.key_idea: Can behaves differently from ordinary verbs — it never changes form, never needs 'to' before the next verb, and never needs do/does to build a question or negative, because it's already an auxiliary itself. The same word covers three different jobs: saying what someone is able to do, saying what's allowed or possible, and politely asking for something.
examples: Diana can paint very well.
Can I open the window?
Can I get a sandwich and a juice, please?
He can't drive.
common_mistakes: Adding 'to' after can: 'I can to swim' instead of 'I can swim.'
Adding -s for he/she/it, or using do/don't with can: 'He cans swim' or 'He don't can swim' instead of 'He can swim' / 'He can't swim.'

topics.formula: am / is / are + verb-ing. Short forms: I'm, he's / she's / it's, we're / you're / they're — negative: 'm not, isn't, aren't.
topics.key_idea: Present continuous describes something happening right now, or something temporary happening around now — this week, these days — rather than a permanent habit. That's the key difference from present simple: present continuous is for now-and-temporary, present simple is for generally-true. Short forms follow the same rule as elsewhere with 'be': fine in negative short answers, not in positive ones.
examples: I'm cooking dinner.
She's watching a documentary.
I'm reading an interesting article at the moment.
'Are you cooking dinner?' 'Yes, I am.'
common_mistakes: Dropping the -ing and just using am/is/are with the base verb: 'I am write a book' instead of 'I am writing a book.'
Using a short form in a positive short answer: 'Yes, I'm' instead of 'Yes, I am.'

topics.formula: Stative verbs (be, have = possess, like, love, hate, prefer, need, want, know, and similar) stay in present simple even when talking about right now — they don't take the -ing form.
topics.key_idea: Most verbs describe actions, but a group of verbs describe states instead — feelings, ownership, mental states — and these don't work in the continuous form at all, even when the meaning is clearly 'right now.' Instead of switching to -ing, they just stay in present simple.
examples: I love this song.
They own a small farm.
I understand the instructions.
He needs a break right now.
common_mistakes: Putting a stative verb into the continuous form: 'I'm liking this song' or 'They are having a new car' instead of 'I like this song' / 'They have a new car.'

topics.formula: Present simple = usually/generally true, or a permanent situation. Present continuous = happening right now, or a temporary situation.
topics.key_idea: The two tenses often describe the same kind of action, so the real decision is about the situation, not the verb: is this something generally true or a settled habit (present simple), or something happening right now, or only for a limited time (present continuous)? The same verb can go either way depending on which of those is meant.
examples: I read the newspaper. / I'm reading the newspaper right now.
I work at a bakery. / I'm working at a bakery this month, just temporarily.
What does Farida do? / What is Farida doing?
common_mistakes: Asking 'What do you do?' when the real question is about right now, or 'What are you doing?' when asking about someone's job — the two questions look similar but ask about completely different things.

topics.formula: base verb, no subject (Open the door. / Don't touch that.). For suggestions that include the speaker: let's + verb, or let's not + verb.
topics.key_idea: The imperative drops the subject entirely and just uses the base verb — it's the same simple form used for instructions, orders, invitations, advice, and warnings. When the speaker wants to include themselves in the suggestion rather than direct it at someone else, 'let's' (let us) takes over instead.
examples: Close the window, please.
Don't drop that box.
Try some cake.
Let's watch a movie.
common_mistakes: Adding a subject where none belongs: 'You open the door' instead of just 'Open the door,' when giving a direct instruction.
Using the plain imperative instead of 'let's' when the speaker is included too: 'Go to the pool!' instead of 'Let's go to the pool!' when the speaker wants to go along.

topics.formula: was (I / he / she / it) / were (you / we / they) — negative short forms: wasn't / weren't. No short forms exist for the positive.
topics.key_idea: Was and were are just the past-tense versions of am/is/are — am and is both become was, and are becomes were. They work the same way present 'be' does, for identity, feelings, or location, just moved into the past, usually alongside a past time word like yesterday or last week. One fixed expression worth remembering separately: 'born' is always paired with was/were, even though the person obviously still exists now.
examples: I was at the office yesterday.
You were early for the meeting.
Diana was busy, but Marcus wasn't.
Where were you born? I was born in Kenya.
common_mistakes: Trying to contract was/were in a positive sentence — there's no short form; only the negative contracts, to wasn't/weren't.
Using am/is/are with 'born' instead of was/were: 'I am born in Sweden' instead of 'I was born in Sweden,' even though it's still true today.

topics.formula: regular verbs: + -ed (watch → watched). Some regular verbs double the final consonant first (stop → stopped). Irregular verbs change completely and don't take -ed (go → went, have → had) — these just have to be learned individually.
topics.key_idea: Past simple describes finished actions or states, or things that used to happen regularly but don't anymore — always with a sense that it's over. Most verbs are regular and just add -ed, but a large group of very common verbs are irregular and change in their own unpredictable way, so they can't be formed with a rule.
examples: We cleaned the house last Sunday.
Marcus texted me last night.
When I was young, I read comics every day.
I called the office, but it was closed.
common_mistakes: Adding -ed to an irregular verb: 'I goed to the shop' instead of 'I went to the shop.'
Forgetting to double the final consonant on some regular verbs: 'stoped' instead of 'stopped.'

topics.formula: did / didn't + subject + base verb, for negatives and questions with any verb except be. Be still uses was/were directly, without did (Was he there? / They weren't happy.)
topics.key_idea: For ordinary verbs, did takes over as the auxiliary for every past-tense negative and question, and the main verb drops back to its base form — never -ed, never the irregular past form — since did already carries the 'past' meaning by itself. The one big exception is the verb be, which never uses did at all; it just keeps using was/were directly, the same as in positive sentences.
examples: I didn't study yesterday.
Did you visit the museum?
We didn't sleep at 6.
Was she at the party?
common_mistakes: Keeping the verb in its past form after did/didn't: 'Did you went to the concert?' instead of 'Did you go to the concert?' — did already shows it's past, so the main verb goes back to base form.
Using did/didn't with the verb be: 'They didn't be happy' or 'Did he be at home?' instead of 'They weren't happy' / 'Was he at home?'

topics.formula: love / like / enjoy / hate / don't mind + verb-ing. forget / hope / learn / need / offer / plan / remember / start / want + to + verb. The second verb's form never changes, no matter what tense the first verb is in.
topics.key_idea: Some verbs are always followed by the -ing form of the next verb, and others are always followed by 'to' plus the next verb — which category a verb belongs to just has to be learned per verb, since there's no rule that predicts it from the meaning alone. Whichever pattern a verb uses stays fixed even when the first verb changes tense.
examples: I love cooking dinner.
I hope to finish soon.
When I was young, I hated cleaning my room.
I wanted to leave early.
common_mistakes: Changing the second verb's form to match the tense of the first: 'I hated went to school' or 'I wanted to went home' instead of 'I hated going to school' / 'I wanted to go home' — the second verb stays in its fixed form.
Mixing up which pattern a verb takes: 'I enjoy to travel' instead of 'I enjoy travelling,' since enjoy belongs to the -ing group.

topics.formula: would like (or 'd like) + to + infinitive = wanting something specific. like + verb-ing = a general preference or enjoyment.
topics.key_idea: Would like and like look related but mean different things: 'I'd like to study English' means I want to do that, while 'I like studying English' means I generally enjoy it as an activity. 'Would you like...?' is also the standard way to offer something or invite someone to do something.
examples: I'd like to study English.
I like studying English.
Would you like a cup of coffee?
Would you like to dance with me?
common_mistakes: Mixing up the two: saying 'I like to buy a new computer' when the meaning is really 'I want one' — that should be 'I'd like to buy a new computer' instead.

topics.formula: have/has + got (I've got, she's got) — negative: haven't/hasn't got — question: Have/Has...got? Only exists in the present; the past just uses had on its own, without got.
topics.key_idea: Have got means exactly the same as have — both are correct, and have got is just more common in spoken British English while have is more common in American English. The one real trap is tense: have got only works in the present. There's no past form like 'had got'; the past simply uses had.
examples: I've got a bike.
Have you got a laptop?
She's got curly hair.
I had a cold last week.
common_mistakes: Trying to use 'got' in the past: 'I had got a car' instead of just 'I had a car.'
Adding an extra do/does to the have-got form: 'Do you have got a car?' instead of 'Have you got a car?' or plain 'Do you have a car?'

topics.formula: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms (a car / cars) and always need a determiner in the singular. Uncountable nouns only have one form (money, milk) and never take a/an.
topics.key_idea: Some things can be counted one by one (a book, two books), and others can't (money, milk, advice) — those get treated as a mass rather than separate units, so they never take a/an and never become plural. A few nouns can go either way depending on meaning: 'coffee' as a drink in general is uncountable, but 'a coffee' meaning one cup is countable.
examples: I have a bicycle.
I need information.
She gave me some feedback.
I had two teas this morning.
common_mistakes: Using a/an with an uncountable noun: 'a money' or 'a furniture' instead of just 'money' or 'furniture.'
Leaving a singular countable noun without any determiner: 'I have car' instead of 'I have a car.'

topics.formula: a/an + singular countable noun. some + plural countable or uncountable noun, in positive sentences (or offers/requests). any + plural countable or uncountable noun, in negatives and most questions.
topics.key_idea: A/an only works with one countable thing at a time. Once there's more than one, or the noun can't be counted at all, some and any take over instead — some in positive sentences, any in negatives and ordinary questions. One exception worth remembering: questions that offer or ask for something use some, not any, even though they're technically questions.
examples: I have a nephew and a niece.
He gave me some advice.
She didn't send me any updates.
Would you like some water?
common_mistakes: Using a/an with a plural or uncountable noun: 'a sugar' or 'a beautiful places' instead of just 'sugar' or 'beautiful places.'
Using any in an offer or request instead of some: 'Can I have any tea?' instead of 'Can I have some tea?'

topics.formula: there is + singular noun (there's for short) / there are + plural noun (no short form). Past: there was / there were. Negatives: there isn't / aren't, there wasn't / weren't.
topics.key_idea: There is/are says that something exists, and whether you use is or are depends only on the noun right after it — singular or plural — the same as with be anywhere else. When a list of several things follows, the verb agrees with just the first item in the list, not the whole group. In the past, is/are simply become was/were.
examples: There is a nice cafe near my office.
There are some books on the shelf.
There was a dog in the yard yesterday.
There isn't any milk left.
common_mistakes: Mismatching there is/are with the noun: 'There is two chairs' instead of 'There are two chairs.'
Trying to contract there are: there's no short form for it — only there is contracts, to there's, and never in a positive short answer.

topics.formula: there = introducing something for the first time, or saying it exists. it = referring back to something already mentioned, or a subject-less use for time, weather, and distance.
topics.key_idea: There introduces something new into the conversation ('there's a party tomorrow'), while it refers back to something already mentioned, or fills the subject spot when there isn't really a 'thing' to talk about at all — like time, weather, or distance. It's easy to reach for it out of habit even when the sentence already has a real subject — in that case, the real subject does the job, and it shouldn't be added at all.
examples: There's a concert next week. It's going to be amazing!
It's half past nine.
It's really foggy this morning.
The hardest part of the job is waking up early.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to switch to it (or they) when mentioning something again, staying with there instead of switching to it or they for the second mention.
Adding it when the sentence already has a real subject: 'The hardest part of the job it's waking up early' instead of 'The hardest part of the job is waking up early.'

topics.formula: next to / beside (at the side of) — between (in the middle of two things) — in front of / behind (facing / at the back of) — opposite (facing, across from) — under (below) — above / over (higher than; over is more common).
topics.key_idea: These prepositions describe where something is relative to something else, not just a general location. Several of them work in natural pairs that are opposite in meaning — in front of vs behind, under vs above/over — which makes them easier to learn together rather than one at a time.
examples: Sit next to me.
I live in a village between two rivers.
Diana stands in front of me in the queue. He is hiding behind the tree.
The dog is under the table. There's a lamp above the desk.
common_mistakes: Mixing up in front of and opposite — in front of means directly ahead in the same row or line, while opposite means facing from across a gap, like the other side of a road or table.
Using between with more than two things — between is for two things or two points specifically; more than two usually needs among instead.

topics.formula: many / much mainly in negatives and questions (many + countable, much + uncountable). a lot of in positive sentences, either type. a few (countable) / a little (uncountable) for a small amount. no / not...any for zero — none in short answers.
topics.key_idea: Which quantity word to use depends on two things at once: is the noun countable or uncountable, and is the sentence positive, negative, or a question. Many/much lean toward negatives and questions, a lot of leans toward positive sentences (though it works elsewhere too), and a few/a little work in any sentence type but specifically signal a small amount.
examples: There isn't much sugar left.
How many photos did you take?
He spends a lot of money on books.
I always add a little salt to the soup.
common_mistakes: Mixing up much and many: 'How much books' instead of 'How many books' — many goes with countable nouns, much with uncountable.
Dropping of after a lot when a noun follows: 'a lot time' instead of 'a lot of time' — of is only optional at the very end of a sentence or in a short answer, like 'I had a lot.'

topics.formula: adjective + -er + than (short adjectives), or more + adjective + than (longer adjectives) — never both together. Opposite: less + adjective + than.
topics.key_idea: Comparatives need exactly one comparing word — either -er on the adjective itself, or more in front of it, never both together. After than, a following pronoun takes the object form (than me, not than I), and much or a bit can go before the comparative to show how big the difference is. If the second thing being compared isn't actually mentioned, than gets dropped too, rather than left hanging at the end.
examples: I am shorter than my sister.
This chair is more comfortable than that one.
My brother is younger than me.
He's a bit shorter than me, but this city is much more expensive than mine.
common_mistakes: Combining both comparative forms: 'more taller' instead of just 'taller' or 'more comfortable.'
Leaving than at the end with nothing after it: 'My brother is taller than' instead of just 'My brother is taller,' when the second thing isn't actually named.

topics.formula: the + adjective + -est (short adjectives), or the + most + adjective (longer adjectives) — for comparing three or more things. Always needs the or a possessive (my / his / Paul's) in front, never used bare.
topics.key_idea: While the comparative compares just two things, the superlative picks out one from three or more — the biggest, the most expensive, and so on. It always needs the or a possessive right before it; it's never left bare the way some other adjectives can be. When naming the group it's picked from, use in before a place or a group word like class, family, or team.
examples: K2 is the second-highest mountain in the world.
He is the tallest student in the class.
This is my most valuable painting.
This is Diana's closest friend.
common_mistakes: Dropping the/a possessive before the superlative: 'He is best in the family' instead of 'He is the best in the family.'
Using of instead of in before a place or group: 'the highest mountain of the world' instead of 'the highest mountain in the world.'

topics.formula: will / won't + base verb — no 'to', no -s, no do/don't. Questions put will before the subject (Will you...?). Short answers: Yes, I will. / No, I won't.
topics.key_idea: Will behaves like can — it's already an auxiliary, so it never needs do/does and the verb after it always stays in its base form. Its main job is talking about the future: predictions (often paired with I think, I hope, I'm sure, perhaps), promises or refusals, and decisions made right at the moment of speaking rather than planned ahead of time.
examples: I'll be at the office next Monday.
I don't think they'll agree.
There's no bread left. I'll go and get some.
Shall I open a window?
common_mistakes: Adding do/don't or -s to will: 'Do you will come?' or 'He wills come' instead of 'Will you come?' / 'He will come.'
Using will for something already planned or decided in advance instead of a decision made right now — will fits the on-the-spot decision.

topics.formula: am / is / are + going to + base verb. If the main verb is go itself, the second go can be dropped (I'm going shopping = I'm going to go shopping).
topics.key_idea: Going to is for the future too, but it works differently from will in two ways: it's used for predictions based on something you can actually see right now (dark clouds, so 'it's going to rain'), and for plans or intentions decided before this moment, not decided on the spot. That's the opposite of will, which fits general predictions and decisions made right now.
examples: Look at that smoke. It's going to spread.
We are going to visit my parents after work.
He's going to start a new job next month.
I'm going running this evening.
common_mistakes: Using will for a plan that was already decided earlier, instead of going to: saying 'I'll go for a swim' as a fixed plan when it should be 'I'm going to go for a swim,' since it was decided before now.
Dropping the to: 'I'm going study biology' instead of 'I'm going to study biology' — to is part of the fixed structure.

topics.formula: verb (+ object) + adverb of manner (He drives carefully. She plays the guitar well.) Most are adjective + -ly (careful → carefully), but some -ly words are actually adjectives, not adverbs (friendly, lovely, silly).
topics.key_idea: Adjectives describe a noun (before it, or after be), while adverbs of manner describe a verb — how the action happens — and go after the verb or after verb + object. The same idea, 'careful,' can show up as an adjective describing a person ('a careful driver') or an adverb describing the action ('drives carefully') — the difference is what it's attached to. A handful of -ly words are actually adjectives despite looking like adverbs, so they can't be used the adverb way.
examples: He speaks quietly.
She sings really beautifully.
Marcus is a great cook. Marcus cooks well.
He's a lovely neighbour.
common_mistakes: Using an adjective where an adverb belongs: 'He drives careful' instead of 'He drives carefully,' since the verb needs describing, not a noun.
Trying to turn an -ly adjective into an adverb: there's no adverb form of friendly, lovely, or silly — they stay adjectives however they're used.

topics.formula: a/an for something mentioned for the first time, or a general job/description. the for something already mentioned, something specific and known, something unique, common places in town, superlatives, and musical instruments.
topics.key_idea: A/an introduces something new, while the signals that both speaker and listener already know exactly what's being talked about — because it was just mentioned, because there's only one of it, or because it belongs to one of a small set of familiar categories: common places around town, superlatives, and musical instruments.
examples: I met an interesting man at the conference. The man was a pilot.
Can you close the window?
The sun is very bright today.
Farida plays the piano.
common_mistakes: Using the for something mentioned for the first time: 'I saw the dog in the park' when it's the first time the dog comes up — that should be 'a dog.'
Forgetting the before a superlative or an instrument: 'This is best restaurant in town' or 'I play guitar' instead of 'the best restaurant' / 'the guitar.'

topics.formula: No article before: plural/uncountable nouns in a general sense, meal names, years / months / days, languages and school subjects, TV as a broadcast service, and next / last + time expression (meaning relative to now).
topics.key_idea: A handful of common categories skip articles entirely, even though English usually needs one somewhere: talking about things in general rather than something specific ('I love music' vs 'the music at the party'), meals, calendar words, languages, and TV as a concept rather than the physical box. Next and last also skip the article when they mean relative to right now — but the same words can need the when they mean something else, like the last day of a trip that already happened.
examples: I don't eat meat.
Lunch is at noon.
She doesn't speak German.
The exam is next Monday.
common_mistakes: Adding an article to a general plural/uncountable noun: 'I love the music' when the meaning is music in general, not one specific piece.
Adding an article before next/last + time when it means relative to now: 'the next Thursday' instead of just 'next Thursday.'

topics.formula: and = addition. but = contrast. or = alternative (and, in negatives, 'not X or Y' instead of 'not X and Y'). so = result. because = reason.
topics.key_idea: Each of these five words signals a different logical relationship between two ideas — is the second idea similar and added on, different and contrasting, an alternative choice, a result, or a reason? Whatever two things get connected with and, but, or or need to match grammatically — both -ing forms, or both to-infinitives, not a mix of the two.
examples: My aunt is a nurse, and my uncle is an architect.
I trained hard, but I lost the race.
I don't like carrots or peas.
It was hot, so we turned on the fan. We turned on the fan because it was hot.
common_mistakes: Using and instead of or in a negative sentence: 'I don't like oranges and lemons' instead of 'I don't like oranges or lemons,' when the meaning is 'not one and not the other.'
Mixing grammatical forms across the connected parts: 'I like dancing and sing' instead of 'I like dancing and singing' — both sides need to match.

topics.formula: verb + object always stay together, right next to each other — nothing goes between them. When both place and time are mentioned, place comes before time.
topics.key_idea: Two ordering rules that are easy to get backwards coming from other languages: the verb and its object can't be separated by anything else, not even a word like 'very much' or 'every day,' and when a sentence mentions both where and when something happens, where comes first, then when.
examples: I enjoy this book a lot.
He walks the dog every morning.
She arrives at the office in the afternoon.
Can you be at the airport at 6pm?
common_mistakes: Splitting the verb and object with another word: 'I like very much pizza' instead of 'I like pizza very much.'
Putting time before place: 'She arrives in the morning at the hospital' instead of 'She arrives at the hospital in the morning.'

topics.formula: (question word) + auxiliary + subject + main verb. The auxiliary can be be, do, have, or a modal (can, will, would, should, etc.), depending on the sentence.
topics.key_idea: Every English question needs an auxiliary right after the subject's usual spot, but which one depends on the sentence: be when be is the main verb, a modal when there's already a modal, and do/does/did for everything else. Have is the trickiest case — it only works as its own auxiliary in have got and the present perfect; for ordinary uses of have, do/does/did still steps in, the same as with any other regular verb.
examples: Have you got a pen?
What have you cooked for dinner?
What time did you have lunch yesterday?
Did you have many toys when you were little?
common_mistakes: Using have as the auxiliary for an ordinary meaning of have, instead of do/does/did: 'Have you to do it now?' instead of 'Do you have to do it now?'
Trying to use a past form of have got: 'Had you got many toys?' instead of 'Did you have many toys?' — have got only exists in the present.

topics.formula: which + noun, for a small or known set of options. what + noun, for an open-ended range of possible answers.
topics.key_idea: Both words go with a noun to ask a question, but which one to use depends on how limited the answer choices are. Which fits when there's a small, often specific set to choose from — sometimes even named directly in the question — while what fits when the possible answers are wide open.
examples: Which jacket do you prefer, the black or the grey?
What phone have you got?
Which month works better for you, June or July?
What month is your birthday?
common_mistakes: Using what when the question already narrows the options to a small, specific set: 'What car do you like, the red or the blue?' instead of 'Which car do you like, the red or the blue?'

topics.formula: Subject questions (question word = the subject): question word + verb directly, no do/does/did in present or past simple (Who won the match?). Object questions: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb, as usual (Who did Jack call?)
topics.key_idea: When the question word is asking who or what did the action, present and past simple skip do/does/did entirely — the question word just takes the subject's place, and the sentence keeps its normal statement order. That's different from asking about the object of the action, which needs the usual auxiliary-before-subject structure. Tenses with a built-in auxiliary, like present continuous or present perfect, keep it either way.
examples: Who scored the goal?
Who did Diana invite?
What broke the window?
Who is fixing the car right now?
common_mistakes: Adding an unnecessary do/did when the question word is the subject: 'Who did win the match?' instead of just 'Who won the match?'
Dropping the auxiliary in an object question, where it's still needed: 'Who Jack called?' instead of 'Who did Jack call?'

topics.formula: Question word ... verb (+ object) + preposition, at the very end of the question — not attached to the front of the question word.
topics.key_idea: When a question needs a preposition that belongs with the verb (play with, work for, talk about), everyday spoken English puts that preposition at the very end of the question rather than up front with the question word. It can feel like it's been left dangling, but that's the normal, natural pattern in conversation.
examples: Who did you go camping with?
What team do you play for?
What are you thinking about?
Who is this gift for?
common_mistakes: Dropping the preposition entirely instead of moving it to the end: 'What company do you work?' instead of 'What company do you work for?'

topics.formula: past simple verb, past simple verb, past simple verb... in the same order the events actually happened, often linked with words like then or after that.
topics.key_idea: When telling a story, past simple verbs are lined up one after another in the same order the events happened — the sentence order mirrors the story order, which is what lets a listener follow along without every event needing its own time expression.
examples: When I got home, I fed the cat and then I made tea.
He woke up, checked his phone, and left for work.
common_mistakes: Switching to present tense partway through a past story out of habit: 'I went home, then I take off my shoes' instead of keeping every event in past simple throughout.
Breaking the chronological order, which makes a spoken narrative harder to follow, since the listener expects the sentence order to match the event order.

topics.formula: was / were + verb-ing. Used with a specific past time expression (at 9, at midday) or alongside a past simple clause (when I saw them...).
topics.key_idea: Past continuous describes something that was already in progress, not finished, at a particular moment in the past — the past version of 'right now.' It's also commonly used to set the scene at the start of a story, painting the background situation before the main events happen.
examples: What were you doing at noon? I was cooking.
They were chatting when I walked in.
It was raining hard, and I was running to the bus stop. Suddenly...
At 3pm, they were still travelling.
common_mistakes: Using past simple when the action was clearly still ongoing at that moment: 'I studied at 9' instead of 'I was studying at 9,' when the point is that it was happening at that exact time, not finished by then.

topics.formula: past simple = a completed, finished action. past continuous = an action already in progress, not finished, at that moment. Often paired: past continuous (longer background action) + past simple (shorter action that interrupts it).
topics.key_idea: The real decision is whether an action was already happening at a certain point, or whether it was a complete, separate event. When both tenses appear in the same sentence, the past continuous usually sets the longer background scene, and the past simple marks the shorter action that interrupts it. The same sentence can mean two different things depending which tense is used: 'she was having a shower' when he arrived means the shower started before he got there; 'she had a shower' when he arrived means it started after.
examples: He was jogging when he twisted his ankle.
We stayed home because it was snowing.
When she called, I was cleaning the kitchen.
When she called, I cleaned the kitchen.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the two in a sentence like 'when she called, I was cleaning/cleaned the kitchen' — the choice changes whether the action started before or after the call, not just the style of the sentence.

topics.formula: to + infinitive, or for + noun, to say why an action is done. For describing what an object is used for, either to + infinitive or for + -ing works.
topics.key_idea: To and for can both express purpose, but they don't take the same kind of word after them — to takes another verb, for takes a noun. The one trap: for + -ing is never used to explain why a person did something, even though for + -ing does work when describing what a thing is generally used for, like a tool or a machine.
examples: I went to the market to buy some fruit.
Let's stop by the cafe for a snack.
I practise daily to improve my Spanish.
This tool is used for measuring distance.
common_mistakes: Using for + -ing to explain why someone did an action: 'I go to the gym for staying fit' instead of 'I go to the gym to stay fit.'
Mixing up to + infinitive with for + noun: 'I went to the shop for buy milk' instead of 'I went to the shop for milk' or 'I went to the shop to buy milk.'

topics.formula: However + comma, at the start of a new sentence (after a full stop or semicolon). Although + subject + verb, with no comma right after although itself — usable at the start or in the middle of a sentence.
topics.key_idea: Both words mean roughly 'but,' but they're built differently. However stands alone as its own sentence opener, always followed by a comma, while although attaches directly to a subject and verb as part of the same sentence, with no comma right after it — only before the whole although-clause, if it comes first.
examples: The traffic was terrible. However, we arrived on time.
Although she was nervous, she gave a great presentation.
I finished the marathon, although I hadn't trained enough.
I want to adopt a dog; however, my flatmate is allergic.
common_mistakes: Adding a comma right after although: 'Although, he had a bad leg' instead of 'Although he had a bad leg' — although goes straight into the subject and verb.
Using however like a mid-sentence conjunction: it needs its own sentence or a semicolon before it, not just a comma.

topics.formula: because + subject + verb (a full clause). because of + noun (just a noun phrase, no verb).
topics.key_idea: Both express a reason, but they take different kinds of grammar after them — because needs a full clause with its own subject and verb, while because of only takes a noun. Mixing them up is one of the most common structural slips at this level.
examples: We postponed the trip because it was snowing.
We postponed the trip because of the snow.
I didn't text you because I didn't want to disturb you.
The shop closed early because of the storm.
common_mistakes: Using because with just a noun, or because of with a full clause: 'because of it was raining' instead of 'because it was raining,' or 'because the rain' instead of 'because of the rain.'

topics.formula: before / after + noun, -ing verb, or subject + verb clause. while + subject + verb, for actions happening at the same time. as soon as / when / once + subject + verb, for 'immediately when.' Comma after the time clause only when it comes first in the sentence.
topics.key_idea: These words link two events in time, and most of them are flexible about what follows — a noun, an -ing form, or a full clause. Two traps worth knowing: 'after' by itself doesn't mean 'next' in a simple sequence — that needs then or after that instead — and every one of these words takes present simple to talk about the future, never will, even though the sentence as a whole is clearly about something yet to happen.
examples: Before I leave the house, I check the weather.
I read a book after dinner.
I listened to music while I was cooking.
As soon as I get paid, I'll transfer the rent.
common_mistakes: Using will after before/after/while/as soon as/when/once when talking about the future: 'When I will get home, I'll call you' instead of 'When I get home, I'll call you.'
Using after alone to mean 'next' in a sequence: 'I got up and had a shower. After, I made breakfast' instead of 'Then/After that, I made breakfast.'

topics.formula: For predictions specifically, will and be going to often overlap and can both sound natural — the evidence-vs-belief rule softens here, unlike with decisions, where the distinction stays sharp.
topics.key_idea: The general rule (going to for predictions based on visible evidence, will for predictions based on general belief) still holds, but in everyday speech about the near future, the two often blur together and either one can sound fine — 'we're going to be late' and 'we'll be late' can mean almost the same thing in the same situation. That flexibility doesn't carry over to decisions, where going to vs will still marks a real difference: decided before, versus decided right now.
examples: The bus leaves in five minutes. We are going to miss it.
Let's hurry. We'll miss the bus.
common_mistakes: Treating the evidence-vs-belief rule for predictions as strictly as the decided-before-vs-decided-now rule for decisions — in practice, the two forms often overlap for predictions specifically, more than the rule alone suggests.

topics.formula: am / is / are + verb-ing, with a future time expression, for something already arranged with a specific time and place — especially common with travel plans and meeting people.
topics.key_idea: Present continuous isn't just for right now — it's also the natural choice for a future plan that's already fixed with someone else, usually with a set time and place, like a booked flight or a meeting you've agreed to. It's not used for predictions at all; that job belongs to will or going to instead.
examples: I'm meeting Diana at 6.
I'm flying to Rome next week.
We're moving house in September.
I'm having lunch with Marcus on Friday.
common_mistakes: Using present continuous for a prediction instead of an arrangement: 'I'm winning the match tomorrow' instead of 'I'm going to win' or 'I'll win,' since a prediction isn't a fixed, already-arranged plan.

topics.formula: present continuous = an arrangement — a specific time and place already fixed, often with someone else. be going to = an intention — a decision made, but not necessarily arranged with anyone.
topics.key_idea: Both can talk about the future, and they often overlap, but the difference is in how settled the plan is: present continuous signals it's already arranged with someone else, at a specific time and place, while going to just signals it's decided, even if nothing's actually been booked or agreed with anyone yet.
examples: I'm leaving at 7 tomorrow.
I'm going to tidy my room this weekend.
'Your bike is broken.' 'I know, I'm going to fix it tomorrow.'
common_mistakes: Using present continuous to imply a fixed arrangement for something that's really just a personal intention with nothing actually arranged: 'I'm washing my car tomorrow' when it hasn't been set with anyone, just decided privately.

topics.formula: who (people) / which (things, animals) / where (places) + clause, to specify exactly which person, thing, or place is meant. that can often replace who or which.
topics.key_idea: These words attach a description directly onto a noun to say exactly which one is meant — who for people, which for things and animals, where for places. That can often stand in for who or which, but the relative pronoun can never be replaced with what, and the clause never keeps an extra pronoun like he or she alongside it.
examples: She thanked the firefighter who rescued her cat.
He wore the jacket which his grandfather gave him.
This is the cafe where we first met.
He's the classmate who/that helped me study.
common_mistakes: Using what instead of that/who/which: 'That's the student what I told you about' instead of 'That's the student that/who I told you about.'
Adding an extra pronoun inside the clause: 'That's the man he tried to steal my wallet' instead of 'That's the man that/who tried to steal my wallet.'

topics.formula: have / has + past participle (regular verbs: same as the -ed past simple form; irregular verbs: the third form, different from the past simple).
topics.key_idea: Present perfect connects the past to now — usually because something recent has an effect on the present, like news you'd share right away. Just, already, and yet are the classic signal words: just for something that happened minutes ago, already for something that happened sooner than expected, and yet (always at the end) for asking or saying something hasn't happened.
examples: I've finished the report!
She's twisted her ankle.
I've just spoken to the manager.
Have you sent the email yet?
common_mistakes: Mentioning a specific past time with present perfect: recent news and events don't come with a 'when' — that calls for past simple instead.
Putting yet somewhere other than the end of the sentence: 'Have you yet washed the dishes?' instead of 'Have you washed the dishes yet?'

topics.formula: have / has + past participle, with ever (in questions), never, or before, to talk about life experiences without saying exactly when.
topics.key_idea: This use of present perfect is about what someone has or hasn't done at any point in their life so far, not a specific moment. Ever asks the general question, never states the negative version, and before adds the sense of 'at some earlier point,' all without pinning the experience to a particular date.
examples: I've climbed Kilimanjaro once.
Have you ever tried sushi?
She has never missed a class.
I think I have met him before.
common_mistakes: Naming a specific time alongside an experience described with present perfect — once a specific 'when' is given, the sentence usually needs to switch to past simple, since it's no longer a general life experience.

topics.formula: have / has + past participle + for + a length of time (for two weeks, for 10 years), or + since + a starting point (since 2010, since I was born), for something that started in the past and is still true now. How long...? asks about the duration.
topics.key_idea: This use describes a situation that began in the past and hasn't stopped — present perfect is what makes that 'still going' meaning possible, which present simple alone can't express. For gives the length of time something has lasted; since gives the starting point it began at.
examples: I've worked here since I graduated.
They have been neighbours for fifteen years.
How long has he played the piano?
We've been waiting for twenty minutes.
common_mistakes: Using present simple for a situation that's still ongoing: 'We are friends since first grade' instead of 'We've been friends since first grade.'
Combining since with ago: 'since 10 years ago' instead of just 'for 10 years' — since needs a fixed point in time, not a length combined with ago.

topics.formula: present perfect = when isn't mentioned or important. past simple = when is stated or asked about. In duration: present perfect + for/since = still true now; past simple + for = finished, no longer true.
topics.key_idea: The real test is whether a specific time gets mentioned. Present perfect fits when only the fact or experience matters, not the moment it happened; as soon as a 'when' comes into the conversation — through a question or an answer — the sentence needs past simple instead. It's very common to start talking about something with present perfect and then drift into past simple once the details come out. The same logic extends to duration: 'He's lived in New York for ten years' means he still lives there, while 'He lived in New York for ten years' means that's over now.
examples: I've tried scuba diving before. / I tried scuba diving last August.
'I've spoken to the landlord.' 'What did he say?' 'He said the repair would take a few days.'
She's worked at that hospital for eight years. / She worked at that hospital for eight years.
How long has he studied French? / How long did he study French?
common_mistakes: Staying in present perfect once a specific time is mentioned or asked about: 'I've broken my arm yesterday' instead of 'I broke my arm yesterday,' since 'yesterday' names a specific time.
Mixing up which tense signals an ongoing situation versus a finished one in a for/since sentence.

topics.formula: some- (affirmative sentences, and offers/requests) / any- (negatives and questions) / no- (with an affirmative verb, not a negated one) / every- (meaning 'all') + -thing / -body / -one / -where. Always a singular verb.
topics.key_idea: These compound words follow the same some/any/no logic as basic quantifiers, just packaged into single words for things, people, and places. No- already carries the negative meaning by itself, so it pairs with a normal, positive verb rather than a negated one — using both together creates a double negative. All of them take a singular verb even though they often refer to more than one thing conceptually, and they can be followed directly by an adjective or a to-infinitive.
examples: There's someone at the door.
There isn't anything in the fridge.
The lights were off, and I could see nobody.
Can we go somewhere calmer? I need something to drink.
common_mistakes: Pairing no- with a negated verb: 'I couldn't see nobody' instead of 'I could see nobody' — nobody already makes the sentence negative.
Using a plural verb with one of these words: 'Everybody are tired' instead of 'Everybody is tired.'

topics.formula: (not) as + adjective + as, to compare two things — often used in the negative to say one thing doesn't reach the same level as another.
topics.key_idea: This is a third way to compare two things, alongside -er/more and less. It's especially common in the negative, where it says the same thing as less...than, just from the opposite direction — 'Peter isn't as considerate as Marta' means exactly the same as 'Marta is more considerate than Peter.'
examples: This cafe isn't as busy as the one downtown.
My laptop isn't as fast as yours.
He's as confident as his sister now.
common_mistakes: Dropping one of the two as's: 'Peter isn't considerate as Marta' instead of 'Peter isn't as considerate as Marta' — one goes before the adjective, one before the second thing being compared.

topics.formula: the + superlative adjective + noun + (that) + present perfect + ever, to say something is the best/worst/etc. example of its kind you've experienced so far.
topics.key_idea: This is a very common way to react strongly to something — combining a superlative with present perfect and ever links the extreme judgment to your whole experience up to now, not just this one moment. It's a fixed, natural-sounding pattern worth learning as a chunk.
examples: This is the funniest show I've ever watched.
He is the kindest teacher I have ever had.
That's the longest queue I've ever seen.
common_mistakes: Using past simple instead of present perfect in this pattern: 'the best movie I ever watched' instead of the natural 'the best movie I've ever watched' — present perfect is what ties it to 'up until now.'

topics.formula: -ly adverbs: more + adverb (comparative) / most + adverb (superlative) — never -er/-est on an -ly adverb. Short adverbs without -ly (fast, hard, early, late): -er / -est, the same pattern as short adjectives.
topics.key_idea: Adverbs compare actions the same way adjectives compare things, but most -ly adverbs can't take -er or -est directly — they need more and most in front instead, unlike the adjective they came from. A handful of short, common adverbs that don't end in -ly break that rule and behave like ordinary short adjectives.
examples: She types more accurately than her colleague.
He drives well but more carefully than his brother.
She runs faster than me.
He always finishes earlier than his teammates.
common_mistakes: Adding -er/-est directly to an -ly adverb: 'quietlier' or 'slowlier' instead of 'more quietly' or 'more slowly.'

topics.formula: too + adjective/adverb. too much + uncountable noun (or after a verb). too many + plural noun. enough + noun, or adjective/adverb + enough (enough comes after, unlike too which comes before). Often followed by to + infinitive.
topics.key_idea: Too always signals a problem — more than needed or wanted — while enough signals the right amount, or, in the negative, not quite reaching it. Position is the easy way to remember which is which: too goes before an adjective, while enough goes after one. Too by itself pairs with adjectives and adverbs directly; for nouns, it needs much (uncountable) or many (countable) in between.
examples: You're too young to drive.
There's too much noise. There were too many cars.
This room is big enough for all of us.
I didn't practise enough, and I lost the match.
common_mistakes: Using too much directly before an adjective: 'I'm too much tired' instead of 'I'm too tired' — too much only goes with a noun or after a verb, not before an adjective.
Confusing too with very: 'I think she is too beautiful' (implies a problem) instead of 'very beautiful' (just intense) — too always means more than wanted or needed.

topics.formula: much/many don't normally appear in affirmative sentences on their own, but too much/too many are the exception — they work fine in affirmative sentences.
topics.key_idea: The rule that much/many belong mainly in negatives and questions has one clear exception: as soon as too is added, they're completely natural in a positive sentence, since too much/too many are really about excess, not just plain quantity.
examples: There's too much pepper in the stew.
You send too many messages.
common_mistakes: Assuming much/many are always wrong in a positive sentence and avoiding them even after too — too much and too many are fully natural in affirmative sentences, unlike much/many alone.

topics.formula: a few / a little = some, a small but sufficient amount (positive). few / little (without a) = almost none, not enough (negative).
topics.key_idea: Adding or dropping the word 'a' completely flips the meaning here, even though the words otherwise look identical. A few/a little says there's a small amount, but it's enough; few/little on its own says there's barely any, and it's a problem.
examples: There's little bread left; we should buy more.
There are a few apples in the bowl.
I understand very little Japanese.
I understand a little Japanese.
common_mistakes: Using few/little and a few/a little as if they mean the same thing — dropping 'a' turns a small-but-fine amount into an almost-nothing, insufficient amount.

topics.formula: most + noun (general majority, no article). most of + the / this / that / my / us / them (majority of a specific group). the most + adjective/adverb (superlative — a completely different meaning).
topics.key_idea: Most has two separate jobs that look similar but aren't. Talking about a majority: bare most goes with a general noun, and most of adds in when there's a specific, defined group (marked by the, a possessive, or a pronoun). The most, on the other hand, isn't about majority at all — it's the superlative, describing the highest degree of an adjective or adverb.
examples: Most people prefer working from home.
Most of the guests at the wedding danced.
Most of them agreed with the plan.
This is the most reliable car you can buy.
common_mistakes: Adding the before most when talking about a majority: 'The most students like online learning' instead of just 'Most students like online learning.'
Using bare most before a specific, defined group instead of most of: 'Most students in my class' reads better as 'Most of the students in my class.'

topics.formula: verb-ing as the subject of a sentence (Reading is good for you), or right after a preposition (tired of waiting). Negative: not + verb-ing.
topics.key_idea: Beyond following certain verbs, the -ing form shows up in two other common spots: at the very start of a sentence when a verb itself is the subject being talked about, and directly after a preposition, since a preposition can never be followed by a plain infinitive. The negative just adds not in front of the -ing form.
examples: Exercising every day is good for your health.
I'm afraid of flying.
He enjoys not having to commute at weekends.
common_mistakes: Using a plain infinitive after a preposition instead of the -ing form: 'tired of to wait' instead of 'tired of waiting' — prepositions are always followed by the -ing form, never to + infinitive.

topics.formula: do / does / did (in negatives and questions), or any modal verb (will, can, must, should, might, may, etc.) + infinitive without to.
topics.key_idea: Two very common situations always use the plain infinitive, with no to at all: right after do/does/did in a negative or question, and right after any modal verb. Both do and modals already function as auxiliaries, so the main verb after them stays in its simplest, bare form.
examples: He didn't finish the report.
Does Marcus live near you?
You must be careful.
I won't forget.
common_mistakes: Adding to after a modal verb or after do/does/did: 'I can to play the guitar' or 'Does Marcus to live near you?' instead of 'I can play the guitar' / 'Does Marcus live near you?'

topics.formula: adjective + to + infinitive (It's important to arrive early). question word + to + infinitive (I don't know what to eat). Negative: not to + infinitive.
topics.key_idea: To + infinitive shows up right after an adjective describing how something is, and right after a question word when the sentence isn't asking a full question but describing a choice or lack of knowledge, like 'what to eat' or 'how to play.' The negative simply adds not before to.
examples: It's essential to double-check your work.
I don't know where to park.
I want to learn how to swim.
She decided not to attend the meeting.
common_mistakes: Dropping to after a question word: 'I don't know what eat' instead of 'I don't know what to eat.'

topics.formula: go + -ing (sports and activities: go shopping, go swimming). go to work / bed / school / university / prison (no article, for their normal purpose). go to a / the + place. go for a + short activity (a walk, a swim, a drink). go on a + trip-type noun (a holiday, a cruise, an excursion).
topics.key_idea: Go combines with different structures depending on what kind of activity or place follows. Most sports and many other activities pair with go + -ing. A handful of very common destinations (work, bed, school, university, prison) drop the article entirely when used for their normal purpose — a student 'goes to school,' but a parent visiting for a meeting 'goes to the school.' Short activities take go for a, while trips and holidays take go on a.
examples: I want to go fishing this weekend.
What time do you go to bed?
They couldn't go to university because of the strike.
She went on an excursion with her class.
common_mistakes: Adding the to work, bed, school, university, or prison when meaning their normal purpose: 'go to the bed' instead of 'go to bed.'
Mixing up for a and on a: 'go on a walk' or 'go for a cruise' instead of 'go for a walk' and 'go on a cruise' — short activities use for a, trips use on a.

topics.formula: must + infinitive without to, no -s, no do/does needed (mustn't for negative, must + subject for questions). have to + infinitive, needs do/does/did for negatives and questions, no contraction to 've, and only have to has past (had to) and future (will have to) forms.
topics.key_idea: Must behaves like a true modal — no -s, no to, and it makes its own negative and question forms without any help from do. Have to looks similar in meaning but grammatically behaves like an ordinary verb, needing do/does/did to form negatives and questions, and it can never contract to 've the way other modals contract. Must also has a real gap: no past or future tense of its own, so had to and will have to fill in for those.
examples: I must finish this report.
Must we wear uniforms?
Do you have to wake up early tomorrow?
Last week, I had to work overtime.
common_mistakes: Using do/does/did with must, or adding to after it: 'Do we must arrive early?' or 'I must to go' instead of 'Must we arrive early?' / 'I must go.'
Trying to use must for the past or future: 'Last night, I must finish my essay' instead of 'Last night, I had to finish my essay.'

topics.formula: must = an obligation based on the speaker's own opinion. have to = an obligation that comes from somewhere else — a rule, another person's decision.
topics.key_idea: Both express obligation, but the source of that obligation is different: must signals that the speaker themselves thinks something is necessary, while have to signals that the obligation comes from outside — a boss, a doctor, a rule — not from the speaker's own judgment.
examples: I must exercise more.
I have to exercise more. My doctor said so.
You must be quiet in here.
We have to be quiet in here. It's the library rule.
common_mistakes: Using must to report someone else's rule rather than a personal opinion: reporting a manager's meeting time as 'I must get up early' instead of 'I have to get up early,' when the obligation actually comes from the manager, not the speaker.

topics.formula: mustn't = prohibited, not allowed to. don't have to = not necessary, no obligation either way.
topics.key_idea: These look like a matching negative pair, but they mean nearly opposite things. Mustn't says an action is forbidden — you're not allowed to do it. Don't have to says an action simply isn't required — you're free to do it or not, with no rule stopping you either way.
examples: You mustn't park here.
You don't have to bring anything. I've got it covered.
You mustn't touch the paintings.
You don't have to stay late.
common_mistakes: Using mustn't when the real meaning is 'no obligation': saying 'You mustn't come to the party' when the real meaning is 'You don't have to come to the party' — the first forbids it, the second just makes it optional.

topics.formula: should / shouldn't + infinitive without to, to give advice. I think you should... for positive advice — but I don't think you should... (not 'I think you shouldn't') for negative advice. ought to / ought not to work as more formal alternatives.
topics.key_idea: Should and shouldn't are the everyday way to give advice — what is or isn't a good idea. When advice gets wrapped in 'I think,' negative advice moves the negative onto think itself rather than onto should: 'I don't think you should call her,' not 'I think you shouldn't call her,' even though both technically make sense. Ought to and ought not to mean exactly the same as should/shouldn't, just slightly more formal.
examples: You seem exhausted. You should take a short nap.
I think you should ask for a second opinion.
I don't think you should message him tonight; he's still upset.
He ought not to skip meals so often.
common_mistakes: Putting the negative on should instead of think when giving negative advice with an opinion: 'I think you shouldn't message him' instead of the more natural 'I don't think you should message him.'

topics.formula: if + present tense (the if-clause) + will / a modal (may, might, can, must, should) / an imperative (the main clause) — for a realistic future possibility. Comma after the if-clause only when it comes first.
topics.key_idea: First conditional talks about a realistic possibility and its likely result. The if-clause always stays in present tense, even though its meaning is about the future — will (or another modal, or even an imperative) belongs in the other clause, not both. Either clause can come first, but a comma is only needed when the if-clause leads.
examples: If it snows, the flight will be delayed.
If you don't set an alarm, you'll oversleep.
If your desk is clear, you can leave early.
If you get lost, text me your location.
common_mistakes: Using will in the if-clause itself: 'If you will finish your homework, I'll let you watch TV' instead of 'If you finish your homework, I'll let you watch TV' — the if-clause stays present tense no matter how future the meaning is.

topics.formula: This is the same pattern as first conditional, just with when / before / after / until / as soon as instead of if: present tense in that clause, will / a modal / an imperative in the main clause.
topics.key_idea: Until belongs in the same family as before, after, while, as soon as, and when — all of them take present tense for a future meaning, matched with will, a modal, or an imperative in the other clause, exactly like first conditional's if-clause.
examples: I won't leave until you arrive.
As soon as you're ready, we can go.
Before you sign it, read it carefully.
common_mistakes: Assuming will is the only option for the main clause — a modal or an imperative works just as naturally, the same as in first conditional.

topics.formula: mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs — stand alone, with no noun after them, unlike possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), which always need a noun.
topics.key_idea: Possessive pronouns replace a possessive adjective plus the noun entirely, so nothing follows them — 'the dog is mine' says the same thing as 'the dog is my dog,' just without repeating the noun a second time. His is the one word that stays exactly the same in both roles; every other one changes form.
examples: The umbrella is mine.
The grey scarf is hers.
The garden is ours.
My phone is old, but her phone is new. / Mine is old, but hers is new.
common_mistakes: Adding a noun after a possessive pronoun, or using a possessive adjective where a pronoun is needed: 'The dog is my' instead of 'The dog is mine,' or 'This is mine dog' instead of 'This is my dog.'

topics.formula: if + past simple + would (or could) + infinitive, for an imaginary or hypothetical present or future situation — even though the verb is past tense, the meaning isn't about the past at all.
topics.key_idea: Second conditional imagines something that isn't real or isn't likely, and describes what would follow if it were. The past tense in the if-clause is just a grammatical signal for 'imaginary,' not an actual past meaning. Was is common in speech, but were is the more formal choice for I/he/she/it — and were specifically is the only option in the fixed advice expression 'if I were you.'
examples: If I had a bigger kitchen, I'd cook every night.
Would you move abroad if you got a great job offer?
If you learned to code, you could switch careers.
If I were you, I would ask for more time.
common_mistakes: Using would in the if-clause itself: the if-clause always stays in past simple, with would/could reserved for the other clause only.
Using was instead of were in the fixed expression 'if I were you': 'If I was you...' instead of 'If I were you...'

topics.formula: First conditional (if + present, will) = a realistic, possible future. Second conditional (if + past, would) = a hypothetical or unlikely/imaginary situation.
topics.key_idea: Both talk about a condition and its result, but the difference is how real the speaker treats the situation as being. First conditional treats it as genuinely possible; second conditional treats it as imaginary, unlikely, or simply not true right now — even the exact same event can shift from one to the other depending on how the speaker actually feels about its likelihood.
examples: If I'm not busy this weekend, I'll help you move.
If I weren't busy this weekend, I'd help you move.
common_mistakes: Using first conditional grammar to describe something the speaker already knows is untrue or unlikely, instead of switching to second conditional to signal that shift in meaning.

topics.formula: am / is / are + past participle (present) or was / were + past participle (past). The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one; the original doer is optional, added with by if it's mentioned at all.
topics.key_idea: Passive flips the focus from who did something to what happened to something or someone — the receiver of the action becomes the subject, and the doer becomes optional. It's especially useful when the doer is unknown, obvious, or just not the point of the sentence, which is exactly why passive shows up so often in formal or written English, like news reports.
examples: The office is cleaned twice a week.
The letters aren't opened until Monday.
The event was postponed.
The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
common_mistakes: Forgetting be, or using the wrong form of it: 'The window broken by someone' instead of 'The window was broken by someone' — passive always needs be plus the past participle, not the past participle alone.
Adding by as a routine habit rather than only when the doer genuinely adds useful information.

topics.formula: used to + base verb, for past habits or past states that are no longer true. Negatives/questions: did / didn't + use to (no 'd'). Never also works for the negative.
topics.key_idea: Used to signals that something regularly happened, or was true, in the past, but isn't anymore — it's specifically about that contrast with now, not just any past action. It works for repeated actions and states (was, had, liked) alike. In negatives and questions, the d disappears from use, since did already carries the past tense.
examples: I used to collect stamps every summer, but I rarely do now.
She used to be quite shy in school.
He didn't use to enjoy cooking.
We never used to disagree about anything.
common_mistakes: Keeping the d in negatives or questions: 'He didn't used to enjoy cooking' instead of 'He didn't use to enjoy cooking' — did already makes it past, so use stays in its base form.

topics.formula: used to = repeated past habit/state, with no specific time mentioned. past simple = a one-time action, or any action once a specific time is given. usually / normally + present simple = a current habit — used to is never used for the present.
topics.key_idea: Used to and past simple can describe the same repeated habit, but as soon as a specific time gets mentioned, or the action only happened once, used to isn't an option anymore — past simple takes over.
