And since used to is strictly for the past, a present-day habit needs usually or normally with present simple instead, never used to.
examples: I often visited my grandparents on weekends.
Last month, I visited my grandparents twice.
I normally wake up early on weekdays.
common_mistakes: Using used to with a specific past time mentioned: 'Last month, I used to visit my grandparents twice' instead of 'Last month, I visited my grandparents twice.'
Using used to for a present habit: 'I use to wake up early' instead of 'I usually wake up early.'

topics.formula: might (not) / may (not) + base verb, to say something is possibly true or will possibly happen — used when the speaker isn't sure. may I...? asks for permission.
topics.key_idea: Might and may work interchangeably here to express genuine uncertainty — not a strong prediction, just a real possibility either way. Might not/may not work the same way for the negative possibility. The one place they're not interchangeable is in questions asking for permission, where may I...? is the natural, common choice, but might isn't typically used that way.
examples: He might be at the gym.
It might not snow tonight.
They may not agree with the plan.
May I sit here?
common_mistakes: Using might I...? to ask permission instead of may I...? — may is the natural choice for permission questions.

topics.formula: get in / out of (car, taxi, van) — get on / off (bike, motorbike, bus, train, plane). To say how you travel: by + transport, or on foot — or a movement verb (walk, drive, fly, cycle), or take + transport for public transport.
topics.key_idea: Small private vehicles you sit inside of use in/out of, while anything you sit on top of or board — bikes, motorbikes, and public transport — uses on/off. Describing how you got somewhere works two ways: either by + the vehicle (or on foot), or a specific movement verb, with take standing in as that verb for public transport specifically, since there's no single verb for 'busing' or 'training' somewhere.
examples: I have to get off the train at the next station.
She stepped out of the taxi.
I go to school by bike. I go to work on foot.
I took the metro to the stadium.
common_mistakes: Using in/out of for a bus, train, or bike instead of on/off: 'get out of the bus' instead of 'get off the bus.'
Combining by with take: 'I took by bus' instead of just 'I took a bus' or 'I went by bus.'

topics.formula: so + auxiliary + subject, to agree with a positive statement (So am I). neither/nor + auxiliary + subject, to agree with a negative statement (Neither do I). Match the same auxiliary as the first sentence — do/does/did if there wasn't one. Alternative: ...too (positive) / ...either (negative) at the end of a full sentence instead.
topics.key_idea: These are quick ways to say 'me too' or 'me neither' without repeating the whole sentence. The auxiliary after so or neither has to match whatever's in the original sentence — the same modal, be, or have — and if the original sentence had no auxiliary at all, do/does/did steps in. Neither is already a negative word by itself, so the verb after it stays in its normal, positive form rather than being negated again. Too and either do the exact same job, just placed at the end of a full sentence instead of inverted at the start.
examples: 'I'm from Toronto.' 'So am I.'
'I'm not hungry.' 'Neither am I.'
'Diana loves spicy food.' 'So does Marcus.'
'I didn't finish.' 'I didn't finish either.'
common_mistakes: Adding a negative to the verb after neither: 'Neither didn't I' instead of 'Neither did I' — neither already makes the sentence negative.
Using too after a negative statement, or either after a positive one — too matches positive statements, either matches negative ones.

topics.formula: had / hadn't + past participle — the same form for every person. Can contract to 'd (I'd left, she'd gone).
topics.key_idea: Past perfect exists to talk about something that happened even earlier than another point already being discussed in the past — it's the 'past before the past.' The contraction 'd is shared with would, so the word right after it tells you which one it is: a past participle means had, an infinitive means would.
examples: I hadn't tried Korean food before last month.
When she checked her bike, she noticed someone had let the air out of the tires.
My colleague mentioned that he had already sent the invoice.
I realized she'd left her umbrella at my place.
common_mistakes: Confusing the contraction 'd for would when it actually means had, or vice versa — check what follows it: a base verb signals would, a past participle signals had.

topics.formula: past simple, past simple, past simple... = events told in the order they happened. past perfect = signals an event happened before the other past event being described, out of the story's normal chronological order.
topics.key_idea: When two past events are mentioned together, past simple for both implies they happened in the order they're mentioned, while switching one to past perfect signals it actually happened earlier, regardless of the order the sentence mentions them in. The clearest comparison: 'when I arrived, she left' means she left after I got there, but 'when I arrived, she had left' means she was already gone before I arrived.
examples: When the meeting started, everyone sat down.
When the meeting started, everyone had already sat down.
He fixed the printer and used it again the next morning.
He used a printer that he had fixed himself.
common_mistakes: Using past simple for both events when one clearly happened before the other, leaving the sequence ambiguous or implying the wrong order.

topics.formula: Reporting verb (said/thought, etc.) + (that) + backshifted tense and pronouns. Present becomes past, present continuous becomes past continuous, will becomes would, and so on. I / my / we / our shift to he / his / she / her / they / their as needed; you / your shifts to match whoever the listener actually is now.
topics.key_idea: Reported speech moves what someone said into a new time and a new speaker, so both the verb tense and the pronouns have to shift to match that new perspective — not because the grammar demands change for its own sake, but because 'I' and 'now' meant something different when the original words were spoken. That is optional and often left out entirely.
examples: Farida: 'I don't have a car.' → Farida said that she didn't have a car.
Marcus: 'I am busy.' → He said that he was busy.
'I will support you.' → He said that he would support me.
She said she was running late.
common_mistakes: Leaving the tense and pronouns unchanged from the original quote: reporting 'I am tired' as 'He said that I am tired' instead of 'He said that he was tired,' which describes the wrong person and the wrong time.

topics.formula: tell + somebody + (that) + clause (tell requires a person as its direct object). say + (that) + clause, or say something to somebody (say never takes a person directly after it without to).
topics.key_idea: Say and tell aren't interchangeable, because they take different grammar after them — tell always needs a person named right after it, while say never does unless to comes first. Getting this backwards is one of the most common mistakes at this level.
examples: They told me (that) they would come.
They said (that) they would come.
He said (that) he didn't have a bike.
He told me (that) he didn't have a bike.
common_mistakes: Using say with a person directly after it, or tell without one: 'They said me' instead of 'They told me,' or 'He told that he didn't have a car' instead of 'He said that he didn't have a car.'

topics.formula: verb + indirect object + direct object (no preposition), or verb + direct object + to/for + indirect object. Some verbs use to (give, send, show, tell...), others use for (buy, cook, make, find...).
topics.key_idea: Verbs like give, send, or buy can take both a direct object (the thing) and an indirect object (the person), and English allows two word orders for this: the person right after the verb with no preposition, or the thing first, followed by to or for plus the person. Which preposition to use isn't random — it splits along two groups of verbs, one that uses to and another that uses for, and this doesn't change no matter which word order is chosen.
examples: I sent my colleagues an update.
I sent an update to my colleagues.
Can you get some water for grandma?
I sent them an update.
common_mistakes: Using to or for when the indirect object is placed right next to the verb: 'I sent to my colleagues an update' instead of 'I sent my colleagues an update' or 'I sent an update to my colleagues.'
Mixing up which preposition a verb takes: 'give a present for him' instead of 'give a present to him.'

topics.formula: get + noun (receive, obtain, buy, or take: get an email, get the train). get + adjective (become: get angry, get married, get dark). get to + place (arrive: get to work). Exception: get here / get there / get home — no to.
topics.key_idea: Get is one of the most flexible verbs in English, and its meaning depends entirely on what follows it — a noun gives it a receiving/obtaining sense, an adjective gives it a 'become' sense, and to plus a place gives it an 'arrive' sense. Three very common destinations — here, there, and home — drop the to entirely, unlike every other place.
examples: My daughter got her diploma last month.
It's getting late.
What time did you get to the airport?
Do you usually get home early?
common_mistakes: Adding to before here, there, or home: 'get to home late' instead of 'get home late' — these three destinations never take to.
Missing the 'become' meaning and assuming get always means 'receive': 'get angry' means to become angry, not to receive anger.

topics.formula: do = tasks, duties, and routine activities — the action or process itself (do homework, do the dishes, do exercise). make = creating or producing something — the result (make dinner, make a decision, make a mistake).
topics.key_idea: The general rule is process versus result: do focuses on carrying out an activity, especially routine chores, study, and work, while make focuses on producing something that didn't exist before — food, plans, decisions, noise, money. Most housework verbs pair with do, but make your bed is a well-known exception worth memorizing on its own.
examples: I'll do the laundry after work.
I do the vacuuming every evening, but I make my bed every morning.
I made an error in the report.
He makes good money as a freelance designer.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two: 'make the laundry' instead of 'do the laundry,' or 'do an error' instead of 'make an error' — these are fixed collocations, not freely interchangeable based on logic alone.
Applying the general do-for-housework rule to make your bed, which is the well-known exception.

topics.formula: Some verbs are stative with one meaning and dynamic with another — have (possess = stative; experience/do = dynamic), be (identity = stative; behavior = dynamic), think (opinion = stative; actively reflecting = dynamic), look/taste/see/smell/feel (perception = stative; deliberate action = dynamic).
topics.key_idea: A handful of very common verbs aren't simply 'always stative' — whether they can go in the continuous depends on which meaning is being used. Have meaning possess never goes in the continuous, but have meaning experience an event does; think meaning 'believe' stays in simple tenses, but think meaning 'actively reflect' can be continuous. The test isn't the word itself, it's whether that particular meaning describes a state or a voluntary action.
examples: I have a bicycle. / They are having a picnic on Saturday.
Marcus is an architect. / He is being unusually quiet today.
I think it's a great plan. / She is thinking about her exam.
This cake tastes amazing. / I am tasting the sauce.
common_mistakes: Assuming a verb is always stative just because it commonly is: treating look, have, or think as permanently blocked from the continuous, when the specific meaning in context actually determines whether it can take -ing.

topics.formula: Intransitive phrasal verbs (no object) are always inseparable. Transitive separable phrasal verbs allow verb + particle + object OR verb + object + particle — but a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle. Transitive inseparable phrasal verbs always keep the object after the whole verb + particle, even with a pronoun.
topics.key_idea: The object's behavior is what reveals which type a phrasal verb is. If there's no object at all, it's automatically inseparable. If there is an object, check whether it can move: separable ones let a full noun go either before or after the particle, but force a pronoun specifically between the verb and particle; inseparable ones never let anything — noun or pronoun — come between the verb and its particle.
examples: She's gone out.
You need to take off your shoes. / You need to take your shoes off. / You need to take them off.
I am waiting for the bus. / I am waiting for it.
common_mistakes: Putting a pronoun object after a separable phrasal verb's particle instead of between the verb and particle: 'put on it' instead of 'put it on.'
Trying to split an inseparable phrasal verb: 'look my notebook for' or 'look it for' instead of 'look for my notebook' / 'look for it.'

topics.formula: no longer = mid position (after the subject, or after be / a modal / an auxiliary), used in a sentence that it makes negative by itself. any longer / anymore = end position, used in a sentence that's already negative, or in a question.
topics.key_idea: All three express the same idea — something used to be true but isn't anymore — but they don't work the same way grammatically. No longer does the negating itself, so it goes with an otherwise positive sentence, sitting in the middle. Any longer and anymore need a sentence that's already negative (or a question), and they sit at the very end instead.
examples: I no longer drink soda.
We are no longer roommates.
We don't live in that city any longer.
Why don't you call us anymore?
common_mistakes: Using no longer in an already-negative sentence, creating a double negative: 'I don't no longer drink soda' instead of 'I no longer drink soda' or 'I don't drink soda any longer/anymore.'
Placing any longer or anymore in the middle of the sentence instead of at the end.

topics.formula: anymore (one word) = a time adverb meaning 'not now like before.' any more (two words) = a determiner meaning 'additional, more than what we have.'
topics.key_idea: These look nearly identical but mean completely different things, and the space is the only clue. Anymore as one word is about time — something that used to happen but doesn't now. Any more as two words is about quantity — asking for or referring to an extra amount of something.
examples: I don't eat sugar anymore.
Do you want any more coffee?
common_mistakes: Using anymore (one word) when asking about additional quantity: 'Do you want anymore coffee?' instead of 'Do you want any more coffee?' — the quantity meaning always needs two words.

topics.formula: on time = punctually, at the expected/scheduled moment. in time (for + noun / to + infinitive) = soon enough, not too late — often just in time for the very last moment.
topics.key_idea: On time is about matching a schedule exactly — arriving when you were expected to. In time is about having enough time left to still do something, which could be well before the deadline or right at the very last second. They answer different questions: on time asks 'was it punctual,' in time asks 'was there enough time left.'
examples: I hope the train arrives on time.
We got to the concert in time to find good seats.
He reached the station just in time to catch his train.
common_mistakes: Using on time when the meaning is really 'not too late,' not 'punctual': saying 'We got there on time to find good seats' when the intended meaning is 'in time to find good seats.'

topics.formula: at the end (of + noun) = the final part of something physical or a period of time. in the end = finally, eventually — how a situation was resolved, the opposite of at first.
topics.key_idea: At the end is literal and needs a noun to attach to — the end of a street, a book, a year. In the end is about outcome, not location, and works as a standalone phrase describing how things eventually turned out, often at the start of a sentence followed by a comma.
examples: There's a bakery at the end of the lane.
The course finishes at the end of September.
In the end, we chose the smaller apartment.
It was a difficult project, but in the end, it worked out.
common_mistakes: Using at the end without a following noun when the meaning is really 'eventually': 'At the end, it worked out' instead of 'In the end, it worked out.'

topics.formula: may (not) + base verb, to directly give or deny permission — not just ask for it. Might is not used this way; it's may specifically. May also suggests a slightly stronger possibility than might when both are used for speculation.
topics.key_idea: Beyond asking for permission with may I...?, may also works to directly grant or refuse it in a statement — 'you may sit anywhere' actually gives permission, not just asks about it. Might never fills this role, even though it's often interchangeable with may for possibility. On that note, if there's ever a subtle difference between the two for speculation, may tends to suggest a slightly stronger likelihood than might, though in casual speech most people don't distinguish them.
examples: You may leave whenever you're ready.
You may not bring outside food.
May I ask a question?
common_mistakes: Using might to give or deny permission: 'You might leave whenever you're ready' instead of 'You may leave whenever you're ready' — might doesn't work for granting permission, only may does.

topics.formula: present simple, for future events that are fixed on a schedule or timetable — transport, opening hours, timetables, official events.
topics.key_idea: This is a distinct use of present simple that isn't about habits or permanent facts at all — it's for future events that are part of a fixed schedule, like a train timetable or a shop's opening hours. The event itself is in the future, but because it's officially scheduled rather than personally arranged, present simple is used instead of present continuous or will.
examples: The bus departs at 9.
The shop opens at 10.
My dentist appointment is on Thursday at 3.
common_mistakes: Using will or present continuous for a fixed timetable event instead of present simple: 'The train will leave at 4' sounds like a prediction rather than a scheduled fact — present simple fits better for something on an official timetable.

topics.formula: present continuous, to describe a situation, trend, or trait that is gradually changing or developing over time — not a single action, but a change in progress.
topics.key_idea: Beyond describing an action happening right now, present continuous also captures change itself — something that's shifting, improving, or developing over a longer stretch of time. The 'progress' here isn't a single moment; it's a trend that's still unfolding.
examples: Traffic in the city is getting worse every year.
More people are switching to electric cars.
Her English is improving a lot.
common_mistakes: Using present simple for an ongoing trend instead of present continuous: 'The population increases every year' sounds more like a repeated fact, while 'The population is increasing' better captures an ongoing, unfolding change.

topics.formula: Will you + base verb + please?, to politely ask someone to do something for you.
topics.key_idea: This is a different job for will than offers or predictions — here the speaker is asking the listener to do something, not offering to do it themselves or guessing what will happen. It's one of several polite request forms in English, alongside could you and would you.
examples: Will you close the window, please?
Will you pass me that book?
Will you help me carry these boxes?
common_mistakes: Confusing a request with an offer: 'Will you post this letter?' (asking the listener to post it) is a different meaning from 'I'll post this letter' (the speaker offering to post it) — the subject determines who's expected to act.

topics.formula: present perfect + today / this week / this month / this year (a time period that hasn't finished yet), or + lately / all + period (all day, all my life). Also used with a number of times (three times, twice) to count experiences up to now.
topics.key_idea: Present perfect fits naturally with a time expression as long as that period of time is still ongoing — 'today' while it's still today, 'this week' while the week isn't over. That's different from a finished time period like 'yesterday,' which needs past simple instead. The same tense also works for counting how many times something has happened up to this point.
examples: I've called him twice today.
Has she texted you this week?
I've been quite busy lately.
I've read this article three times.
common_mistakes: Using present perfect with a finished time period: 'I've seen him yesterday' instead of 'I saw him yesterday,' since yesterday is already over.

topics.formula: has/have gone to + place = the person is still there, hasn't come back. has/have been to + place = the person went and already returned.
topics.key_idea: These look almost identical but describe opposite situations. Gone to means the trip isn't over — the person is currently away. Been to means the trip is finished and the person is back, which is also the form used for general life experience of having visited somewhere.
examples: Diana has gone to the market; she'll be back soon.
We have been to Portugal four times.
He's gone to pick up the kids.
I've been to Cairo, but I've never been to Istanbul.
common_mistakes: Using been to when the person is still away, or gone to when they've already returned: saying 'She's been to the shop' when she's currently still out, instead of 'She's gone to the shop.'

topics.formula: have/has + been + verb-ing, for actions that started in the past and are still going, or have only just stopped. Common with for/since/how long/lately/all + period.
topics.key_idea: This tense highlights the activity itself, often with a visible result right now — red eyes because someone's been crying, tired arms because someone's been painting. It can describe something still happening, or something that only just finished, and it's especially natural when repeating or emphasizing how long something has been going on.
examples: Have you been crying? Your eyes are red.
Sorry for the mess, I've been baking.
He's been calling you all morning.
How long have you been learning Korean?
common_mistakes: Using present perfect simple when the point is really about an ongoing process with a visible result: saying 'I have painted' instead of 'I've been painting' when explaining why you're covered in paint right now.

topics.formula: Stative verbs must use present perfect simple, never continuous. For dynamic verbs describing an ongoing duration, continuous is more natural, especially to emphasize how long. Simple = a fully finished action, or counting how many/how much. Continuous = maybe still going (or just stopped), or the result comes from the process itself.
topics.key_idea: With a stative verb there's no choice — present perfect simple is the only option. With a dynamic verb, the choice depends on what's being emphasized: continuous stresses the ongoing activity and its duration, often with the process itself explaining a present result, while simple points to a finished, countable outcome. 'How long' pairs naturally with continuous; 'how many/how much' pairs with simple.
examples: We've had this sofa for ages.
Who has eaten the last cookie? / Who has been eating the cookies?
I've painted the fence, and now it looks great. / I've been painting the fence, that's why my hands are covered in paint.
I've sent thirty emails today. / I've been sending emails all morning.
common_mistakes: Using continuous with a stative verb: 'I've been having this car for years' instead of 'I've had this car for years.'
Using simple when the emphasis is really on ongoing duration or a process-based result: 'I have washed the car' instead of 'I've been washing the car' to explain why you're sweaty right now.

topics.formula: during + noun, answers 'when' (during the concert). for + length of time, answers 'how long' (for two hours). while + subject + verb, for two things happening at the same time.
topics.key_idea: These three all relate to time, but they answer different questions and take different grammar after them. During tells you when something happened within a period, for tells you how long something lasted, and while introduces a second, simultaneous action with its own subject and verb — where during would need a noun instead.
examples: Several people fell asleep during the lecture.
We waited for almost two hours.
I listened to a podcast while I was jogging.
I fell asleep during the movie. / I fell asleep while I was watching the movie.
common_mistakes: Using during instead of for when the meaning is duration, not timing: 'I ran during one hour' instead of 'I ran for one hour.'
Using during with a full clause instead of a noun: 'I fell asleep during I was watching the film' instead of 'I fell asleep while I was watching the film,' or 'I fell asleep during the film.'

topics.formula: any + comparative, in negative sentences (not any better). no + comparative, with a positive verb (no better).
topics.key_idea: These are two ways of saying the same thing — that something isn't better, faster, or more expensive than something else — but they pair with opposite verb forms. Any needs a negative verb to go with it, while no already carries the negative meaning itself, so it pairs with a plain positive verb instead.
examples: This laptop is no faster than the old one.
This laptop isn't any faster than the old one.
The new route is no shorter than the old one.
common_mistakes: Mismatching any/no with the wrong verb form: 'Your performance was any better than mine' instead of 'wasn't any better' or 'was no better' — any needs a negative verb, no doesn't.

topics.formula: the least + adjective = the opposite of the most. After a superlative: in + a place or group (in the class, in the world); of + a time period or a number of people (of the year, of my brothers).
topics.key_idea: The least is simply the bottom end of the scale, the mirror image of the most. And the word that follows a superlative isn't always in — it depends on what's being compared against: a place or named group uses in, while a stretch of time or a specific number of people uses of.
examples: He's the least talkative person in the office.
It was the happiest day of my life.
She's the tallest of the sisters.
This is the most popular restaurant in town.
common_mistakes: Using in where of belongs, or the reverse: 'the best evening in my life' instead of 'the best evening of my life' — a period of time takes of, not in.

topics.formula: a/an + noun, meaning 'each' or 'per' — used for rates, frequency, prices, and speeds.
topics.key_idea: Beyond introducing something new or meaning 'one,' a/an also does the job of 'per' when talking about how often something happens or at what rate — hours a day, times a week, dollars a month, kilometers an hour.
examples: I exercise four times a week.
She earns $30 an hour.
We drive at about 60 miles an hour on this road.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article entirely in this pattern: 'three times week' instead of 'three times a week.'

topics.formula: What a/an + adjective + singular countable noun! Such a/an + adjective + singular countable noun.
topics.key_idea: Both are used to react strongly to something, and both need a/an in front of a singular countable noun, even though the sentence is expressing a big reaction, not just introducing something new for the first time.
examples: What a lovely surprise!
That was such a boring lecture!
You are such a generous person.
common_mistakes: Dropping the a/an in this pattern: 'What fantastic idea!' or 'Such horrible day!' instead of 'What a fantastic idea!' / 'Such a horrible day!'

topics.formula: no article with home/work/bed/hospital/school/university/prison when used for their normal purpose (living, working, sleeping, being treated, studying, being imprisoned). the + same word when referring to the literal building or object instead.
topics.key_idea: These words drop the article when they're being used for what they're actually for — being in bed to sleep, being in hospital as a patient. But the same word needs the as soon as it's just referring to the physical place or object itself, not its function — going to the hospital to visit someone, finding something under the bed.
examples: He's still at work.
I need to go to the hospital to visit my uncle.
She's been in bed with a fever.
I found my glasses under the bed.
common_mistakes: Using the when the place is meant in its normal function, or dropping the when it's meant literally: 'She's in the bed all morning' (should be no article, for resting) or 'I found the keys under bed' (should be 'under the bed,' a literal object).

topics.formula: noun + number, no article (room 15, page 86, platform 3).
topics.key_idea: When a number identifies a specific noun like a room, page, or platform, no article is needed at all — the number itself does the identifying job that the or a would normally do.
examples: Please go to gate 12.
Turn to page 45.
Meet me at exit 7.
common_mistakes: Adding an article before this pattern: 'Go to the page 86' instead of just 'Go to page 86.'

topics.formula: Most place names (countries, cities, continents, mountains) take no article. But country names that are plural, or built around State(s)/Republic/Kingdom/Union, take the: the US, the UK, the Philippines, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic.
topics.key_idea: Place names are one of the few noun categories that generally skip articles altogether, but there's a specific, learnable exception: if the country's name is grammatically plural, or built around a word like State, Republic, or Kingdom, it needs the, just like any other plural or descriptive noun phrase would.
examples: She grew up in the United Arab Emirates.
I've always wanted to visit the Bahamas.
He works for the government of the Czech Republic.
They moved to Poland last year.
common_mistakes: Adding the to an ordinary country name, or leaving it off a plural/Republic-Kingdom-State name: 'the Spain' instead of just 'Spain,' or 'I live in Netherlands' instead of 'I live in the Netherlands.'

topics.formula: another + singular noun, or alone as a pronoun (one more). other + plural noun (other doctors) — never 'others' before a noun. others (always a pronoun, never + noun) = more of the same kind. the other(s) = the specific remaining one(s) in a known group, with or without a noun.
topics.key_idea: The core split is determiner versus pronoun: another and other go before a noun (another cup, other doctors), while others is always alone, never followed by a noun. Adding the changes the meaning from 'more of the same general kind' to 'the specific ones left in a group you already know about' — the other kids means the remaining kids in this particular group, not just any additional kids.
examples: Could I have another slice of cake?
I need to talk to other teachers about this.
I've read one of his books, but I'd like to read another.
Some students passed, but others didn't.
common_mistakes: Adding a plural ending to other as a determiner: 'I want to talk to others doctors' instead of 'other doctors' — other stays the same whether it's followed by a noun or not.
Using other instead of others as a pronoun: 'We need to find other' instead of 'We need to find others,' since others never appears without a noun attached, unlike other.

topics.formula: could = the past form of can, for past ability, past permission, and polite requests. can/could + see/hear/smell/feel/taste, instead of the continuous form of these stative perception verbs.
topics.key_idea: Could is simply can moved into the past — same uses (ability, permission, polite requests), just earlier in time. Separately, perception verbs like see, hear, smell, feel, and taste are stative, so they never take the continuous form the way an action verb would; can (or could, in the past) does that job instead.
examples: She could ride a bike by the age of five.
Could you turn the music down, please?
Can you smell something burning?
I can taste too much salt in this soup.
common_mistakes: Using the continuous form of a perception verb instead of can/could: 'I'm hearing something odd!' instead of 'I can hear something odd!'

topics.formula: be able to + infinitive, a more formal alternative to can/could for ability. Required (not can) for any form other than plain present or past: to-infinitive, -ing, present perfect, future, etc.
topics.key_idea: Be able to means roughly the same as can, just more formal, but it has one job can/could genuinely can't do: filling in every verb form can and could don't have. Can and could only exist as simple present and past forms — there's no infinitive, -ing, or perfect form of can — so be able to has to step in whenever the sentence needs one of those.
examples: They weren't able to reach an agreement.
I'd like to be able to speak three languages.
She hasn't been able to sleep well lately.
Will you be able to attend the meeting?
common_mistakes: Trying to use can in a form it doesn't have: 'I'd like to can visit her' instead of 'I'd like to be able to visit her.'

topics.formula: General ability (present or past): can/could or be able to, either works. A specific, one-time past achievement (positive): was/were able to or managed to — NOT could. Negative: couldn't still works fine for a specific occasion.
topics.key_idea: For a general skill someone had over time, could and was/were able to are interchangeable. But for something that happened once, in one specific situation, positive sentences can't use could at all — that specifically requires was/were able to or managed to. This restriction only applies to positive sentences; couldn't is perfectly fine for a specific occasion when something didn't happen.
examples: My grandmother could swim very well as a child.
Despite the storm, the sailors were able to reach the shore.
He managed to fix the engine just in time.
It was so noisy that we couldn't hear each other.
common_mistakes: Using could for a specific, one-time past success: 'The building was flooding, but the staff could evacuate in time' instead of 'were able to evacuate' or 'managed to evacuate' — could only works here in the negative, or for a general, repeated ability.

topics.formula: 've/'s got to + infinitive, an informal spoken alternative to have to, meaning exactly the same thing.
topics.key_idea: In everyday spoken English, have got to (usually contracted to 've got to) is just a more casual way of saying have to — same meaning, same obligation, just a different register. It's common in conversation but not typically used in formal writing.
examples: I've got to finish this report by Friday.
She's got to renew her passport soon.
We've got to leave before the traffic gets bad.
common_mistakes: Dropping to after got: 'I have got go' instead of 'I've got to go.'

topics.formula: mustn't = can't = not allowed to, all expressing prohibition.
topics.key_idea: These three all say the same thing — that something is forbidden — and can generally be swapped for each other. Can't and not allowed to are just more everyday-sounding alternatives to the more formal mustn't.
examples: You mustn't feed the animals here.
You are not allowed to feed the animals here.
Visitors can't bring food into the museum.
common_mistakes: Assuming mustn't and don't have to are similar in strength just because they're both negative forms — mustn't is as strong as can't (forbidden), while don't have to is much weaker (simply optional).

topics.formula: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves — used when the subject and object are the same person, after a preposition referring back to the subject, or to emphasize that the subject alone did the action. by/on + myself/yourself/etc. = alone, without help.
topics.key_idea: Reflexive pronouns point back to the subject of the sentence, which happens in three main situations: when the subject and object are literally the same person, after a preposition that refers back to the subject, or simply to stress that no one else was involved. A number of everyday verbs (dress, shave, wash, relax, hurry, concentrate, open) don't take a reflexive pronoun in English even though learners from many other languages expect one, since English treats these as complete on their own.
examples: He cut himself while cooking.
We really enjoyed ourselves at the festival.
She's proud of herself for finishing the marathon.
The kids got dressed by themselves.
common_mistakes: Adding a reflexive pronoun to a verb that doesn't need one in English: 'I washed myself and dressed myself' instead of just 'I washed and dressed' — several everyday verbs are complete without one.
Forgetting the reflexive when the action really does return to the subject: 'I saw me in the mirror' instead of 'I saw myself in the mirror.'

topics.formula: each other / one another, when two or more people do the same thing to each other — a mutual action, not a self-directed one.
topics.key_idea: Reciprocal pronouns describe an action going both ways between people — person A does something to person B, and B does the same back to A — which is different from a reflexive pronoun, where someone acts on themselves alone. Each other and one another mean the same thing and can generally be swapped.
examples: The old friends hadn't seen each other in years.
The teammates always support one another.
They've known each other since childhood.
common_mistakes: Using a reflexive pronoun where the action is really mutual between two people: 'They introduced themselves' (each person introduced only their own self) versus 'They introduced each other' (each one introduced the other person) — these describe different situations.

topics.formula: -ed adjective = describes how someone feels (bored, tired, surprised). -ing adjective = describes what causes that feeling (boring, tiring, surprising).
topics.key_idea: Both forms come from the same verb, but they describe opposite ends of the same feeling: -ed goes on the person experiencing it, -ing goes on whatever is causing it. A film can be boring, which is why a person watching it feels bored — the two words are related but never interchangeable.
examples: I'm exhausted after that hike.
That documentary was fascinating.
She was embarrassed by the mistake.
common_mistakes: Using -ing to describe how someone feels, or -ed to describe what caused it: 'I'm boring' (says the person themselves is dull) instead of 'I'm bored' (says the person feels bored) — mixing these up actually changes the meaning, not just the grammar.

topics.formula: had + past participle, with stative verbs and for/since/how long/always, for a situation that had already been going on before a specific point in the past. Also used with a number/amount to say how much or how many had happened by that point.
topics.key_idea: This is the 'past before the past' version of present perfect's duration use — instead of counting up to now, it counts up to some earlier moment already being discussed. A situation had already lasted a certain amount of time, or a certain quantity had already been reached, by the time the main past event in the story happened.
examples: By the time she turned thirty, she had lived in five different countries.
The day the shop closed, it had been open for exactly ten years.
We had driven 300 kilometers before we stopped for lunch.
common_mistakes: Using past simple for a duration that had already been ongoing before the main past event: 'By the time he retired, he worked at the firm for thirty years' instead of 'he had worked at the firm for thirty years' when the point is how long the situation had already lasted by that specific moment.

topics.formula: be used to + noun or -ing = accustomed to something, not finding it strange anymore (a state). get used to + noun or -ing = becoming accustomed to it (a process). In both, to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive — so the verb after it takes -ing, never the base form.
topics.key_idea: These look almost identical to the past-habit 'used to,' but they're a completely different structure. Be used to describes an ongoing state of familiarity, get used to describes the process of arriving at that familiarity, and in both cases to acts as a preposition — which is exactly why a following verb needs the -ing form, unlike used to + infinitive for past habits, where to is part of the verb itself.
examples: It took a while, but I'm used to the cold weather now.
She's still getting used to her new schedule.
I'll never get used to waking up this early.
common_mistakes: Using the base infinitive after be/get used to instead of -ing: 'I'll get used to work with John' instead of 'I'll get used to working with John' — to here is a preposition, so it needs -ing, unlike the past-habit used to.

Confusing be used to (a state of present familiarity) with the unrelated used to + infinitive (a past habit that's over): 'I used to drive on the left' (I did it regularly in the past) means something completely different from 'I'm used to driving on the left' (I find it normal now).

topics.formula: be (in whatever form the tense needs) + past participle. Present perfect passive: have/has been + past participle. Future passive: will be + past participle.
topics.key_idea: Passive isn't limited to just present and past simple — it works with any tense at all, since the rule is always the same: take whatever form of be that tense normally uses, and add the past participle after it. Present perfect passive uses have/has been, future passive uses will be, and so on for every other tense.
examples: The bridge has been closed for repairs.
New regulations will be introduced next year.
The proposal is being reviewed by the committee.
common_mistakes: Getting stuck only forming passive in present or past simple, and reverting to active voice when a different tense is needed — 'has cancelled' (active, present perfect) becomes 'has been cancelled' (passive), following the same be-plus-past-participle pattern.

topics.formula: must + base verb, when confident something is true (a deduction, not an obligation). can't + base verb, when confident something is NOT true — never mustn't for this. can is not used for deduction at all. + be + -ing, for a deduction about something happening right now.
topics.key_idea: These same modal words also work for logical deduction, not just obligation or possibility — must signals 'I'm confident this is true,' based on evidence or reasoning, and its negative counterpart is can't, not mustn't, even though mustn't is the normal negative of must elsewhere. Can itself is never used this way at all. Adding be + -ing lets the deduction apply to something happening right now, rather than a general fact.
examples: You must be freezing in that thin jacket.
This can't be the right address; the building looks abandoned.
They must be on vacation; their lights have been off for days.
common_mistakes: Using mustn't for a confident negative deduction: 'It mustn't be true' instead of 'It can't be true' — can't is the negative of must specifically for deduction.
Using can for deduction: 'She can be tired after that shift' instead of 'She might/may be tired' or 'She must be tired,' depending on how confident the speaker is.

topics.formula: unless + present tense = if...not. Used in first conditional sentences as an alternative to 'if...don't/doesn't'.
topics.key_idea: Unless is a shortcut for a negative condition — it packs 'if...not' into one word. Since the negative is already built in, the clause after unless stays positive; adding a second negative would say the opposite of what's intended.
examples: I won't sign the contract unless the terms change.
She won't come to the party unless you invite her personally.
Unless it cools down, we'll cancel the hike.
common_mistakes: Adding a second negative inside the unless clause: 'I won't go unless I don't save some money' instead of 'I won't go unless I save some money' — unless already means 'if not,' so the clause itself stays positive.

topics.formula: if + past perfect (the if-clause) + would / could / might + have + past participle (the main clause), for an imaginary result of something that didn't actually happen in the past.
topics.key_idea: Third conditional looks back at the past and imagines a different outcome — something that could have happened, if an earlier condition had been different, but didn't. Both parts of the sentence describe events that are already over and can't be changed; the whole sentence is a hypothetical replay of the past, not a real possibility going forward.
examples: If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the flight.
If we had checked the weather, we would have brought umbrellas.
He could have won the race if he hadn't fallen.
common_mistakes: Using would have in the if-clause instead of past perfect: 'If you would have left earlier' instead of 'If you had left earlier' — the if-clause needs past perfect, not would have.
Forgetting have after would/could/might: 'I would arrived on time' instead of 'I would have arrived on time.'

topics.formula: reported question = question word (or if/whether for yes/no questions) + subject + verb, in normal statement word order — no do/does/did, and no question mark.
topics.key_idea: A reported question loses its question-like word order entirely — the subject goes back before the verb, just like in a normal statement, and do/does/did disappears completely, the same as with subject questions. Yes/no questions need if or whether to introduce them, since there's no question word to do that job.
examples: 'Where do you work?' → He asked me where I worked.
'Are you coming tonight?' → She asked if I was coming tonight.
'How much does it cost?' → I wondered how much it cost.
common_mistakes: Keeping question word order or the auxiliary do/does/did in a reported question: 'He asked me where did I live' instead of 'He asked me where I lived.'

topics.formula: ask / tell + object + to + infinitive, to report an order, instruction, or request. Negative: not to + infinitive.
topics.key_idea: Reporting a command or instruction doesn't use a full reported clause with 'that' — it switches to a to-infinitive structure instead, naming who the instruction was directed at right after ask or tell.
examples: 'Sit down.' → The teacher told the students to sit down.
'Please wait here.' → He asked us to wait there.
'Don't touch the paintings.' → The guide told us not to touch the paintings.
common_mistakes: Reporting a command as if it were a statement, with a full clause: 'She told me that I close the door' instead of 'She told me to close the door.'

topics.formula: forget/remember + to + infinitive = the task itself (do it or not). forget/remember + -ing = a memory of something that happened. try + to + infinitive = make an effort to achieve something. try + -ing = experiment with something to see if it helps. stop + to + infinitive = pause one activity in order to do another. stop + -ing = quit doing something.
topics.key_idea: With this small group of verbs, choosing -ing or to + infinitive doesn't just change the style — it changes the actual meaning. Forget and remember split between the task itself (to + infinitive, something you need to do or did) and a memory of an event (-ing, something that happened). Try splits between genuine effort toward a goal (to + infinitive) and experimenting with an option (-ing). Stop splits between pausing to do something else (to + infinitive) and quitting an activity entirely (-ing).
examples: I forgot to send the invoice.
I'll never forget meeting her for the first time.
Why don't you try adding a bit of lemon to the sauce?
We stopped to check the map. / I stopped smoking two years ago.
common_mistakes: Mixing up remember to do (the task) and remember doing (the memory): 'I remember to visit Paris as a child' instead of 'I remember visiting Paris as a child,' when talking about an actual memory.

Confusing stop to do (pausing for a different activity) with stop doing (quitting): 'I stopped to smoke' (means I paused something else in order to smoke) when the intended meaning was 'I stopped smoking' (I quit).

topics.formula: so much / so many, another exception allowing much/many in affirmative sentences (to show an extreme result). plenty of, an alternative to a lot of/lots of, before both countable and uncountable nouns.
topics.key_idea: So much and so many work like too much/too many — they're additional exceptions where much/many are completely natural in a positive sentence, here used to build up to a result ('so many people that we had to leave'). Plenty of is simply a third way of saying 'a lot of,' with the same countable-or-uncountable flexibility.
examples: There was so much noise that I couldn't concentrate.
So many people showed up that we ran out of chairs.
We've got plenty of time before the train leaves.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the result clause that usually follows so much/so many: 'There was so much traffic' on its own sounds incomplete without a following 'that...' clause explaining the consequence.

topics.formula: no + countable (plural) or uncountable noun, in an affirmative sentence, meaning zero — an alternative to not any.
topics.key_idea: No works directly before a noun in a positive sentence to say there's zero of something, doing the same job as not any but without needing a negative verb. It's a plain determiner here, different from the compound words nobody or nothing, which stand in for a noun rather than going in front of one.
examples: There's no water left in the bottle.
I have no regrets about the decision.
There were no seats available.
common_mistakes: Combining no with a negative verb: 'There isn't no biscuits left' instead of 'There are no biscuits left' or 'There aren't any biscuits left' — no already makes the sentence negative on its own.

topics.formula: none, a pronoun meaning 'zero,' standing alone with no noun after it. none of + noun (countable or uncountable), when naming what there's zero of.
topics.key_idea: None does the same job as no, but as a pronoun rather than a determiner, so it never sits directly in front of a noun — either it stands completely alone, or it connects to a noun through of.
examples: 'How many tickets are left?' 'None.'
I wanted some cake, but there was none left.
None of the volunteers showed up.
common_mistakes: Using none directly before a noun without of: 'None students came' instead of 'None of the students came.'

topics.formula: all + noun (no the) = people/things in general. all + the/my/etc. + noun = a particular, specific group. both + noun, or both + the/my/etc. + noun, work the same way for exactly two people or things — the (of) is often optional but never changes the meaning the way it does with all.
topics.key_idea: With all, dropping or including the changes the meaning — no the means a general statement about everything of that kind, while the/my/etc. narrows it down to one particular group you have in mind. Both refers to exactly two, and works with or without a determiner in a very similar pattern, though the meaning shift isn't as sharp as it is with all.
examples: All children need affection.
All the children in this class are under six.
Both brothers work in finance.
Both the brothers I mentioned live abroad.
common_mistakes: Using all + the with a general meaning, or all alone when a specific group is meant: 'All the drivers break speed limits' (implying every driver everywhere) when the intended meaning was really about one particular group of drivers.

topics.formula: all of / both of + us/you/them, before the verb, as the subject — of is required, never optional here. us/you/them + all/both, after the verb, as the object.
topics.key_idea: With pronouns specifically, all and both need of when they come before the verb as part of the subject — unlike with ordinary nouns, this of can't be dropped. When the pronoun is the object instead, all/both simply follows it directly, with no of at all.
examples: All of them were late.
Both of us were surprised.
The manager praised them all.
She thanked us both.
common_mistakes: Dropping of before a pronoun subject: 'All them agreed with the plan' instead of 'All of them agreed with the plan' — of is required with pronouns, even though it's optional with ordinary nouns.

topics.formula: all/both in mid position: before an ordinary verb, after be (when it's the only verb), after the first auxiliary verb, or after the subject in a question.
topics.key_idea: All and both can sit inside the sentence, close to the verb, instead of attaching directly to a noun or pronoun — this mirrors where frequency adverbs like always or often go, following essentially the same positioning rules.
examples: We both agree with the plan.
The guests were all delighted.
They have all left already.
common_mistakes: Placing all/both in the wrong spot relative to an auxiliary verb: with more than one auxiliary, all/both goes after the first one, not the last — 'They have finished all' instead of 'They have all finished.'

topics.formula: either + singular noun = one or the other of two. neither + singular noun = not one and not the other. either of / neither of + the/my/etc. + noun, or + us/you/them. Neither pairs with a positive verb (it's already negative); either used alone typically pairs with a negative verb — not either means the same as neither.
topics.key_idea: Either and neither work like a two-option version of some and no — either picks one out of exactly two, neither rules out both. Both take a singular noun and a singular verb, even though they're technically talking about two things. Since neither already carries the negative meaning, the verb after it stays positive; the reverse pattern, not either, means exactly the same thing as neither.
examples: You can sit on either side of the table.
Neither answer was correct.
Can either of you lend me a pen?
I don't like either of the options.
common_mistakes: Using a negative verb with neither: 'Neither Sam nor his brother can't attend' instead of 'Neither Sam nor his brother can attend' — neither is already negative.

Using either with a positive verb standing alone for a negative meaning: 'I trust either of them' when the meaning is 'I don't trust either of them' — either needs a negative verb to carry that meaning on its own.

topics.formula: both X and Y / either X or Y / neither X nor Y, to connect the two specific things or people being talked about.
topics.key_idea: These paired connectors work like and, or, and a doubled-up not, but they're built for exactly two named items — both...and adds them together, either...or presents a choice between them, and neither...nor rules both of them out at once.
examples: Both Marcus and Diana attended the conference.
You can either call me or send a message.
I enjoy neither jogging nor swimming.
He neither called nor wrote.
common_mistakes: Mismatching the pairs, like starting with either but finishing with nor: keeping each pair together matters — either...or, neither...nor, both...and.

topics.formula: any / anything / anybody / anywhere, in a positive sentence, meaning 'it doesn't matter which one' — a completely different use from the negative/question 'any' that means 'some, at all'.
topics.key_idea: Any and its compound forms have a second job beyond negatives and questions — in a positive sentence, they can mean that the choice genuinely doesn't matter, any one will do just as well as another. This is a distinct meaning from the more familiar negative use, even though the word looks identical.
examples: You can pick any seat you like.
Any doctor here could confirm that.
We can meet any day next week.
common_mistakes: Missing this meaning and assuming any/anybody/anywhere can only appear in negatives and questions — in a positive sentence, they're not a mistake at all when the meaning is 'it doesn't matter which.'

topics.formula: so + adjective/adverb (+ that...) — intensifies an adjective or adverb directly. such a + (adjective) + singular countable noun (+ that...) — intensifies a noun phrase. such + (adjective) + uncountable or plural noun (+ that...) — same, without a/an.
topics.key_idea: So and such both mean 'very' or 'really,' but which one to use depends on what's being intensified: so goes directly before an adjective or adverb with nothing else attached, while such goes before a full noun phrase, adding a if the noun is singular and countable. Both are often followed by a that-clause spelling out the result of being that extreme.
examples: You are so talented!
He is so kind that everyone loves him.
She is such a brilliant scientist.
We had such terrible luck on this trip.
common_mistakes: Using so before a noun phrase, or such before a bare adjective: 'She is so a brilliant actress' instead of 'She is such a brilliant actress,' or 'You are such stubborn' instead of 'You are so stubborn.'

topics.formula: who/which/that can be dropped entirely from a defining relative clause when it's immediately followed by a subject + verb (i.e., when it's the object of the clause, not the subject).
topics.key_idea: A defining relative clause can lose its pronoun completely, but only in one specific situation: when the pronoun is standing in for the object of the clause, meaning a new subject and verb come right after it. If the pronoun is itself the subject of the clause, it can't be dropped.
examples: Is this the jacket (that) you bought yesterday?
She's not the person (who) I thought she was.
This is the cafe (that) I mentioned earlier.
common_mistakes: Dropping the pronoun when it's actually the subject of the clause: 'I saw a man was very tall' instead of 'I saw a man who was very tall' — that pronoun can't be omitted here, since nothing else acts as the subject.

topics.formula: Non-defining relative clause, set off by commas, adding extra (non-essential) information. That can never replace who/which here, and the pronoun can never be omitted.
topics.key_idea: Non-defining clauses add a side note about someone or something already fully identified — remove the clause and the sentence still says exactly who or what is meant. That's the opposite of a defining clause, which is essential for identifying the person or thing in the first place. Because the information is optional, that specifically isn't allowed here, and the pronoun always stays, unlike in a defining clause.
examples: My neighbor, who works as a pilot, travels constantly.
This restaurant, which just opened last month, is already popular.
My cousin who lives in Berlin is a doctor. / My cousin, who lives in Berlin, is a doctor.
common_mistakes: Using that in a non-defining clause, or dropping the pronoun: 'My laptop, that I bought last year, broke already' instead of 'which,' or 'My colleague, I deeply respect, is retiring' instead of keeping 'who.'

topics.formula: 'd better (had better) + base verb, for strong advice or a warning, often implying something bad will happen otherwise. Negative: 'd better not. Despite the past form 'had,' the meaning is about right now or the immediate future.
topics.key_idea: Had better is stronger and more urgent than should — it's less about a good idea and more about avoiding a bad outcome, and it can sound like a warning or even a threat depending on the context. Even though had looks like a past tense, the whole expression is really about the immediate present or future, never the actual past.
examples: We'd better hurry, or we'll miss the train.
You'd better call her before it's too late.
You'd better not forget your passport.
common_mistakes: Adding to after had better: 'I'd better to take a look' instead of 'I'd better take a look' — the verb after had better stays in its base form, with no to.

topics.formula: it's time (for someone) + to + infinitive = someone should do something now or soon. it's (about) time + subject + past simple = the same idea, but stronger, often implying it's overdue — and using a past tense verb despite talking about now/the future.
topics.key_idea: Both forms say someone should act, but the past simple version carries an extra edge of complaint or criticism — it's time you did something usually implies you should already have done it, and the past tense here is purely grammatical, a marker of this specific structure, not an actual reference to the past.
examples: It's time for you to make a decision.
It's time to leave.
It's time you apologized to her.
It's about time you started saving money.
common_mistakes: Using a present tense verb in the it's time + subject structure: 'It's time you fix that leak' instead of 'It's time you fixed that leak' — this specific pattern always takes past simple, even though the meaning is about now or the future.

topics.formula: positive statement + negative tag / negative statement + positive tag, using the same auxiliary as the main sentence (or do/did if there isn't one) + subject pronoun. Special case: I am... → ...aren't I?
topics.key_idea: A question tag turns a statement into a quick question by flipping the polarity — positive gets a negative tag, negative gets a positive tag — while reusing whatever auxiliary the sentence already has. How the voice moves at the end changes the meaning: falling intonation mostly just seeks agreement with something the speaker already believes, while rising intonation signals genuine uncertainty, really asking for information.
examples: You're coming to the wedding, aren't you?
She doesn't like spicy food, does she?
They won't be late, will they?
I'm doing the right thing, aren't I?
common_mistakes: Matching the tag's polarity to the statement instead of flipping it: 'She's coming, is she?' instead of 'She's coming, isn't she?' — the tag needs the opposite polarity from the main sentence.
Using 'am I not' instead of the irregular 'aren't I': 'I'm late, am I not?' is old-fashioned; 'aren't I' is the standard tag for I am.

topics.formula: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing (never a clause directly), or despite/in spite of + the fact that + clause. Even though works just like although (a clause-based contrast word), just slightly more emphatic.
topics.key_idea: Despite and in spite of mean the same as although, but they need a noun or an -ing form right after them, not a full clause — if a full clause is really needed, the fact that has to be inserted first to bridge the grammar. Even though is simply a stronger-sounding version of although and follows exactly the same clause-based pattern.
examples: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.
They finished the project in spite of the tight deadline.
We went hiking despite the fact that it was freezing.
Even though we were tired, we kept working.
common_mistakes: Following despite/in spite of directly with a clause: 'Despite he was tired, he kept working' instead of 'Despite the fact that he was tired, he kept working,' or simply 'Despite his tiredness, he kept working.'

topics.formula: in order to / so as to + infinitive, more formal alternatives to plain to + infinitive for purpose. Negatives: in order not to / so as not to. so that + subject + verb (usually with a modal: could, would, can), another way to express purpose with a full clause.
topics.key_idea: These are all more formal or more explicit ways of saying why something is done, useful especially in writing. In order to and so as to work exactly like to + infinitive, just dressier, and their negatives are built by inserting not before to. So that goes further, opening up a full clause with its own subject, almost always paired with a modal verb.
examples: We left early in order to avoid the traffic.
She whispered so as not to wake the baby.
He saved money so that he could travel next year.
common_mistakes: Placing not after to instead of before it: 'in order to not be late' instead of 'in order not to be late.'

topics.formula: as / since + clause, more formal alternatives to because, usable at the start or end of a sentence. due to + noun, a more formal alternative to because of.
topics.key_idea: These are simply more formal versions of the reason words already covered — as and since work exactly like because (clause-based), just more common in writing than speech, and due to works exactly like because of (noun-based), with the same more formal tone.
examples: As the shop was closed, we went home.
Since prices have gone up, fewer people are eating out.
The trip was cancelled due to the storm.
common_mistakes: Using due to with a full clause instead of a noun: 'due to it was late' instead of 'due to the late hour' or 'because it was late.'

topics.formula: verb + a specific, fixed preposition + object — the preposition doesn't follow logical rules, it's simply part of that verb and has to be learned per verb (e.g. listen to, wait for, look at, believe in, depend on, remind someone of, argue with, complain about).
topics.key_idea: A lot of English verbs are always followed by one particular preposition before their object, and there's rarely any logical reason why that preposition and not another — it's simply a fixed pairing that has to be memorized verb by verb, the same way a phrasal verb's particle does. Getting the verb right but the preposition wrong is a very common, very noticeable mistake.
examples: She apologized for the delay.
He's applying for a scholarship.
They succeeded in convincing the investors.
I'm relying on your support.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition, or none at all, with a verb that needs one: 'listen music' instead of 'listen to music,' or 'wait Sandra' instead of 'wait for Sandra' — the preposition is a fixed part of the verb, not optional and not interchangeable with a different one that might seem logical.

topics.formula: adjective + a specific, fixed preposition (+ noun or -ing) — like verb-preposition pairs, the choice isn't logical and has to be learned per adjective (e.g. good at, afraid of, interested in, keen on, angry with, worried about).
topics.key_idea: Just like certain verbs, certain adjectives are always followed by one particular preposition, and that pairing has to be memorized rather than reasoned out. The same feeling can even take different prepositions depending on what it's directed at — angry at yourself, but angry with someone else.
examples: She's very good at chess.
I'm not interested in politics.
He's proud of his achievements.
We're worried about the exam results.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition with an adjective, or one borrowed from a similar-sounding adjective in another language: 'afraid from the dark' instead of 'afraid of the dark,' or 'interested on' instead of 'interested in.'

topics.formula: since + starting point, normally with present or past perfect, marking when an ongoing duration began. from + starting point, used more broadly, including for future/scheduled starting points, or paired with to/until/till to mark both a start and an end point.
topics.key_idea: Both mark a starting point, but since is specifically tied to talking about an ongoing duration with perfect tenses — how long something has been true, counting from that point. From is more general-purpose and doesn't require that ongoing-duration meaning at all; it's the one used for scheduled changes, timetables, or whenever a clear endpoint (to, until, till) is also being given.
examples: I've been a member since 2015.
The store is open from nine to five.
She's lived here since she was ten.
The offer is valid from Monday.
common_mistakes: Using since where from fits better, especially with a to/until endpoint or a non-perfect tense: 'I work since 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.' instead of 'I work from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.'

topics.formula: number + singular noun (hyphenated) + noun, as a compound adjective — the measurement noun stays singular, never plural, even though the number is more than one. number + part of the body + -ed, when the noun is a body part.
topics.key_idea: These compound adjectives combine a number with a unit of measurement or a body part, joined by hyphens to show they work as a single describing word. The measurement noun always stays singular, since adjectives don't have plural forms in English, even though it looks like it should match the number. When the noun is a body part specifically, -ed gets added at the end.
examples: A three-week holiday.
A ten-minute walk.
A five-year-old child.
A four-legged table.
common_mistakes: Making the noun plural to match the number: 'a three-weeks course' instead of 'a three-week course' — the noun in a compound adjective is always singular.
Forgetting the -ed when the compound adjective ends in a body part: 'a four-arm robot' instead of 'a four-armed robot.'

topics.formula: would rather / would sooner + base verb (no to), for a present or future preference. Negative: would rather not + base verb. Question: Would + subject + rather + base verb?
topics.key_idea: Would rather (or the less common would sooner) expresses a preference, similar to would prefer, but the verb after it is the bare infinitive, with no to — a common trap since would prefer does take to. Both words mean exactly the same thing, and either can replace the other throughout.
examples: I'd rather stay home tonight.
Would you rather walk or take the bus?
I'd rather not discuss this now.
common_mistakes: Adding to, or using the -ing form, after would rather: 'I'd rather to skip the meeting' or 'I'd rather skipping the meeting' instead of 'I'd rather skip the meeting.'

topics.formula: would rather / would sooner + a different subject + past simple, to say what you'd like someone else to do — the past tense form is used, but the meaning is present or future. Negative: would rather + subject + didn't.
topics.key_idea: This structure only comes into play when the person expressing the preference and the person expected to act are different — as soon as there's a second subject involved, the verb switches to past simple, purely as a grammatical marker, not an actual reference to the past.
examples: I'd rather you told me the truth.
Would you rather we left now?
She'd rather I didn't come with her.
common_mistakes: Using this structure when the subject is the same both times: 'I'd rather I left now' instead of the simpler 'I'd rather leave now,' which is correct when there's only one subject involved.
Putting not before the subject instead of before the verb in the negative: 'I'd rather not you told him' instead of 'I'd rather you didn't tell him.'

topics.formula: preposition + whom + subject + verb, a more formal way to ask a question that would otherwise end in a preposition + who.
topics.key_idea: Moving the preposition to the front of a question, instead of leaving it dangling at the end, is the more formal option — and when it moves to the front, who has to become whom. This pairing (fronted preposition + whom) only really shows up together; whom on its own without a preposition in front sounds old-fashioned in everyday speech.
examples: To whom should I address this letter?
She's the colleague with whom I share an office.
Who did you go with? / With whom did you go?
common_mistakes: Fronting the preposition but keeping who instead of switching to whom: 'With who did he travel?' instead of 'With whom did he travel?'

topics.formula: negative auxiliary/modal + subject + verb, to ask for confirmation of something the speaker already believes, or to express surprise or annoyance. Without a contraction, not goes directly after the subject.
topics.key_idea: A negative question isn't really asking whether something is false — it's usually checking that something the speaker already assumes is true, or reacting with surprise or annoyance that it might not be. The full, uncontracted form moves not to right after the subject rather than attaching it to the auxiliary.
examples: Isn't it a bit late to call?
Doesn't she usually arrive on time?
Wasn't the meeting supposed to start at nine?
common_mistakes: Misplacing not in the uncontracted form: 'Did not she call you back?' instead of 'Did she not call you back?' — not goes after the subject, not right after the auxiliary, when it isn't contracted.

topics.formula: polite opener (Could you tell me...? / Do you know...? / I wonder...) + normal statement word order (subject + verb), not question word order. For yes/no questions with no question word, use if or whether.
topics.key_idea: Indirect questions are the polite version of a direct question, and the key grammar change is that the embedded part stops behaving like a question at all — it goes back to ordinary subject-before-verb order, with no do/does/did. Without a question word to introduce it, if or whether does that job instead.
examples: Could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?
Do you know what time the shop closes?
I wonder why he left so early.
common_mistakes: Keeping question word order or do/does/did inside the embedded question: 'Could you tell me what time is it?' instead of 'Could you tell me what time it is?'

topics.formula: (Yes,/No,) + subject + auxiliary verb, with the OPPOSITE polarity from what was just said, to disagree.
topics.key_idea: This is the disagreeing counterpart to so am I / neither do I — instead of matching the polarity of what someone said, the auxiliary flips it, showing that the speaker's own situation is actually different.
examples: 'I'm not hungry.' 'I am.'
'She didn't call.' 'She did.'
'You won't finish on time.' 'Yes, I will.'
common_mistakes: Matching the same polarity instead of flipping it when disagreeing — the auxiliary's polarity is what signals whether it's agreement or disagreement.

topics.formula: auxiliary verb alone, standing in for a repeated verb phrase within the same sentence, usually linked with but or and. If the first clause has no auxiliary, do/does/did fills in.
topics.key_idea: Rather than repeating the whole verb phrase a second time when contrasting two people or situations in one sentence, English just reuses the auxiliary on its own — the listener understands the rest is implied.
examples: I don't enjoy cooking, but my roommate does.
He can't drive, and neither can his sister.
I thought I had missed the bus, but I hadn't.
common_mistakes: Repeating the full verb phrase instead of just the auxiliary: 'Tom can play the guitar, and Tina can't play the guitar' instead of the more natural 'and Tina can't.'

topics.formula: auxiliary + subject?, echoing the same auxiliary and the same polarity as what was just said, to show interest or surprise — do/does/did if the original sentence had no auxiliary.
topics.key_idea: A reply question isn't really asking for new information — it's a quick, natural way to react to what someone just said, showing you're listening and reacting. It copies the auxiliary and polarity of the original statement exactly, rather than flipping it the way a normal question tag does.
examples: 'Marcus hasn't replied yet.' 'Hasn't he? That's odd.'
'I can fix this myself.' 'Can you? Impressive.'
'She left without saying anything.' 'Did she? How strange.'
common_mistakes: Flipping the polarity as if making a question tag — reply questions keep the same polarity as the original statement, unlike tags added onto the end of your own sentence.

topics.formula: stress the existing auxiliary verb to add emphasis, or insert do/does/did before the base verb in present/past simple sentences that don't normally have an auxiliary — most often used to contradict what someone else has said.
topics.key_idea: To emphasize a verb, especially when contradicting someone, English leans on whatever auxiliary is already there by stressing it. Present and past simple don't have one in a positive sentence, so do/does/did gets inserted purely to carry that emphasis, with the main verb staying in its base form.
examples: 'Why aren't you eating?' 'I am eating!'
'She doesn't trust him.' 'She does trust him. She told me herself.'
'You didn't lock the door.' 'I did lock the door, but it must have come open.'
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add do/does/did for emphasis in present/past simple, and just repeating the plain verb: 'I want to save our marriage' (flat) instead of 'I do want to save our marriage' (emphatic, contradicting someone).

topics.formula: imperative + will you?, for a request. Let's + shall we?, for a suggestion — two fixed exceptions to the normal question tag pattern.
topics.key_idea: Ordinary statements build their tag from the sentence's own auxiliary with flipped polarity, but imperatives and let's suggestions don't have a normal subject and verb to work from, so they use their own fixed tags instead — will you? for a command, shall we? for a suggestion that includes the speaker.
examples: Pass me the salt, will you?
Let's order pizza, shall we?
Turn off the lights, will you?
common_mistakes: Trying to build a normal flipped-polarity tag for an imperative or let's sentence — there's no auxiliary to flip, so will you and shall we are simply the fixed forms for these two cases.

topics.formula: the + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + subject + verb, to link two things that change together. be can be dropped. Works with a comparative noun phrase (the more exercise) or a bare clause (the more you read) too. Shorthand: the + comparative, the better.
topics.key_idea: This doubled structure shows that as one thing increases or decreases, another changes along with it — cause and effect, moving together. Be is often left out when it would otherwise appear, and the pattern flexes to work with adjectives, adverbs, nouns, or a full clause. A common shorthand version drops the second half down to just 'the better,' to say simply that more of something is preferable.
examples: The earlier you book, the cheaper the tickets.
The more languages you speak, the easier travel becomes.
The harder you train, the stronger you get.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the second the, or using a regular comparative sentence instead of the doubled structure: 'Harder he works, more stressed he is' instead of 'The harder he works, the more stressed he is.'

topics.formula: the + adjective (no noun, no plural -s), to refer to a whole group of people sharing that quality — an alternative to adjective + people.
topics.key_idea: A small set of adjectives can stand in for a whole category of people just by adding the in front, with no noun and no plural ending, even though the meaning is plural. This only works for a specific, limited list of adjectives describing groups (the poor, the elderly, the unemployed), not adjectives freely in general.
examples: The government promised new housing for the homeless.
This charity supports the visually impaired.
The wealthy often have access to better healthcare.
common_mistakes: Adding a plural -s to the adjective: 'the poors' instead of 'the poor' — these stay in their plain adjective form, never pluralized.
