topics.formula: the + nationality adjective ending in -ch/-sh/-ese/-ss (the English, the Chinese), or the + plural nationality noun (the Belgians, the Brazilians), to mean 'all the people of that nationality.'
topics.key_idea: Nationality words split into two grammatical types: some are adjectives that only change meaning by adding the (the English), and others are true plural nouns that just add -s (the Belgians). For a single person specifically, the -ch/-sh/-ese/-ss group usually needs -man/-woman added (an Englishman), unless a special separate noun already exists for that nationality (a Spaniard, a Scot).
examples: The Japanese are known for their punctuality.
The Germans invented this technology.
A Norwegian moved in next door.
A Dutchman gave us directions.
common_mistakes: Using a nationality adjective alone for one person without adding -man/-woman or the special noun: 'a French' instead of 'a Frenchman/Frenchwoman,' or 'a Spanish' instead of 'a Spaniard.'

topics.formula: opinion + size + age + shape + colour + origin + material + purpose + noun (often remembered with the mnemonic OSASCOMP). Determiners (a, the, my, this, some, etc.) come before all of it.
topics.key_idea: When more than one adjective describes the same noun, they follow a fairly fixed order rather than a random one — what the speaker thinks of it comes first, and the most fixed, physical facts (like material or purpose) sit closest to the noun. It's rare to actually need more than two or three adjectives at once, but when it happens, this order is what makes the phrase sound natural.
examples: A stunning old wooden cabin.
She wore a beautiful long red dress.
They bought a tiny modern Japanese car.
common_mistakes: Putting a fact adjective before an opinion adjective: 'a modern amazing attic' instead of 'an amazing modern attic' — opinion always comes first when it's paired with a fact adjective.

topics.formula: had been + verb-ing, for a dynamic action that had been going on (continuously or repeatedly) even before the main past event in the story.
topics.key_idea: This is the 'past before the past' version of present perfect continuous — it highlights an ongoing or repeated activity that was already happening, or had just stopped, at the point some other past event took place. It works with dynamic verbs specifically, the same restriction present perfect continuous has.
examples: I was relieved. I had been searching for my passport for an hour.
We had been driving for two hours when we finally saw the sign.
She had been rehearsing the speech for weeks before the event.
common_mistakes: Using past perfect simple when the point is really an ongoing or repeated process leading up to the main event: 'I had waited for him' instead of 'I had been waiting for him,' when the emphasis is on the duration and frustration of the wait itself, not just the fact that it happened.

topics.formula: Adverbs of manner most commonly go in final position. Mid position is mainly literary style, or standard with passive verbs. Initial position is literary only. Well, badly, hard, and fast never go in mid position.
topics.key_idea: Manner adverbs are flexible about where they can go, but not equally so — final position is by far the most natural everyday choice, while mid and initial position both carry a more formal, written, storytelling feel, except with passive verbs, where mid position is completely normal. A handful of common manner adverbs simply refuse mid position altogether.
examples: He answered the questions politely.
The letter was carefully written.
Quietly, she closed the door behind her.
common_mistakes: Placing well, badly, hard, or fast in mid position — these adverbs need final position, unlike most other manner adverbs.

topics.formula: Adverbs of time normally go in final position. They can also go in initial position for emphasis, or to connect and structure a text.
topics.key_idea: Final position is the everyday default for time adverbs, but moving one to the front of the sentence is a deliberate choice — it draws attention to the timing itself, or helps link one sentence to the next as part of a larger narrative.
examples: We'll finish the project eventually.
It got dark very quickly.
Three years later, they finally reunited.
common_mistakes: Overusing initial position for time adverbs without a real reason for emphasis — final position is the more neutral, everyday choice.

topics.formula: Comment (viewpoint) adverbs — obviously, luckily, unfortunately, honestly, ideally, etc. — normally go in initial position, followed by a comma.
topics.key_idea: These adverbs don't describe how an action was done — they express the speaker's own attitude or judgment about the whole sentence, which is exactly why they usually sit outside the main clause, right at the front.
examples: Fortunately, nobody was injured in the accident.
Frankly, I don't think this plan will work.
Surprisingly, the team won the final.
common_mistakes: Confusing a comment adverb with a manner adverb and placing it mid-sentence as if it described the verb: 'We honestly arrived late' (sounds like describing how honestly they arrived) instead of 'Honestly, we arrived late' (the speaker's own comment on the whole situation).

topics.formula: nearly / hardly / quite / rather, etc. → mid position. very / extremely / incredibly, etc. → directly before the adjective or adverb they modify. much / a lot / a bit → after the verb. a little → before the adjective or adverb.
topics.key_idea: Degree adverbs don't all follow one rule — the specific word decides where it goes. Most of the common ones sit in mid position like frequency adverbs, but the strongest intensifiers (very, extremely) always attach directly to the word they're boosting, while much/a lot/a bit trail after the verb instead.
examples: We were almost caught in the rain.
It's extremely difficult to get tickets.
He doesn't complain much.
I'm a little nervous about the interview.
common_mistakes: Placing very or extremely in mid position instead of right before the adjective/adverb — these need to sit directly next to the word they intensify, not floated earlier in the sentence like a frequency adverb.

topics.formula: When multiple adverbs stack at the end of a sentence, the order is usually manner, place, time — except with a verb of movement, where it becomes place, manner, time. A verb and its object can never be separated by an adverb.
topics.key_idea: When several adverbs pile up at the end, there's still a preferred order rather than a free-for-all, and it shifts slightly depending on whether the verb itself describes movement. One rule stays fixed no matter what: an adverb can never wedge itself between a verb and its object.
examples: They danced gracefully on the stage last night.
He walks to work every day.
I like tea a lot.
common_mistakes: Placing an adverb between a verb and its object: 'I like a lot pizza' instead of 'I like pizza a lot,' or 'He speaks very well English' instead of 'He speaks English very well.'

topics.formula: will be + verb-ing, for an action that will be in progress at a specific point in the future. Also used instead of present continuous for a settled future arrangement.
topics.key_idea: Future continuous captures a moment in the future and describes what will already be happening at that exact point — not the whole action, just a snapshot of it in progress. It can also replace present continuous for a firmly planned future event, giving the same 'already decided' meaning with a slightly different tense.
examples: This time tomorrow, we'll be flying to Tokyo.
At noon, I'll be presenting to the board.
We'll be staying with relatives next weekend.
common_mistakes: Using plain will + infinitive when the meaning is really 'in progress at that moment': 'This time next week, we'll travel to Paris' instead of 'we'll be travelling to Paris,' which specifically pictures the journey already underway.

topics.formula: will have + past participle, for an action that will be completed before a specific point in the future. Also used for a duration that will have reached a certain length by that future point (will have been + -ing for continuous duration, or will have + past participle for a stative one).
topics.key_idea: Future perfect looks ahead to a point in the future and looks backward from it, confirming that something will already be finished by then. It works the same way for duration — by a certain future moment, a situation will already have lasted a certain amount of time.
examples: By next spring, they will have finished the renovation.
By the time she's forty, she'll have run ten marathons.
We'll have moved into the new office by December.
common_mistakes: Using future simple instead of future perfect when the meaning is 'already done by then': 'By 2050, researchers will find a cure' instead of 'will have found a cure,' which changes whether the discovery happens before or at that point.

topics.formula: if + present tense (the if-clause) + present tense (the main clause), for something that is always true or always happens under that condition. If can usually be swapped for when with no change in meaning.
topics.key_idea: Zero conditional isn't really about a hypothetical future — it's a general truth or an automatic result, true every time the condition is met, not just once. Because it's describing something universal rather than a specific future possibility, when works just as well as if in almost every case.
examples: If you freeze water, it turns into ice.
When metal is heated, it expands.
If plants don't get sunlight, they die.
common_mistakes: Using will in the main clause, treating it like a first conditional: 'If water reaches 100 degrees, it will boil' instead of 'it boils' — zero conditional describes something that just always happens, with present tense throughout.

topics.formula: Zero conditional (if/when + present, present) = a general truth, true every time. First conditional (if + present, will) = one particular, real possibility.
topics.key_idea: The same event described with these two conditionals means something different — zero conditional treats it as a rule that always plays out that way, while first conditional treats it as a specific, one-time future scenario that may or may not happen.
examples: If you don't sleep enough, you feel tired.
If you don't sleep enough tonight, you'll feel tired tomorrow.
common_mistakes: Mixing the two forms within one sentence — using will with an if-clause meant to express a general truth, or plain present tense in the main clause when the meaning is really about one specific future occasion.

topics.formula: in case + present tense, to describe a precaution taken regardless of whether the possible event happens or not.
topics.key_idea: In case looks similar to if but means something different — an if-action only happens as a response to the condition being true, while an in case action happens beforehand, as a precaution, no matter what ends up happening.
examples: I'll bring an extra charger in case mine runs out.
Take a jacket in case it gets cold.
Write down the address in case you forget it.
common_mistakes: Confusing in case with if: treating 'I'll take my umbrella in case it rains' as meaning the umbrella is only taken if it rains, when the real meaning is that it's taken regardless, purely as a precaution.

topics.formula: when / as soon as / until / before + present perfect (instead of present simple), for a future time clause, to emphasize that the action will be fully completed first.
topics.key_idea: Present perfect can replace present simple after these future time words without changing the basic meaning, but it adds a subtle emphasis on completion — making clear the first action needs to be finished before the second one happens.
examples: I'll leave as soon as I finish this email. / I'll leave as soon as I've finished this email.
We won't start until everyone arrives. / We won't start until everyone has arrived.
common_mistakes: Assuming present perfect is required here rather than optional — present simple works fine in these same sentences; present perfect just adds a stronger sense of 'completely finished first.'

topics.formula: Second and third conditional can use the continuous aspect in either clause when the situation is about something ongoing rather than a single event: past continuous or past perfect continuous in the if-clause, and be + -ing (continuous infinitive) or have been + -ing (perfect continuous infinitive) in the main clause.
topics.key_idea: Conditionals aren't limited to the simple aspect — when the hypothetical situation is really about something in progress rather than a single completed action, the continuous form fits more naturally in either half of the sentence, following the same simple-versus-continuous logic that applies everywhere else in English.
examples: If you weren't studying right now, we could go out.
If it weren't for her, I might not be working here today.
He could have been injured if he hadn't been wearing a seatbelt.
common_mistakes: Assuming conditionals can only use the simple aspect — continuous forms work perfectly well in both the if-clause and the main clause whenever the meaning calls for an ongoing action rather than a single event.

topics.formula: wish + subject + past simple, for something unlikely or impossible right now or in the near future. wish + subject + past perfect, for a past regret. If only works the same way as wish, just more emphatic. Were can replace was after I/he/she/it.
topics.key_idea: Wish reaches for something different from reality, and the tense tells you when: past simple points at the present or near future, wishing things were different right now, while past perfect reaches back and expresses regret about something that already happened. If only carries the exact same grammar, just with more emotional weight.
examples: I wish I had more free time.
We wish we lived closer to the beach.
I wish I hadn't sold my old car.
If only you had told me sooner.
common_mistakes: Using present tense instead of past simple/perfect after wish: 'I wish I have more time' instead of 'I wish I had more time' — wish always pulls the verb one step back into the past, regardless of the actual time being talked about.

topics.formula: wish + person/thing + would + infinitive, for something that's currently annoying the speaker and that they want to change or stop. Cannot be used to wish about the speaker's own behavior.
topics.key_idea: This version of wish is specifically about frustration with a habit or ongoing situation — usually someone else's behavior, or something like the weather — and expresses a desire for it to change or stop, not just a general 'I wish things were different.' It can never be used to wish about oneself.
examples: I wish you would stop interrupting me.
I wish it would stop snowing.
If only they would answer their phone.
common_mistakes: Using this structure to wish about oneself: 'I wish I would stop biting my nails' instead of 'I wish I didn't bite my nails' or 'I wish I could stop biting my nails' — wish + would only works for someone or something other than the speaker.

topics.formula: A handful of feeling adjectives don't pair with a regular -ing form for the 'causing' meaning — they use a separate, irregular adjective instead: offended → offensive, stressed → stressful, delighted → delightful, impressed → impressive, scared → scary.
topics.key_idea: The -ed/-ing pattern is reliable for most feeling verbs, but a few common ones break from it — instead of adding -ing to make the 'causing' version, English uses a completely different adjective ending, often -ive or -ful, that has to be learned separately rather than derived from the rule.
examples: That comment was offensive.
This deadline is stressful.
It was a delightful evening.
The results were impressive.
common_mistakes: Applying the regular -ing rule to these words: 'a stressing job' or 'an offending comment' instead of 'a stressful job' or 'an offensive comment.'

topics.formula: would + infinitive, an alternative to used to for repeated past actions — but NOT for past states or situations (stative verbs), where only used to works.
topics.key_idea: Would offers another way to talk about a repeated habit from the past, similar to used to, but it's more limited: it only works for actions someone did again and again, never for a state or situation that was simply true back then. Used to covers both cases, which is why it's the safer, more flexible default when in doubt.
examples: Every summer, we would visit our grandparents' farm.
My uncle would always bring us gifts when he came to visit.
We would go for long walks by the lake.
common_mistakes: Using would for a past state instead of a repeated action: 'I would be blond as a child' or 'I would live with my mum' instead of 'I used to be blond' / 'I used to live with my mum' — would only works for repeated actions, never states.

topics.formula: need + to + infinitive = it's necessary to do something (active). need + -ing = the same meaning, but with a passive sense (something needs to be done to it), used for things needing to be dealt with.
topics.key_idea: Need follows the same to-infinitive pattern as most verbs meaning something is necessary, but it has a second, passive option — need + -ing — that only makes sense when the subject is the thing receiving the action, not doing it. 'Your car needs cleaning' means someone needs to clean it, not that the car itself needs to do any cleaning.
examples: I need to renew my passport.
This wall needs painting.
The carpet needs vacuuming.
common_mistakes: Using need + -ing when the subject is actually doing the action, not receiving it: 'I need seeing you' instead of 'I need to see you' — the passive -ing form only works when the subject is the one something is being done to.

topics.formula: must have + past participle, confident something WAS true or happened. can't/couldn't have + past participle, confident something did NOT happen or wasn't true — never mustn't have.
topics.key_idea: This is the past-tense version of must/can't for deduction — instead of speculating about now, it looks back and draws a confident conclusion about something that already happened, based on evidence available now. The negative still follows can't, never mustn't, exactly as it does for present deduction.
examples: I can't find my umbrella! I must have left it on the bus.
You can't have finished already; it's only been five minutes.
She can't have forgotten; she never forgets appointments.
common_mistakes: Using mustn't have instead of can't/couldn't have for a confident negative deduction about the past: 'She mustn't have passed the test' instead of 'She can't have passed the test.'

topics.formula: could have + past participle = something was possible in the past but didn't happen. could/might/may have + past participle = it's possible (uncertain) that something did happen. Negative: might not/may not have — never could not have for this meaning.
topics.key_idea: Could have does double duty here — it can describe an unrealized possibility from the past (something that could have happened but didn't), or, alongside might/may have, express genuine uncertainty about whether something actually did happen. For the negative version of that uncertainty, might not or may not is needed; could not have doesn't work the same way.
examples: You could have called to say you'd be late.
They might have already left by now.
She may not have received the email yet.
common_mistakes: Using could not have instead of might not/may not have to express negative uncertainty about the past: 'She could not have heard us' (sounds like a confident deduction that she didn't) when the intended meaning was uncertain possibility, 'might not have heard us.'

topics.formula: should have / ought to have + past participle, for something that was expected to happen but didn't (or shouldn't have happened but did) — commonly used for criticism or regret.
topics.key_idea: This structure looks back at what would have been the right or expected action and points out that reality didn't match it, which is exactly why it so often comes across as criticism, whether directed at someone else or at oneself.
examples: You should have double-checked the numbers before submitting.
He ought to have apologized sooner.
You ought to have asked for permission first.
common_mistakes: Using should/ought to alone (without have) when talking about the past: 'You should already finish the report' instead of 'You should have already finished the report' — have is essential to shift the meaning into the past.

topics.formula: be bound/sure + to + infinitive, to express strong certainty about the future. there is/are bound/sure to be, for certainty that something will exist.
topics.key_idea: Bound and sure both express a very high degree of confidence about what will happen, functioning as adjectives rather than modal verbs, always paired with to and an infinitive.
examples: This plan is bound to fail if we don't prepare properly.
The concert is sure to sell out quickly.
There are bound to be delays during rush hour.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to before the infinitive: 'He is bound win' instead of 'He is bound to win.'

topics.formula: It is likely/unlikely that + clause. Subject + be likely/unlikely + to + infinitive. Can take comparative/superlative forms or degree words (very, quite) since likely/unlikely are ordinary adjectives.
topics.key_idea: Likely and unlikely are regular adjectives, not modals, which is exactly why they behave like other adjectives — they take very or quite in front, and they have comparative and superlative forms, none of which a modal verb could ever do.
examples: It's likely that the meeting will be postponed.
She is likely to get the promotion.
They are unlikely to change their minds.
common_mistakes: Mixing the two structures together: 'It's likely to that he wins' instead of choosing either 'It's likely that he will win' or 'He is likely to win,' not a blend of both.

topics.formula: In affirmative sentences: after the auxiliary (or before the main verb if there's no auxiliary). In negative sentences with a contraction: before the auxiliary. In negative sentences without a contraction: after the auxiliary, before not.
topics.key_idea: Definitely and probably follow the same mid-position logic as frequency adverbs in positive sentences, but their placement shifts in the negative depending on whether the auxiliary is contracted — contracted negatives put them first, but the full, uncontracted form squeezes them in between the auxiliary and not.
examples: She'll definitely be at the party.
He's probably still at the office.
They probably won't notice the difference.
We will definitely not be attending.
common_mistakes: Using the same position for both the contracted and uncontracted negative: 'They won't probably find any evidence' instead of 'They probably won't find any evidence.'

topics.formula: would prefer + noun or to + infinitive, for a specific, one-time preference. Can add rather than or instead of + infinitive without to, to show the alternative being passed over.
topics.key_idea: Would prefer works like would rather but takes a to-infinitive instead of a bare one, and it's specifically about a choice on this particular occasion, not a general lifelong preference. Rather than and instead of both introduce the option being rejected, and rather than specifically pairs with a bare infinitive, not a to-infinitive.
examples: I would prefer to take the train rather than fly.
I'd prefer to stay in instead of going out tonight.
He would prefer to wait rather than rush the decision.
common_mistakes: Using to after rather than: 'I would prefer to be early rather than to be late' instead of 'rather than be late' — rather than takes the bare infinitive, without to.

topics.formula: prefer + noun or -ing verb, for a general, ongoing preference (not tied to one occasion). prefer X to Y, where to is a preposition, so a following verb takes the -ing form.
topics.key_idea: Plain prefer (without would) is for describing what someone generally likes better, across every occasion, not just right now. When comparing two specific options with to, that to behaves like a preposition rather than part of an infinitive, which is why the verb after it needs -ing.
examples: I prefer tea to coffee.
She prefers reading to watching TV.
common_mistakes: Using the bare or to-infinitive after prefer X to instead of -ing: 'He prefers walking to cycle' instead of 'He prefers walking to cycling' — to here is a preposition, needing the -ing form after it.

topics.formula: look/smell/taste/sound/feel + adjective, to describe a quality directly. + like + noun, to compare it to something. + as if/as though + clause (or informally, + like + clause), to describe an impression using a full clause.
topics.key_idea: These sense verbs link the subject to a description in three different ways depending on what follows — a plain adjective describes the quality itself, like introduces a noun for comparison, and as if or as though (or informally, like) opens up a full clause to describe a fuller impression or guess about the situation.
examples: This bread tastes strange.
That sounds like a great idea.
You look as if you've seen a ghost.
He sounds like he's had a rough day.
common_mistakes: Using like before an adjective instead of before a noun or clause: 'You sound like nervous' instead of 'You sound nervous' — an adjective attaches directly, with no like needed.

topics.formula: It + is/was/has been + past participle of a reporting verb (say, believe, think, report, etc.) + that + clause, to report something without committing to whether it's true — common in news and formal writing.
topics.key_idea: This structure lets a writer or speaker pass along information while staying at arm's length from it — it doesn't say who exactly believes or reports it, just that it's generally claimed or thought. It works with any tense of be, matching the reporting verb's own timing.
examples: It is believed that the ancient city lies beneath the desert.
It has been reported that the company is planning layoffs.
It was rumored that the deal had fallen through.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the passive be, using the reporting verb actively without a clear subject: 'Is said that they are in Las Vegas' instead of 'It is said that they are in Las Vegas.'

topics.formula: subject + is/are/was/were + past participle of reporting verb + to + infinitive (same time or future), + to be + -ing (in progress at the same time), or + to have + past participle (earlier than the reporting).
topics.key_idea: This is the second way to distance a claim from its source, putting the real subject at the front instead of it, which is exactly why an infinitive has to follow the reporting verb instead of a full clause. Which infinitive form to use depends purely on timing: plain to + infinitive for something happening now or later, to be + -ing for something in progress, and to have + past participle for something that already happened before the reporting itself.
examples: The chef is said to have trained in Paris.
She is expected to win the award.
They are believed to be hiding in the mountains.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong infinitive form for the timing involved: 'She is thought to leave last week' instead of 'She is thought to have left last week,' since the leaving happened before the reporting.

topics.formula: have/get + object + past participle, for something someone else does for you (paid, asked, or persuaded), usable in any tense. Have isn't an auxiliary here, so do/does/did is needed for negatives and questions. Can also describe something bad happening to you (a negative experience).
topics.key_idea: This structure shifts the focus from who performed an action to who arranged for it or experienced it — the object gets something done to it, without saying exactly who did the doing. Have is the standard choice, get the more informal one, and the same structure extends beyond services paid for to negative experiences that simply happened to someone.
examples: We're having the kitchen renovated.
You should get your blood pressure checked.
He had his bike stolen outside the station.
common_mistakes: Treating have as an auxiliary in this structure: 'Haven't you your house painted?' instead of 'Don't you have your house painted?' — do/does/did is needed here, since have is acting as a main verb, not an auxiliary.

topics.formula: have + person + bare infinitive (no to), when naming who does something for you. get + person + to + infinitive, for the same idea, often implying persuasion was needed.
topics.key_idea: These say the same basic thing as have/get something done, but they name the actual person doing the work instead of leaving them unnamed. The grammar differs slightly between the two: have takes a bare infinitive, while get needs to, and get often carries a hint that some convincing was involved.
examples: We had a plumber fix the leak.
I got my sister to proofread my essay.
She had her assistant book the flights.
common_mistakes: Adding to after have, or forgetting it after get: 'We had the plumber to fix the sink' instead of 'had the plumber fix the sink,' or 'I got a friend help me move' instead of 'I got a friend to help me move.'

topics.formula: having + past participle (perfect gerund), to emphasize that the -ing action was already completed before the time being talked about. Often interchangeable with the plain -ing form when the timing is already clear from context.
topics.key_idea: The perfect gerund makes explicit what the plain -ing form usually leaves implicit — that the action happened and finished before now. When context already makes the sequence obvious, the two forms mean almost the same thing, but perfect gerund adds a bit of emphasis on completion.
examples: He admitted taking the last cookie.
She regretted quitting so early. / She regretted having quit so early.
He denied having broken the vase.
common_mistakes: Assuming the perfect gerund is always required to show past time — in most contexts the plain -ing form already implies the same sequence, and perfect gerund is optional extra emphasis, not a strict grammatical requirement.

topics.formula: what/which/when/where/who/how + ever, meaning 'it doesn't matter which one' — any option from the full range is fine. Whichever specifically implies a limited, defined set of choices, unlike whatever.
topics.key_idea: Adding -ever to a question word turns it into a free-choice word, saying that any option works and the specific choice genuinely doesn't matter. Most of these words work the same way across a general, open-ended range, but whichever stands apart slightly — it's used when there's a limited, known set of options to pick from, not an unlimited range.
examples: Choose whatever flavor you like.
Call me whenever you're ready.
You can sit wherever there's space.
Whoever finishes first can leave early.
common_mistakes: Using whatever when the options are actually limited and known: 'Choose whatever destination' instead of 'Choose whichever destination' when picking from a specific, defined list of choices.

topics.formula: everything / everybody, not all alone, as the subject of a sentence meaning 'every person/thing.'
topics.key_idea: All can't stand completely alone as a sentence's subject the way everything or everybody can — it always needs either a noun right after it or of + a pronoun/determiner attached. When there's truly nothing else to attach it to, everything or everybody takes over instead.
examples: Everything was ruined by the storm.
Everybody enjoyed the concert.
common_mistakes: Using all by itself as a subject: 'All is big in the U.S.' instead of 'Everything is big in the U.S.'

topics.formula: all + day/night/week/month/year, etc. (no article, no preposition), meaning 'the entire' period.
topics.key_idea: This is a fixed pattern for talking about a whole stretch of time — no article and no preposition go with it, unlike most other time expressions.
examples: We worked all night to finish the project.
It rained all week.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition or article before this pattern: 'We didn't see them in all the day' instead of 'We didn't see them all day.'

topics.formula: either of / neither of + plural noun can take a singular OR plural verb (plural is more informal). In either...or / neither...nor with mismatched number, the verb usually agrees with the closer element.
topics.key_idea: The strict singular-verb rule for either and neither loosens up a bit in practice — when a plural noun follows either of or neither of, a plural verb is common informally too. And when either...or or neither...nor connects a singular and a plural item, the verb typically matches whichever one is physically closest to it.
examples: Neither of the applicants is/are qualified.
Either Sara or her brothers is/are coming to help.
Neither Tom nor his colleagues is/are happy with the decision.
common_mistakes: Rigidly forcing a singular verb in every either/neither construction — plural agreement is genuinely acceptable, especially informally, once a plural noun is directly involved.

topics.formula: already goes in mid position: before the main verb, after be (when it's the only verb), after the first auxiliary/modal, or after the subject in questions. In already vs yet questions: already asks about something the speaker expects or suspects already happened; yet asks with no assumption either way.
topics.key_idea: Already usually sits in the same mid-position spot frequency adverbs do, though informal speech sometimes moves it to the very end instead. In questions specifically, already and yet aren't interchangeable in meaning — already signals the speaker already suspects or expects the answer is yes, often with a note of surprise at the timing, while yet is a neutral, genuinely open question.
examples: She has already left for the airport.
I've already eaten, thanks.
Have you already submitted the application? That was fast!
Have you submitted the application yet?
common_mistakes: Using already in a negative sentence: 'It isn't already dark' instead of 'It isn't dark yet' — already belongs in questions and affirmative sentences, not negatives.

topics.formula: still = a situation continuing, unchanged — same mid position as already, but in negative sentences it goes before the negative verb specifically. Often used with present perfect to show surprise or impatience, especially in the negative — a stronger, more emotional cousin of yet.
topics.key_idea: Still marks something as ongoing rather than newly happening, and its position shifts slightly in negatives, sitting right before the negative verb rather than after it. When still and yet both work in a negative sentence, they say almost the same thing, but still adds a layer of surprise or impatience that plain yet doesn't carry.
examples: He's still working on the report.
I still don't understand this rule.
She still hasn't replied.
She hasn't replied yet. / She still hasn't replied.
common_mistakes: Placing still after the negative verb like a normal mid-position adverb: 'She hasn't still arrived' instead of 'She still hasn't arrived' — still specifically goes before the negative verb.

topics.formula: British English typically pairs already/yet with present perfect. American English commonly pairs them with past simple instead.
topics.key_idea: This is purely a regional difference in which tense feels natural alongside already and yet — both versions are understood everywhere, but British speakers lean toward present perfect and American speakers toward past simple for the exact same meaning.
examples: I've already booked the tickets. / I already booked the tickets.
Have you finished the assignment yet? / Did you finish the assignment yet?
common_mistakes: Assuming one version is 'more correct' than the other — this is a dialect preference, not a grammar rule with a right and wrong answer.

topics.formula: needn't + infinitive (no to) = don't need to + infinitive, for present absence of necessity. Needn't is more formal/British, often used to give permission not to do something. Don't need to is preferred for general, non-specific necessity.
topics.key_idea: Need behaves as both a normal verb (don't need to) and a modal verb (needn't) with basically the same present-tense meaning, though needn't leans more formal and British, and specifically suits giving someone permission to skip something right now. For a general truth about necessity rather than one specific situation, don't need to is the more natural choice.
examples: You needn't bring anything; we have everything covered.
You don't need to bring anything; we have everything covered.
Employees don't need to work weekends.
common_mistakes: Using needn't for a general statement rather than a specific occasion: 'People needn't get a degree' sounds less natural than 'People don't need to get a degree' for a broad, general claim.

topics.formula: needn't have + past participle = something was done, but turned out to be unnecessary. didn't need to + infinitive = something wasn't necessary, and (usually) wasn't done.
topics.key_idea: These look like simple past-tense versions of needn't and don't need to, but they mean genuinely different things. Needn't have specifically describes an action that did happen, only for it to turn out unnecessary in hindsight. Didn't need to is more neutral about whether the action happened at all — it usually implies it simply wasn't done, because it wasn't required.
examples: You needn't have printed all these documents.
You didn't need to print all these documents.
Since the room was already clean, I didn't need to tidy it.
common_mistakes: Using needn't have to describe something that didn't happen: 'He started to feel better, so I needn't have called the doctor' sounds like the doctor was called unnecessarily, when the intended meaning was that the doctor was never called at all — didn't need to is correct there instead.

topics.formula: quite + gradable adjective/adverb = 'less than very, but to a large degree.' quite + non-gradable (extreme) adjective = 'completely, absolutely.' quite + a/an + noun (or adjective+noun) = an intensifier before a noun phrase. quite a few/a lot/a bit = a larger amount.
topics.key_idea: Quite genuinely changes meaning depending on what kind of adjective follows it — with an ordinary, scalable adjective it's a moderate booster, but with an extreme, all-or-nothing adjective it means something closer to 'completely.' It also works before noun phrases (always with an article) and can boost a few/a lot/a bit to suggest a bigger quantity.
examples: The film was quite entertaining.
I'm quite certain we've met before.
That was quite an achievement.
Quite a lot of people attended.
common_mistakes: Reading quite the same way regardless of the adjective type: 'quite good' means moderately good, but 'quite amazing' means completely amazing — the adjective itself determines which meaning applies.

topics.formula: rather + adjective/adverb, more formal than pretty, often adding intensity to something negative, or emphasizing something unexpectedly positive. rather + a + noun, or a + rather + noun, before a noun phrase. rather + verb, for opinions (mainly British English).
topics.key_idea: Rather is flexible in tone — it commonly sharpens a negative or lukewarm judgment, but it can just as easily emphasize something surprisingly good. Before a noun, the article can go either right before or right after rather, and rather can even attach directly to certain opinion verbs, a pattern more common in British than American English.
examples: The service was rather slow.
His performance was rather impressive.
We've had rather a busy week. / We've had a rather busy week.
I rather doubt he'll show up.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the article when rather modifies a full noun phrase: 'We've had rather dull morning' instead of 'We've had rather a dull morning' or 'We've had a rather dull morning.'

topics.formula: pretty + adjective/adverb (informal, moderate-to-large degree). fairly + adjective/adverb (the weakest of these intensifiers, 'acceptable but not very'). Before adjective+noun: pretty needs an article right before it (a pretty busy day); fairly's article goes before fairly itself too (a fairly common surname).
topics.key_idea: Pretty and fairly sit at different points on the intensity scale — pretty leans stronger and more casual, fairly is the mildest of this whole group, closer to 'acceptable' than 'impressive.' Both need an article directly in front of them when modifying a full noun phrase, unlike rather, which allows the article in two different spots.
examples: The exam was pretty tough.
We had a pretty good time.
The town is fairly small.
It was a fairly straightforward task.
common_mistakes: Placing the article after pretty or fairly instead of before: 'pretty a busy day' instead of 'a pretty busy day.'

topics.formula: In a future time clause, present simple can mean an action happening AT THE SAME TIME as the main clause event, while present perfect specifically means the time-clause action is COMPLETED FIRST, before the main clause event. When both readings make equal sense, either form works with little difference; when they'd produce a real ambiguity, present perfect resolves it. Present perfect cannot be used when the two events genuinely happen as one and the same, essentially simultaneous action.
topics.key_idea: The simple-vs-perfect choice in a future time clause isn't just a formality — it can genuinely change what's being said, since present perfect specifically signals that the first action finishes before the second one starts. When a sentence could be read either way (during or after), present perfect removes the ambiguity by clearly ruling out the 'during' reading. But when the two clauses are really describing the same single moment, only present simple works.
examples: I'll relax when I finish this chapter. / I'll relax when I've finished this chapter.
We can leave when the guests arrive.
When I graduate, I'll travel for a year.
common_mistakes: Assuming present simple and present perfect are always interchangeable in these clauses — sometimes the choice genuinely changes the meaning (simultaneous vs sequential), and using present perfect for two genuinely simultaneous events, like 'When I've called Jack, I'll invite him,' sounds wrong.

topics.formula: Standard English uses only one negative word per clause. A negative verb (don't/isn't/etc.) pairs with any-words (anything, anybody, anywhere, ever) or a positive word (some), not with no-words (nothing, nobody, nowhere, never, no, none).
topics.key_idea: In standard English, stacking two negative words together doesn't add extra negation — it's simply considered incorrect, even though many languages do use double negatives correctly, and native speakers use them informally too, especially in music and casual speech. Once a sentence already has a negative verb, everything after it switches to the any- family instead of the no- family.
examples: I don't want anything.
She didn't go anywhere last weekend.
I don't have any siblings.
They never say anything nice.
common_mistakes: Combining a negative verb with a no-word: 'We didn't see nobody' instead of 'We didn't see anybody' or 'We saw nobody' — pick one negative, not both.

topics.formula: A deliberate double negative (not + a negative word or negative-prefix adjective) gives a softer, more nuanced meaning than a plain positive — different from the accidental double negative that's simply a mistake. Negative-prefix adjectives (unusual, impossible, inappropriate) inside a negative sentence are always fine and don't count as an error.
topics.key_idea: Not every double negative is wrong — when it's clearly intentional, it creates a careful, hedged meaning that's different from and more nuanced than just saying the positive outright. This is completely separate from adjectives or adverbs that happen to start with a negative prefix (un-, im-, in-); using one of those inside an otherwise negative sentence is always correct, since the prefix is part of the word itself, not a second negation stacked on the sentence's grammar.
examples: It's not that I didn't enjoy the trip, but it was exhausting.
I can't not mention how proud I am of you.
It's not unusual for prices to rise in December.
Her answer wasn't unreasonable at all.
common_mistakes: Confusing an intentional, nuanced double negative with the ungrammatical kind — the correct version uses not with a full negative-prefix word or a deliberately structured clause, not a no-word like nothing or nobody stacked onto a negative verb.

topics.formula: have + noun, meaning 'take' (a shower, a meal, a lesson), 'give' (a party), 'encounter' (trouble, difficulty), or 'experience/enjoy' (fun, a good time, weather). In these meanings, have is dynamic, so it works fine in continuous forms, and needs do/does/did for questions and negatives.
topics.key_idea: Have is enormously flexible, taking on a completely different practical meaning depending on the noun that follows it — none of these actually mean 'possess.' Because these uses describe an action or activity rather than a state, have behaves like an ordinary dynamic verb here, unlike the possession meaning of have, which is stative and can't go in the continuous.
examples: I'm going to have a swim before breakfast.
We're having a barbecue this weekend.
Did you have any difficulty finding parking?
We had a great time at the reunion.
common_mistakes: Treating every use of have as stative (possession) and avoiding the continuous form: 'I have a lot of problems with my new computer' instead of 'I'm having a lot of problems,' when the meaning is really 'experiencing,' a dynamic sense.

topics.formula: haven't + noun (dropping got entirely), an older-fashioned way to express negative possession — mainly heard in British English, in fixed phrases.
topics.key_idea: In a small number of set expressions, got can disappear from haven't got altogether while the possession meaning stays exactly the same, though this style now sounds a bit dated or very British.
examples: I haven't time to explain right now.
I haven't a clue what happened.
I haven't the faintest idea where he went.
common_mistakes: Assuming got must always follow haven't for possession — while it's the most common pattern, dropping it is genuinely correct too, if slightly old-fashioned.

topics.formula: to have + past participle (perfect infinitive), to show that the action happened before the time of the main verb.
topics.key_idea: The perfect infinitive shifts the timing of an infinitive one step into the past relative to the main verb, similar to how the perfect gerund works for -ing forms — it marks that whatever's being described was already finished by the time of the main action.
examples: I'm relieved to have finished the exam.
He claimed to have witnessed the accident.
She seems to have forgotten our meeting.
common_mistakes: Using a plain infinitive when the meaning is really 'before the main verb's time': 'He pretended to lose my number' instead of 'He pretended to have lost my phone number,' which shifts the losing to before the pretending.

topics.formula: yet (meaning 'but'), + subject + verb, usually after a comma or and. while/whereas + clause, at the start or middle of a sentence, to contrast two facts or ideas — largely interchangeable.
topics.key_idea: These add two more ways to signal contrast beyond however and although. Yet works almost like a stronger but, most naturally mid-sentence after a comma. While and whereas both set two facts side by side to highlight how they differ, and can usually be swapped for each other freely.
examples: The task was simple, yet it took hours to complete.
While I respect his opinion, I disagree with it.
My brother enjoys hiking, whereas I prefer swimming.
common_mistakes: Confusing this contrastive yet with the completion-related yet used with present perfect ('haven't finished yet') — they're unrelated meanings of the same spelling.

topics.formula: in order for + someone/something + to + infinitive, when the person or thing doing the purpose-action is different from the sentence's main subject.
topics.key_idea: Plain in order to assumes the same subject is doing both actions, but when a different person or thing needs to be involved in achieving the purpose, for names them explicitly right after in order.
examples: We need more volunteers in order for the event to succeed.
She simplified the instructions in order for beginners to follow along.
common_mistakes: Using plain in order to when a different subject is actually involved: 'We need to mobilize the media in order to listen to us' doesn't make sense — for the Government has to be inserted to name who's actually being asked to listen.

topics.formula: (used) for + -ing verb, to describe what an object or action is generally for — its function or purpose.
topics.key_idea: This is a different job for for than the purpose-of-an-action use covered elsewhere — here it explains what something is made or intended for in general, often with used made explicit or implied.
examples: This device is (used) for measuring humidity.
The room is used for storing old furniture.
common_mistakes: Using to + infinitive without used to describe an object's function: 'This knife is to cut plastic' sounds unnatural — for + -ing works on its own, while to + infinitive normally needs used in front of it in this context.

topics.formula: owing to / on account of + noun, additional formal alternatives to due to and because of, all meaning the same thing.
topics.key_idea: These simply add to the growing list of formal ways to introduce a reason before a noun — due to, because of, owing to, and on account of are all interchangeable, differing only in how formal or old-fashioned they sound.
examples: The flight was delayed owing to bad weather.
She left the meeting early on account of a family emergency.
common_mistakes: Following owing to or on account of with a full clause instead of a noun — like due to and because of, these need a noun phrase, not a subject+verb clause.

topics.formula: so + clause, at the end of a sentence, informal. for this reason, at the start of a new sentence, followed by a comma. as a result / consequently / therefore, more formal, usually starting a sentence with a comma, but consequently/therefore can also go in mid position (before the verb, after be, or after the first auxiliary).
topics.key_idea: These all express the same basic idea — this is why something happened — arranged along a scale from casual (so) to quite formal (consequently, therefore), with formality generally paired with starting a fresh sentence rather than joining onto the same one. Consequently and therefore are flexible enough to slot into mid position too, unlike the others.
examples: I overslept, so I missed the bus.
Sales have dropped significantly. For this reason, the company is cutting costs.
The bridge was damaged in the storm. As a result, traffic was rerouted.
He has therefore decided to resign.
common_mistakes: Treating all of these as equally interchangeable regardless of register — so fits casual speech, while consequently and therefore are reserved for more formal writing.

topics.formula: one / you / we, to talk about people in general, not one specific person. One is the most formal and rarely spoken; one's is its possessive form. Whichever pronoun is chosen, it should stay consistent throughout a piece of writing.
topics.key_idea: All three of these can step outside their normal, specific meaning to make a general statement about people as a whole. One sounds noticeably more formal and old-fashioned than you or we, and is mostly reserved for writing, though its possessive one's shows up a bit more often. Whichever one is chosen, switching between them mid-text reads as inconsistent.
examples: One should always be polite to strangers.
You never know what tomorrow will bring.
We must accept that mistakes happen.
Honesty always shapes one's reputation.
common_mistakes: Switching between generic pronouns within the same piece of writing — pick one and keep it consistent throughout.

topics.formula: they, for a general or unspecified group not including the speaker/listener (people in charge, people in a place). they/them/their, informally, for one person of unknown or unspecified gender — very common after words like someone, everyone, nobody.
topics.key_idea: They does double duty for generic reference. On its own, it points to some vague 'they' in charge or in a place, without naming who exactly. It also works for a single person when their gender isn't known or doesn't matter, especially following an indefinite pronoun like someone or everyone — a widely used pattern, even though some traditional grammar guides object to it.
examples: They say it's going to be a cold winter.
They're building a new stadium downtown.
Anyone who wants to join should bring their own equipment.
Somebody left their bag on the train.
common_mistakes: Assuming singular they is always ungrammatical — it's extremely common in both speech and writing, especially after indefinite pronouns, even though some traditional style guides discourage it.

topics.formula: Object pronouns (not reflexive) after prepositions of place (in front of, behind, near, etc.), and after with when it means 'accompanied by' — even when they refer back to the subject.
topics.key_idea: The general rule that a reflexive follows a preposition referring back to the subject has two real exceptions: prepositions describing physical location use an ordinary object pronoun instead, and with specifically stays as an object pronoun when it means 'together with,' rather than switching to a reflexive form.
examples: She placed her bag on the table in front of her.
They left their shoes behind them.
He took his daughter with him to the market.
common_mistakes: Using a reflexive pronoun after a preposition of place or after with meaning 'accompanied by': 'in front of herself' or 'with himself' instead of 'in front of her' / 'with him.'

topics.formula: each other's / one another's, the possessive form of the reciprocal pronouns, showing something belongs mutually to both parties.
topics.key_idea: Just like ordinary nouns, each other and one another can take a possessive 's, letting them describe something that belongs to or is shared between the two parties involved.
examples: The dancers borrowed each other's costumes.
The colleagues respected one another's opinions.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the apostrophe-s, or misplacing it: 'each others arms' instead of 'each other's arms.'

topics.formula: there + be, usable in any tense, with modals, in the passive, or as there seem(s) to be / there tend(s) to be / there is/are sure/likely/bound to be. there used to be, negative: there didn't use to be.
topics.key_idea: There + be isn't limited to plain present or past — it flexes into every tense and modal combination the same way an ordinary sentence would, and it also pairs with a small set of fixed follow-up verbs (seem, tend) or certainty expressions (sure, likely, bound) to add nuance about how confident the speaker is.
examples: There will be fireworks tonight.
There has been a lot of confusion about the schedule.
There must be a reason for the delay.
There used to be a cinema on this street.
common_mistakes: Limiting there + be to just present/past simple — it works with modals, passive voice, and perfect/continuous forms just as naturally as an ordinary sentence would.

topics.formula: there is no use/point (in) + -ing = it's pointless to do something. there is no need (for someone) + to-infinitive = something isn't necessary. It's no use + -ing is an equally valid alternative to there is no use + -ing, using it as the preparatory subject instead.
topics.key_idea: These are fixed expressions for dismissing an action as pointless or unnecessary — no use and no point both take the -ing form, while no need switches to a to-infinitive instead, and can optionally name who the lack of necessity applies to.
examples: There is no point in arguing about this.
There is no use complaining now.
There is no need to apologize.
It's no use trying to convince him.
common_mistakes: Using a to-infinitive after no use/no point, or -ing after no need — mixing up which grammar pattern goes with which expression.

topics.formula: It + be/seem + adjective (or noun) + to + infinitive, or + that + clause, when the real subject is long — the infinitive or clause is postponed to the end, and it fills the empty subject position at the front.
topics.key_idea: English generally avoids starting a sentence with a long, heavy subject, so it steps in as a placeholder up front while the real subject — a to-infinitive phrase or a whole that-clause — moves to the end, where it reads more naturally.
examples: It's important to arrive early.
It would be wonderful to visit Japan someday.
It's surprising that she agreed so quickly.
It's a pity that you can't join us.
common_mistakes: Trying to start the sentence with the long infinitive or clause instead of using it: 'To hear from you again is nice' is grammatically possible but sounds much less natural than 'It's nice to hear from you again.'

topics.formula: It takes (someone) + a length of time + to + infinitive, to say how long something requires.
topics.key_idea: This is a fixed way of expressing duration needed for a task, with it as the placeholder subject standing in for the whole activity being timed.
examples: It takes about twenty minutes to walk to the station.
How long does it take to learn a new language?
common_mistakes: Dropping it, or misordering the parts — this structure always needs it at the start, with the time expression coming before the to-infinitive.

topics.formula: It + be + the emphasized element + who/that + the rest of the sentence, to single out and stress one specific part of a statement.
topics.key_idea: A cleft sentence takes an ordinary statement and splits it apart to shine a spotlight on just one piece of it — the person, thing, or detail placed right after it was/is gets all the emphasis, as if answering an implied 'who/what/when exactly?'
examples: It was Elena who organized the surprise party.
It's my laptop that keeps crashing.
It was last summer that they got married.
common_mistakes: Using this structure without a clear element to emphasize — cleft sentences exist specifically to highlight one piece of information, so they read oddly if there's nothing particular being singled out.

topics.formula: get + past participle, an informal alternative to be + past participle for passive voice — especially common for things that happen unexpectedly or unfortunately.
topics.key_idea: Get can substitute for be in the passive, giving a more casual, dynamic feel, and it's especially natural when describing something sudden, negative, or out of the subject's control, like an accident or a piece of criticism.
examples: He got fired for missing too many deadlines.
She got promoted after just six months.
My car got damaged in the storm.
common_mistakes: Assuming get-passive works identically to be-passive in every context — get-passive is informal and works best for sudden or negative events, and sounds odd in more neutral, formal, or descriptive passive statements.

topics.formula: by the way / incidentally, to introduce something unrelated that just came to mind. anyway / in any case, to return to the main point after a digression, or to add a stronger, clinching reason. as I was saying, to pick back up after being interrupted.
topics.key_idea: These all manage the flow of a conversation around a digression — by the way and incidentally introduce a tangent, while anyway, in any case, and as I was saying bring the conversation back on track, whether after a side note or an actual interruption.
examples: By the way, did you get my message?
Anyway, we finally found a solution.
As I was saying, before we were interrupted...
common_mistakes: Using by the way for something closely connected to the main topic — it specifically signals a shift to something unrelated, not a natural continuation.

topics.formula: actually / in fact / as a matter of fact, to introduce something that contradicts or is more surprising than what was just said or expected.
topics.key_idea: These all flag a bit of a twist — what follows corrects, sharpens, or surprises against the previous statement or a common assumption.
examples: I thought he was shy, but actually, he's quite outgoing.
Everyone assumed the show was cancelled, but in fact, it sold out.
common_mistakes: Using actually just to mean 'currently' or 'right now' — its main discourse function here is signaling a contrast or correction, not simply timing.

topics.formula: after all, to add a supporting reason, or to note something is true despite doubts. at least, to introduce a positive point within something negative, or to soften a claim.
topics.key_idea: Both add a kind of counterbalance to a statement — after all backs up a claim with a reason that should already be obvious, while at least finds something positive to hold onto within an otherwise negative situation, or dials back the certainty of a claim.
examples: Don't blame yourself; after all, you did your best.
The trip was expensive, but at least we made great memories.
He knows the answer, or at least he claims to.
common_mistakes: Confusing their functions — after all supports a point with a reason, while at least specifically softens or finds a silver lining; they aren't interchangeable.

topics.formula: all in all, to sum up after weighing everything about a specific situation. on the whole, to make a general statement, true in most cases.
topics.key_idea: Both wrap things up with an overall judgment, but all in all is used to conclude a specific discussion after considering its various parts, while on the whole makes a broader generalization about what's usually true.
examples: There were a few delays, but all in all, the event went smoothly.
On the whole, customers seem satisfied with the new product.
common_mistakes: Using on the whole for a one-off, specific conclusion instead of a general truth — that's the job all in all does instead.

topics.formula: besides (informal), furthermore (formal), what's more (informal), all used to add extra supporting information to what's just been said.
topics.key_idea: These three all add another point onto an existing statement, but they sit at different points on the formality scale — furthermore belongs in formal writing, while besides and what's more suit everyday conversation.
examples: I don't want to go out tonight; besides, I'm exhausted.
The device is more efficient. Furthermore, it's cheaper to produce.
They found new evidence. What's more, it confirms their theory.
common_mistakes: Using furthermore in casual conversation, where besides or what's more would sound much more natural.

topics.formula: obviously, to introduce something easy to see or understand. basically, to introduce the most essential point. in other words / that is to say, to restate something more simply or precisely.
topics.key_idea: These all help make an idea clearer — obviously flags something that shouldn't need much explanation, basically strips a topic down to its core point, and in other words or that is to say rephrases what's already been said in plainer or more precise terms.
examples: Obviously, we need more funding to finish the project.
Basically, the plan is to launch the product next spring.
He said he needed space; in other words, he wanted to end things.
common_mistakes: Using in other words to introduce genuinely new information rather than a rephrasing of something already said.

topics.formula: otherwise, after an instruction or suggestion, to say what will happen if it isn't followed. regarding / as regards / as far as...is concerned, meaning 'about,' to introduce a topic.
topics.key_idea: These serve two very different jobs — otherwise sets up a consequence for not following advice or an order, while regarding and its formal cousins simply announce what topic is about to be discussed.
examples: Submit the form by Friday; otherwise, your application won't be considered.
Regarding your request, we'll respond within 48 hours.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that as far as needs is/are concerned to complete the phrase, or using otherwise outside this specific consequence structure.

topics.formula: on the other hand, to introduce a contrasting fact or point of view — often paired with on the one hand earlier in the same discussion.
topics.key_idea: This phrase sets up a full-sentence-level contrast, weighing one perspective against another, and it's commonly used together with on the one hand to frame both sides of an issue explicitly.
examples: Working remotely offers flexibility. On the other hand, it can feel isolating.
On the one hand, the salary is attractive. On the other hand, the hours are long.
common_mistakes: Using on the other hand without a clear first point being contrasted — it needs something to be weighed against, whether stated explicitly with on the one hand or simply implied by the previous sentence.

topics.formula: could/might/may + be + -ing, to say it's possible something is happening right now (uncertain, unlike must be + -ing which signals confidence).
topics.key_idea: This is the continuous form of might/may/could for present possibility — it works the same way the simple form does, just applied to something currently in progress rather than a general state.
examples: She might be sleeping right now.
They could be discussing the merger as we speak.
He may be working from the cafe today.
common_mistakes: Using must be + -ing when the meaning is really uncertain rather than confident — might/may/could be + -ing signals real uncertainty, while must be + -ing signals the speaker feels quite sure.

topics.formula: should/ought to + infinitive, for a present or future situation the speaker expects to be true, based on what's normal or known — a different meaning from should for advice.
topics.key_idea: This use of should isn't recommending anything — it's predicting, based on typical patterns or known facts, that something is probably true right now or will happen as expected. It sits alongside must as a way of expressing confidence, just slightly less certain.
examples: The package should arrive by Friday.
She ought to be finished with the exam by now.
common_mistakes: Reading should here as advice rather than expectation: 'He should be home by now' isn't recommending that he be home, it's predicting that he probably already is.

topics.formula: negative/restrictive adverb + auxiliary + subject (+ verb), for emphatic, formal inversion. If there's no auxiliary, do/does/did steps in. Not must always be followed by another element before the inversion begins.
topics.key_idea: Moving a negative or restrictive adverb to the very front of a sentence, for dramatic emphasis, flips the normal subject-verb order into a question-like structure — exactly the same inversion a question uses, including bringing in do/does/did when the sentence wouldn't normally have an auxiliary. Not on its own can never trigger this pattern; it always needs to be paired with something else first (not until, not often, etc.).
examples: Rarely have I seen such dedication.
Under no circumstances should you share this password.
Not once did he apologize.
common_mistakes: Using bare not to trigger inversion: 'Not can we see such great expressions of art' instead of 'Not often can we see such great expressions of art' — not needs a partner word before the inversion.

topics.formula: Hardly / barely / scarcely...when, and no sooner...than, typically used in narratives with past perfect in the inverted clause. No sooner pairs only with than, never that or when.
topics.key_idea: This is a fixed set of narrative structures for saying one thing happened immediately after another, almost always built on past perfect in the inverted half, with a specific connecting word that has to match — no sooner insists on than, while the others pair with when.
examples: Hardly had we sat down when the waiter arrived.
No sooner had the concert started than the power went out.
common_mistakes: Using than or that after hardly/barely/scarcely instead of when, or using when after no sooner instead of than — each of these has one specific partner word, not an interchangeable one.

topics.formula: With only when / only if / not since / not until, a subordinate clause (subject + verb, no inversion) comes first, and the inversion happens in the sentence's main clause instead — never inside the subordinate clause itself.
topics.key_idea: This is the trickiest inversion pattern, because the inverted part isn't right next to the adverbial — it's the sentence's real, main clause that gets flipped, while the subordinate clause right after only when/not until stays in completely normal word order. Checking the sentence without the fronted adverbial first, to find where the real subject and verb are, is the safest way to get this right.
examples: Only when the results arrive will we know the truth.
Not until she called did I realize something was wrong.
common_mistakes: Inverting the subordinate clause instead of the main clause: 'Only when do I sleep, I can forget' instead of 'Only when I sleep, can I forget' — the subordinate clause after only when/not since stays in normal order; it's the main clause that inverts.

topics.formula: seldom / rarely / never + inversion, following the same pattern as other negative adverbials. Never is often paired with present perfect or past perfect when talking about a lifetime experience.
topics.key_idea: These frequency adverbs trigger the exact same inversion as any other negative adverbial when fronted for emphasis, and never specifically tends to pair with a perfect tense when the point is about something that has (or hadn't) happened at any point up to a given time.
examples: Seldom does he complain about anything.
Never had she felt so proud.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to invert after these words when they're placed at the front for emphasis — they follow the same inversion rule as any other negative/restrictive adverbial.

topics.formula: there + is/are + said/believed/thought/etc. (passive reporting verb) + to be, or there + seem(s)/appear(s) + to be/to have been, to distance a claim about something existing.
topics.key_idea: This extends the distancing pattern to existence claims specifically — instead of naming a person or thing as the subject, there fills that role, followed by the same passive reporting verb or seem/appear structure, plus to be (or to have been, for something already in the past).
examples: There are believed to be several survivors.
There seems to have been a misunderstanding.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to be after the reporting verb or seem/appear: 'There are said new leads' instead of 'There are said to be new leads.'

topics.formula: It seems/appears (that) + clause, or the more formal it would seem/appear (that) + clause. Subject + seem/appear + to + infinitive (simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous), matching the timing of what's being described.
topics.key_idea: Seem and appear offer another way to hedge or distance a claim, separate from passive reporting verbs — they don't attribute the information to anyone specific, just present it as an impression. The infinitive form after seem/appear shifts to match timing exactly the same way it does with passive reporting verbs: simple for now or the future, continuous for something ongoing, and perfect (or perfect continuous) for something already completed or ongoing in the past.
examples: It appears that the shipment was delayed.
It would seem that our plan needs adjusting.
The company seems to be recovering from the crisis.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong infinitive form for the timing — describing something already finished with the simple infinitive instead of the perfect infinitive loses the distinction between 'seems to do' and 'seems to have done.'

topics.formula: apparently, at the start of a sentence, for information that seems to be true based on appearances. allegedly, for a claim (often negative) that hasn't been proven. according to + source, to attribute information to a specific person or group.
topics.key_idea: These are three more distancing tools, each doing a slightly different job — apparently signals the information comes from what seems true, allegedly specifically flags an unproven accusation, and according to names exactly where the information comes from, shifting responsibility for its accuracy onto that source.
examples: Apparently, the store is closing next month.
He allegedly stole funds from the charity.
According to the report, sales increased by ten percent.
common_mistakes: Using allegedly for a positive or neutral claim — it's specifically reserved for unproven wrongdoing, not general uncertainty; apparently or according to fit those other cases better.

topics.formula: would rather/sooner + a different subject + past perfect, to express a preference about something in the past — what someone wishes had (or hadn't) happened.
topics.key_idea: This extends the would rather + different-subject pattern one step further into the past — instead of past simple for a present/future wish about someone else, past perfect expresses regret or preference about something that already happened.
examples: I'd rather you hadn't mentioned that in front of everyone.
She'd rather he had asked first.
common_mistakes: Using past simple instead of past perfect when the preference is about something already in the past: 'I'd rather you didn't speak to her like that' (present/future meaning) instead of 'I'd rather you hadn't spoken to her like that' (past regret) — these mean genuinely different things.

topics.formula: suppose / supposing / imagine / what if, used like if to introduce a hypothetical — present tense for a real, possible situation (like first conditional), past simple for an unreal present/future situation (like second conditional), past perfect for an unreal past situation (like third conditional).
topics.key_idea: These four words all work as substitutes for if, following exactly the same tense logic as the three conditional types — the verb tense used after them signals whether the situation is realistically possible, purely imaginary, or an unchangeable past that didn't happen.
examples: Imagine you won the lottery tomorrow; what would you do first?
What if the interview gets cancelled?
Supposing she hadn't warned us, we would have been late.
common_mistakes: Mismatching the tense with the intended type of hypothetical — using present tense after suppose when describing something clearly unreal, instead of past simple or past perfect as the situation demands.

topics.formula: verb + object + to + infinitive, with verbs like advise, allow, ask, beg, convince, encourage, expect, force, persuade, remind, tell, warn, and want/need/would like/would hate/would prefer.
topics.key_idea: This large family of verbs all follow the same pattern — name who the action applies to right after the verb, then use to + infinitive for what they should (or shouldn't) do. It works the same way whether the verb is about instruction, desire, or persuasion.
examples: She convinced him to apply for the job.
They expect us to finish by Friday.
I'd like you to meet my colleague.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the object, or using a that-clause with a verb that specifically needs this pattern: 'I want that you go' instead of 'I want you to go.'

topics.formula: advise / persuade / remind / teach / tell / warn + object + that-clause, as an alternative to the to-infinitive pattern.
topics.key_idea: A handful of these object-plus-infinitive verbs also allow a full that-clause instead, giving a second, equally correct way to report what was said or advised.
examples: The lawyer advised us that we should appeal the decision.
She reminded them that the deadline was approaching.
common_mistakes: Assuming every object+to-infinitive verb also accepts a that-clause — only this specific smaller group does, not the whole family (like force or convince).

topics.formula: advise / allow + -ing (no object at all), as opposed to advise/allow + object + to-infinitive when a person is named.
topics.key_idea: These two verbs switch grammar entirely depending on whether a specific person is mentioned — with an object, they take a to-infinitive, but drop the object and they switch to the -ing form instead.
examples: The doctor advised resting for a few days.
They don't allow smoking indoors.
common_mistakes: Using to-infinitive without an object: 'He advised to go' instead of 'He advised going' — without a named object, these verbs need -ing.

topics.formula: arrange / ask / plan / wait + for someone + to + infinitive. Also used after certain adjectives, nouns (advantage, mistake, idea, disaster, etc.), and too/enough, when a for-someone phrase is needed before the infinitive.
topics.key_idea: This structure inserts for + a person right before the infinitive whenever the verb, adjective, or noun involved needs to specify who exactly is meant to carry out the action — arrange, plan, and wait all use it as their standard pattern, and it also shows up naturally after evaluative adjectives and nouns, and after too/enough.
examples: I'll arrange for the documents to be delivered tomorrow.
It's crucial for everyone to understand the risks.
It would be a mistake for you to ignore this warning.
common_mistakes: Dropping for before the person in this structure: 'I will arrange you to have a meeting' instead of 'I will arrange for you to have a meeting.'

topics.formula: let / make / help + object + infinitive without to. But in the passive, make specifically switches to be made + to-infinitive.
topics.key_idea: These three verbs are unusual in taking a bare infinitive after their object, unlike most verb+object+infinitive verbs, which need to. Make is the one exception within the exception: once it goes passive, the missing to suddenly reappears.
examples: My parents let me stay out late on weekends.
The coach made the team run extra laps.
Can you help me move this table?
common_mistakes: Keeping the bare infinitive in the passive form of make: 'The staff were made wear their uniform' instead of 'The staff were made to wear their uniform' — to reappears specifically when make becomes passive.

topics.formula: hear / listen / notice / see + object + infinitive without to, for a short, complete action witnessed start to finish. + object + -ing, for a longer action witnessed in progress, without seeing it finish.
topics.key_idea: The choice here isn't about grammar rules so much as what was actually perceived — a bare infinitive says the whole action was witnessed from beginning to end, while -ing describes catching just part of something already underway.
examples: I heard the glass break.
I heard the neighbors arguing for almost an hour.
common_mistakes: Treating the two forms as interchangeable — the choice actually changes the meaning of what was witnessed: complete versus partial, finished versus ongoing.
