topics.formula: dislike / hate / imagine / involve / keep / mind / prevent / not like / remember / resent / risk / stop + object + -ing, where the object of the main verb also functions as the subject of the -ing action.
topics.key_idea: With this group of verbs, the object isn't just receiving the main verb's action — it's simultaneously the one doing the -ing action described afterward, which is exactly the kind of double-duty role a gerund construction like this creates.
examples: I can't stand him complaining all the time.
She resents being told what to do.
We risk losing everything if this fails.
common_mistakes: Using a to-infinitive instead of the -ing form after these verbs' object: 'I hate him to tell me' instead of 'I hate him telling me.'

topics.formula: as long as / provided (that) / providing (that) / on condition (that) / only if + clause, alternatives to if that specifically emphasize the necessary condition for something to happen.
topics.key_idea: These all mean roughly the same as if, but they add extra emphasis — they frame the following condition as essential, the one thing that has to be true for the rest of the sentence to hold. On condition (that) is the most formal of the group.
examples: I'll lend you my car as long as you fill up the tank.
You may leave early provided you finish your tasks.
They'll approve the loan on condition that you provide proof of income.
We'll proceed only if everyone agrees.
common_mistakes: Treating these as identical in tone to plain if — they carry a stronger sense of 'this condition is essential,' which plain if doesn't necessarily convey.

topics.formula: whether or not + clause, or even if + clause, both meaning that something stays true or will happen regardless of which alternative turns out to be the case.
topics.key_idea: These both rule out a condition mattering at all — unlike a normal if-sentence, where the outcome depends on the condition, whether or not and even if both say the outcome is the same either way, so the condition is essentially irrelevant to what happens.
examples: I'll support your decision whether or not I agree with it.
Even if it rains, the festival will go ahead.
common_mistakes: Confusing whether or not / even if with plain if: 'I'll help him if he needs me' means help is conditional on need, while 'I'll help him whether or not he needs me' means the help happens regardless.

topics.formula: past simple/continuous in the if-clause (present/future meaning) + would/should/might have + past participle in the main clause (past meaning) — mixing second and third conditional. Or: past perfect in the if-clause (past meaning) + would/should/might + infinitive in the main clause (present meaning).
topics.key_idea: Mixed conditionals let a sentence talk about two different time periods at once — an unreal present situation with a past consequence, or an unreal past event with a present-day result. The trick is spotting which half of the sentence belongs to which time, since the two clauses genuinely don't match the usual same-time pattern of ordinary conditionals.
examples: If I hadn't missed the flight, I would be there with you now.
If I spoke French, I would have understood the conversation earlier.
If she had taken that job, she would be living in Paris today.
common_mistakes: Forcing both clauses into matching tenses as if it were a standard second or third conditional — mixed conditionals are correct exactly because the two halves refer to different times, not a mismatch to be fixed.

topics.formula: Should + subject + infinitive (instead of if + present, first conditional, formal). Had + subject + past participle (instead of if + past perfect, third conditional, if is dropped entirely). Were + subject + to + infinitive (instead of if + past simple, second conditional, for improbable future events). Negative forms don't contract: not goes after the subject (should you not, had we not, were you not).
topics.key_idea: These formal inversions drop if and move the auxiliary to the front instead, working like a more elegant substitute for each conditional type — should for a real future possibility, had for an unreal past, and were...to for an unlikely future. In every case, the negative stays uncontracted, with not placed after the subject rather than fused onto the verb.
examples: Should you have any questions, feel free to contact us.
Had they arrived on time, they wouldn't have missed the opening.
Were she to accept the offer, she would need to relocate.
common_mistakes: Using a contracted negative in this structure: 'Shouldn't you wish to retake the test' instead of 'Should you not wish to retake the test' — the formal inversion always keeps not separate and uncontracted.

topics.formula: In the second-condition-if-clause + third-condition-result type of mixed conditional, the hypothetical present state described in the if-clause is understood to have also applied at the earlier point in time when the past result took place.
topics.key_idea: This type of mixed conditional carries a hidden logical assumption — since the if-clause describes an ongoing state (not a one-time event), it's understood that state was already true back when the past consequence happened too, not just true right now.
examples: If I were taller, they would have picked me for the team.
If she weren't so stubborn, she would have listened to us back then.
common_mistakes: Missing the implicit backward extension of the present state — assuming the if-clause only describes 'now' and not realizing it also applies to the earlier moment the main clause refers to.

topics.formula: was/were allowed to + infinitive, for past permission (affirmative). couldn't + infinitive also works for past permission, but only in the negative — could is NOT used for one specific instance of affirmative past permission.
topics.key_idea: This is a permission-specific counterpart to the ability rule for could — affirmative past permission needs was/were allowed to, not could, but the negative couldn't works just fine either way, whether the meaning is ability or permission.
examples: Employees were allowed to leave early on holidays.
He was allowed to skip the meeting because of the emergency.
common_mistakes: Using could for affirmative past permission: 'He could receive visits' sounds more like a general ability than a specific instance of permission granted — was/were allowed to is the safer, clearer choice.

topics.formula: subject + be allowed to + infinitive, an alternative to can/could for permission or possibility — but never 'it + be allowed to.' subject + be (not) permitted to + infinitive, more formal, for official rules and laws — 'it + be (not) permitted to' IS possible here.
topics.key_idea: Both express permission, but they differ slightly in formality and in one specific grammar point — be allowed to never takes it as a dummy subject (that job goes to using or an -ing form instead), while be permitted to, being more official and rule-based, does allow it as its subject.
examples: Visitors are allowed to take photos in this gallery.
Smoking is not permitted inside the building.
Guests are permitted to bring one additional person.
common_mistakes: Using it as the subject of be allowed to: 'It is allowed to use mobile phones' instead of 'You are allowed to use mobile phones' or 'Using mobile phones is allowed.'

topics.formula: be supposed to / be meant to + infinitive, to say what someone should or shouldn't do according to a rule, arrangement, or expectation.
topics.key_idea: These describe an expected obligation — what's meant to happen according to plans, rules, or common sense — and they're often used specifically to point out that reality doesn't match that expectation.
examples: We're supposed to submit the form by Monday.
You're not supposed to park here.
common_mistakes: Confusing be supposed to with a stronger obligation like must — it more often describes an expectation or arrangement, and is commonly used to point out a mismatch between what should be happening and what actually is.

topics.formula: smell/taste + of + noun = the real thing is actually present. smell/taste + like + noun = similar to, but not actually, that thing.
topics.key_idea: This small preposition swap changes what's actually being claimed — of says the ingredient or substance is genuinely there, while like just compares the smell or flavor to something else without claiming it's actually present.
examples: The candle smells of lavender.
This drink tastes like cinnamon.
The sauce smells of garlic.
common_mistakes: Using like when the meaning is really 'contains': saying 'smells like garlic' when garlic is actually a genuine ingredient understates the claim compared to 'smells of garlic.'

topics.formula: seem + adjective, seem like + noun, seem as if/though + clause (informally, seem like + clause too).
topics.key_idea: Seem works as a linking verb in exactly the same pattern as look, sound, taste, smell, and feel — a plain adjective describes the impression directly, like introduces a noun comparison, and as if/though (or informally like) opens a full clause.
examples: You seem upset about something.
The wait felt like forever.
It seems as though nobody is home.
common_mistakes: Using like before a plain adjective: 'You seem like tired' instead of 'You seem tired' — an adjective attaches directly, without like.

topics.formula: look = an impression based on appearance, what's seen. seem = an impression based on behavior, voice, or overall manner, not just appearance.
topics.key_idea: These two overlap a lot but draw their impression from different sources — look is purely about how something appears visually, while seem is about the overall vibe someone gives off, often through how they act or sound rather than just how they look.
examples: You look pale; are you feeling okay?
He seems nervous about the presentation.
common_mistakes: Using look and seem interchangeably in every context — some adjectives naturally pair with one but not the other, depending on whether the judgment comes from appearance or behavior.

topics.formula: sense verbs used as linking/copular verbs (look, feel, sound, taste, smell, seem) take an adjective after them, never an adverb — just like be.
topics.key_idea: When these verbs describe a quality rather than an action, they function exactly like be, which is why they need an adjective, not an adverb, even though the temptation is often to reach for the -ly form.
examples: The plan sounds reasonable.
She felt awful after the news.
common_mistakes: Using the adverb form after a linking sense verb: 'You look tiredly' or 'She felt badly' instead of 'You look tired' / 'She felt bad' — these verbs take adjectives, since they're describing a state, not an action.

topics.formula: to be + -ing (continuous infinitive), for an action in progress around the time of the main verb. to have been + -ing (perfect continuous infinitive), for a duration that started earlier and continues up to the main verb's time.
topics.key_idea: These extend the infinitive system the same way continuous and perfect continuous extend ordinary tenses — the continuous infinitive captures something happening right around the main verb's moment, while the perfect continuous infinitive adds duration, describing something that had already been going on for a while by that point.
examples: I'm happy to be joining this team.
You shouldn't be sleeping during class.
I'm proud to have been leading this project for two years.
common_mistakes: Using the simple infinitive when the meaning specifically calls for something in progress or an extended duration: 'I'm glad to spend this weekend with you' loses the sense of 'right now, ongoing' that the continuous infinitive captures.

topics.formula: would like / would hate / would rather / would prefer + (to) have + past participle, when the same subject wishes something had happened earlier or in the past, rather than now or in the future.
topics.key_idea: When these expressions of preference are talking about the same subject wanting a different outcome for a past event, the perfect infinitive is required — the simple infinitive alone shifts the meaning to something present or future instead.
examples: I would like to visit the museum again.
I would like to have visited the museum before it closed.
He would rather stay home tonight. / He would rather have stayed home last night.
common_mistakes: Using the simple infinitive when the meaning is really about the past: 'I would like to see you again' doesn't capture the same regretful, past-focused meaning as 'I would like to have seen you again.'

topics.formula: to be + past participle (passive infinitive), or being + past participle (passive gerund), to describe an action done to the subject rather than by it.
topics.key_idea: Infinitives and gerunds can go passive too, following the normal be + past participle pattern, just slotted into whatever infinitive or gerund form the sentence needs — including combining with perfect forms for something passive that already happened.
examples: She is too young to be allowed to drive.
This machine needs to be repaired.
I don't mind being interrupted occasionally.
He denied having been informed about the changes.
common_mistakes: Using the active infinitive/gerund form when the subject is actually receiving the action: 'This place needs taking care' instead of 'This place needs to be taken care of,' when the place itself isn't doing the caring.

topics.formula: Will you be + -ing...?, a polite, less direct way of asking about someone's future plans.
topics.key_idea: Asking with future continuous sounds more neutral and less demanding than a plain will-question, since it presents the activity as something that might simply be happening anyway, rather than directly asking the person to decide or commit right now.
examples: Will you be attending the conference next week?
common_mistakes: Using a direct will-question when a softer, less presumptuous tone is wanted: 'Will you go home this summer?' can sound more like it's pressing for a decision, while 'Will you be going home?' sounds more like a casual, open inquiry.

topics.formula: be about to + infinitive, for something that will happen in the very near future. be on the brink/verge/point of + noun or -ing, for the same 'about to happen' meaning, often used for more significant or dramatic events.
topics.key_idea: Both express that something is on the cusp of happening, but the grammar differs — about to pairs directly with an infinitive, while brink/verge/point of need of plus a noun or -ing form, and tend to describe bigger, more consequential moments rather than small everyday actions.
examples: We are about to announce the winner.
The village is on the brink of losing its only school.
They are on the verge of signing the contract.
common_mistakes: Using a bare infinitive after brink/verge/point of instead of of + noun/-ing: 'on the verge to win' instead of 'on the verge of winning.'

topics.formula: be due to + infinitive, for a future event that is planned, scheduled, or expected to happen.
topics.key_idea: Due to signals that something is officially or reasonably expected to occur, based on a schedule or plan — similar to timetabled present simple, but usable more broadly for expected events, not just fixed timetables.
examples: The shipment is due to arrive on Thursday.
The CEO is due to give a speech at noon.
common_mistakes: Confusing this due to with the reason-giving due to + noun (meaning 'because of') — this is a completely different structure, be due to + infinitive, about an expected future event.

topics.formula: be + to + infinitive, for official arrangements and expected events (common in news), formal instructions and orders (negative = prohibition), or in an if-clause naming what's needed to achieve a goal.
topics.key_idea: This formal structure covers several related but distinct jobs — reporting planned official events, giving formal commands (with the negative meaning something is forbidden), and setting up an if-clause that spells out a necessary condition for reaching some outcome.
examples: The minister is to visit the flooded region tomorrow.
Staff are to complete the training by the end of the month.
You are not to discuss this matter with anyone.
common_mistakes: Missing that the negative form of be to expresses prohibition, not simply the absence of a plan: 'You are not to leave' means you're forbidden to leave, not just that leaving isn't scheduled.

topics.formula: After and/but/or, a repeated subject (or subject + auxiliary) can be dropped. After be, a repeated adjective or adverb can be dropped too.
topics.key_idea: English often avoids repeating something the listener can easily fill in — a subject connected by and, but, or or, or an adjective/adverb that's already been stated once right after be, can simply be left out without any loss of clarity.
examples: He opened the letter and read it twice.
We could stay or leave early.
They claim the movie is amazing, but I don't think it is.
common_mistakes: Repeating the subject or adjective unnecessarily where ellipsis reads more naturally: spelling everything out ('...but I don't think he is the best') can sound clunky compared to the more natural, trimmed version.

topics.formula: A repeated verb phrase can be dropped after a different auxiliary or modal too, not just the same one. Sometimes two auxiliaries need to stay together in the second clause to keep a past meaning clear (could have, should have).
topics.key_idea: This extends basic verb-phrase ellipsis beyond matching auxiliaries — a completely different modal can still leave the main verb implied. When the implied meaning is specifically about the past, though, two auxiliaries sometimes need to stay together (like could have or should have) so the past sense doesn't get lost.
examples: I'm not saving as much as I should.
She promised to call, but she hasn't.
He didn't win, but he could have.
common_mistakes: Dropping down to a single auxiliary when a past meaning specifically requires two: 'She could' instead of 'She could have,' which loses the intended meaning of an unrealized past possibility.

topics.formula: to (alone), replacing a repeated infinitive or infinitive phrase — a 'reduced infinitive.'
topics.key_idea: When an infinitive verb phrase has already been mentioned, the rest of it can be dropped and only to left standing in its place, avoiding an awkward repetition.
examples: I don't feel like cooking tonight, but I probably should.
'Are you going to apply for the job?' 'I've decided not to.'
common_mistakes: Repeating the full infinitive phrase where a reduced infinitive would sound more natural: 'I really want to travel' isn't wrong, but 'I really want to' flows better once 'travel' has already been established.

topics.formula: one, to replace a singular countable noun already mentioned. ones, for the plural version.
topics.key_idea: These stand in for a noun that's already clear from context, letting a sentence avoid repeating it — one for a single item, ones for more than one.
examples: 'Do you have a charger?' 'Yes, I've got one.'
'Which jacket is yours?' 'The blue one.'
These shoes are worn out; I need new ones.
common_mistakes: Using one/ones for an uncountable noun — this substitution only works for countable nouns, singular or plural.

topics.formula: do so (also does so, did so, doing so — more formal), or do it/do that (more informal), to replace a repeated verb phrase.
topics.key_idea: These let a whole verb phrase be swapped out for a short stand-in, with do so leaning more formal and written, and do it/do that sounding more like everyday spoken English.
examples: If you'd like to cancel, you're welcome to do so.
Avoiding the topic won't help; doing so will only make things worse.
They asked me to leave, and I did it.
common_mistakes: Using do so in casual conversation where do it/do that would sound more natural, or vice versa in formal writing.

topics.formula: if so (or if that is so) = if [the positive situation just mentioned] is true. if not = if [that situation] isn't true.
topics.key_idea: These compress an entire repeated conditional clause down to two or three words, referring back to whatever was just said instead of spelling the condition out again.
examples: Do you need more time? If so, let me know.
The bus should arrive by eight. If not, call the office.
common_mistakes: Using if so/if not without a clear preceding statement for them to refer back to — they only work when the condition they're replacing has just been stated.

topics.formula: verb (think, hope, believe, expect, guess, imagine, presume, suppose, suspect, say, seem, appear, etc.) + so, to avoid repeating a positive clause. For negative meaning: positive verb + not (with be afraid, assume, guess, hope, presume, suspect), or negative verb + so (with believe, expect, imagine, think). Appear, seem, and suppose can go either way.
topics.key_idea: This is a compact way to answer or react to something without restating the whole clause — so stands in for the positive version of what was just said. For the negative version, some verbs move the negative onto the verb itself (I don't think so), while others keep the verb positive and add not instead (I'm afraid not), and a handful of verbs allow either pattern.
examples: 'Is the store open?' 'I believe so.'
'Can we still make it?' 'I'm afraid not.'
'Will they cancel the trip?' 'I don't think so.'
common_mistakes: Mismatching which verbs take positive-verb-plus-not versus negative-verb-plus-so: 'I don't hope so' sounds wrong, since hope specifically pairs with 'I hope not,' not a negated verb.

topics.formula: 's can also be used with time expressions, shops, places, and organisations, not just people and animals — and for these categories, of + noun is often an equally valid alternative.
topics.key_idea: The possessive 's isn't strictly limited to living things — it comfortably extends to organisations, places, and time expressions too, and in these cases, English usually offers both the 's form and an of-phrase as genuinely interchangeable options.
examples: The city's growth has been remarkable. / The growth of the city has been remarkable.
The company's decision surprised everyone.
common_mistakes: Assuming 's is only correct for people and animals — it also works comfortably with places, organisations, and time expressions.

topics.formula: of + possessive 's (or possessive pronoun), used specifically when a determiner (a, some, this, etc.) comes before the noun — 'a friend of Anna's' rather than 'Anna's a friend.'
topics.key_idea: This double genitive solves a grammar clash — a possessive 's can't sit comfortably right after an article or another determiner, so of steps in to carry the possessive meaning while 's stays attached to the person's name at the end.
examples: A colleague of Marcus's recommended this restaurant.
Is that a friend of yours?
common_mistakes: Trying to combine a determiner directly with 's in front of the noun: 'A Anna's friend' doesn't work — of Anna's has to be used instead, after the noun.

topics.formula: of, preferred over 's, for inanimate things, parts of things, abstract nouns, and long noun phrases.
topics.key_idea: The possessive 's naturally suits living, active possessors, so when the 'owner' is really just an object, a part of something, an idea, or a long, unwieldy phrase, of reads far more naturally instead.
examples: We admired the elegance of the building.
The handle of the suitcase broke.
That's the son of the woman who runs the bakery.
common_mistakes: Using 's with a long noun phrase, which becomes awkward: 'the neighbours who live next door's child' instead of the much clearer 'the child of the neighbours who live next door.'

topics.formula: noun + noun (the first noun acting like an adjective, usually singular), as a third alternative to possessive 's or of — school bus, car park, tourist destination.
topics.key_idea: Rather than marking possession explicitly, English often just stacks two nouns together, with the first one modifying the second the way an adjective would. Sometimes more than one form (compound noun, 's, or of) is genuinely possible, but usually one particular version is simply the one people use.
examples: The kitchen table is scratched.
What's the company policy on remote work?
common_mistakes: Assuming a compound noun always has an equally natural 's or of alternative — for many common compounds, like bus stop or toothpaste, only the compound form is actually used in practice.

topics.formula: container + noun (e.g. tea cup, wine glass), for the empty container itself. noun + of + container (e.g. a cup of tea, a glass of wine), for the container together with its contents.
topics.key_idea: This small but useful distinction hinges entirely on word order — flip a container-plus-contents compound around and add of, and the meaning shifts from talking about an empty object to talking about that object actually filled with something.
examples: Could you wash these coffee cups?
Would you like a glass of juice?
common_mistakes: Mixing up the two orders: 'a tea cup' describes an empty cup, while 'a cup of tea' means an actual drink — using one when the other is meant creates real confusion.

topics.formula: The reason why / the thing that / the person who / the place where / the day when + [rest of the sentence] + be + the emphasized element.
topics.key_idea: This type of cleft sentence puts a descriptive phrase first, naming the category of what's being emphasized, and saves the actual emphasized element for after be — the opposite order from starting with it.
examples: The reason why he resigned is still unclear.
The thing that annoys me most is his lateness.
The place where we got married holds special memories.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which relative word fits which category: reason takes why, thing takes that, person takes who, place takes where, and day (or other time nouns) takes when.

topics.formula: In it-cleft sentences, use who/which/that after a noun phrase being emphasized, but only that (not who/which) after an adverbial phrase. When can follow a noun phrase, but not an adverbial phrase.
topics.key_idea: The choice of connecting word after it + be + [emphasized element] depends on what kind of element is being emphasized — a noun phrase has more flexibility (who, which, that, or even when for a time noun), while an adverbial phrase (like a time or place expression that isn't a simple noun) is restricted to that alone.
examples: It's Friday when the results come out.
It's on Friday that the results come out.
common_mistakes: Using when after an adverbial phrase: 'It's on Monday when I have to call' instead of 'It's on Monday that I have to call.'

topics.formula: What (or all, for extra emphasis) + subject + verb + is/was + (to) + infinitive, to focus on a verb or action. What happens/happened is/was (that) + clause, to focus on an entire sentence or event.
topics.key_idea: What steps in as a more flexible alternative to the thing that, and it opens up two more focused patterns — one that highlights specifically what someone does or did, using an infinitive after is/was, and another that highlights an entire situation or event as a whole.
examples: What he did was apologize immediately.
All she wants is to be heard.
What happened was that the printer ran out of ink halfway through.
common_mistakes: Losing the is/was connector between the what-clause and the emphasized element: 'What she did apologize' instead of 'What she did was apologize.'

topics.formula: which/that, as relative pronouns referring back to a noun or a whole previous clause. what is never used as a relative pronoun this way — it works independently, meaning 'the thing/s that.'
topics.key_idea: A common error is reaching for what where which or that is actually needed — what can't refer back to something already mentioned the way a true relative pronoun does. Instead, what stands completely on its own, already built-in with the meaning 'the thing that,' with nothing before it to refer back to.
examples: I returned the jacket which/that I had borrowed.
He offered to drive us, which was very kind.
I couldn't believe what she said.
common_mistakes: Using what as if it were which or that: 'He offered to help us, what was a nice gesture' instead of 'He offered to help us, which was a nice gesture' — what never refers back to something already stated.

topics.formula: preposition + whom/which (formal, less common in speech), or the preposition moved to the end of the clause (informal, most common). After a preposition, only whom or which can be used — never who or that. whose can also follow a preposition.
topics.key_idea: A relative pronoun that's the object of a preposition has two possible homes for that preposition — right before the pronoun, in a formal style, or trailing at the end of the clause, which is the everyday, natural choice. Fronting the preposition comes with a restriction: only whom and which work there, not who or that.
examples: This is the topic about which we disagree.
She's the mentor to whom I owe my career.
That's the reason (that) he left for.
common_mistakes: Using who or that right after a preposition: 'He was a man for who everybody had respect' instead of 'for whom' — a fronted preposition specifically requires whom or which.

topics.formula: when (time), where (place), why (reason), introducing a relative clause. preposition + which is a more formal alternative to each of these.
topics.key_idea: These three relative adverbs pack a preposition and a relative pronoun into a single word, saving the sentence from a more clunky preposition + which construction, which remains available as a more formal option.
examples: The company changed the policy when the complaints increased.
This is the room where we held the ceremony.
Nobody knows the reason why he quit.
common_mistakes: Overusing the formal preposition + which alternative in everyday speech, where the relative adverb alone sounds far more natural.

topics.formula: quantifier (some, any, none, all, both, several, many, few, etc.) + of which/whom/whose, used in non-defining relative clauses to talk about a portion of a previously mentioned group.
topics.key_idea: This structure lets a non-defining clause zoom in on part of a group already introduced — which/whom for things or people, whose for possession — always following the quantifier and of, and always confined to the comma-separated, non-defining kind of clause.
examples: His colleagues, several of whom disagreed, still supported the plan.
The building had many rooms, most of which were empty.
I joined a club, several of whose members are professional athletes.
common_mistakes: Using this structure in a defining relative clause instead of a non-defining one — quantifier + of which/whom/whose only appears in the comma-separated, non-defining type.

topics.formula: -ing participle clause, replacing a full adverbial clause of time, reason, or cause — used mainly in written English.
topics.key_idea: This is a compact way to fold a whole subordinate clause into a single participle phrase, dropping the conjunction and the repeated subject, while keeping the same time (present or past) meaning as the original clause would carry.
examples: Feeling exhausted, she decided to cancel the trip.
Hearing the alarm, everyone rushed outside.
Cooking dinner, I burned my hand on the pan.
common_mistakes: Using this structure in casual speech, where a full adverbial clause sounds more natural — participle clauses are mainly a feature of written English.

topics.formula: having + past participle (perfect -ing participle clause), to emphasize that one action happened before another, often expressing cause. having been + past participle (passive), as an alternative to a since-clause of reason.
topics.key_idea: Adding having marks the participle clause's action as clearly completed before the main clause's action, which is exactly why this form is common for explaining a cause. The passive version, having been, works especially well as a formal, compact substitute for a since-clause explaining a reason.
examples: Having missed the deadline, he apologized to the client.
Not having slept well, I struggled to concentrate.
Having been rejected twice, she almost gave up applying.
common_mistakes: Using the plain -ing form when the sequence of events genuinely needs to be marked as earlier: 'Losing all the games, he felt depressed' loses some of the clear before-and-after sequencing that having lost captures.

topics.formula: past participle clause, usually replacing a passive sentence — often interchangeable with a non-defining relative clause.
topics.key_idea: These clauses compress a passive idea down to just the past participle itself, dropping was/were being entirely, and they can usually be expanded back out into a full non-defining relative clause without changing the meaning.
examples: Written in the 1800s, the novel remains popular today.
Surprised by the news, she sat down quietly.
Founded by two brothers, the company grew rapidly.
common_mistakes: Trying to use the active -ing form when the underlying meaning is actually passive: since the briefcase was found (not doing the finding), found is correct, not finding.

topics.formula: after / before / instead of / without / when / while + -ing participle clause (most commonly), a common and natural way to attach a participle clause to a preposition or conjunction.
topics.key_idea: Participle clauses very often sit right after these connecting words, especially -ing ones, creating a smooth, compact way to link two related actions without needing a full second clause with its own subject.
examples: Before leaving the office, check that all the lights are off.
Instead of complaining, try to find a solution.
People often check their phones while waiting in line.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that these prepositions/conjunctions still need the -ing form directly after them, not a full clause with a repeated subject: 'while driving' is the participle version, not 'while they are driving.'

topics.formula: The subject of the participle clause's implied verb must be the same as the subject of the main clause — using two different subjects (a dangling participle) is a common and serious error.
topics.key_idea: A participle clause has no subject of its own written out, so the sentence's real subject has to logically apply to both the participle action and the main clause's action. When those two things actually happen to different people or objects, the participle clause needs to be a passive past participle instead, matching the object that experiences the action.
examples: If you heat the mixture, it thickens. → Heated, the mixture thickens.
If you water the seeds daily, they grow faster. → Watered daily, the seeds grow faster.
common_mistakes: Creating a dangling participle by mismatching subjects: 'Mixing it with soda, the cocktail tastes even better' illogically implies the cocktail is doing the mixing — switching to the passive past participle (mixed) fixes this.

topics.formula: With verbs that take two objects (bring, get, give, make, offer, promise, send, show, etc.), either object can become the subject of the passive sentence. Starting with the person (indirect object) is more common than starting with the thing (direct object).
topics.key_idea: Ditransitive verbs create a genuine choice in the passive that most verbs don't offer — either the person or the thing involved can become the subject, producing two different but equally correct passive sentences. In practice, English favors putting the person first.
examples: I offered my colleague a ride.
My colleague was offered a ride.
A ride was offered to my colleague.
common_mistakes: Assuming only one passive version is possible: both 'the person was given/sent/shown X' and 'X was given/sent/shown to the person' are correct, though the person-first version is more commonly used.

topics.formula: possessive 's (singular time noun) or ' alone (plural time noun ending in -s), used specifically with time expressions to describe a duration — a genuine exception to the general rule against using 's with inanimate things.
topics.key_idea: Even though inanimate things generally prefer of over the possessive 's, duration-expressing time nouns are a clear exception — they take the possessive form naturally. A useful test: if replacing the possessive with of + the time word still makes sense (two years' experience = an experience of two years), the possessive is the right choice; if it doesn't make sense (like 'nine months of pregnant'), it isn't.
examples: She has ten years' teaching experience.
It's about a twenty minutes' walk from here.
We had a three hours' wait at the airport.
common_mistakes: Dropping the apostrophe in these time expressions: 'two years experience' is commonly seen but not considered correct — the possessive apostrophe belongs there.

topics.formula: number + time noun (singular, hyphenated) + noun = the same meaning as number + time noun (plural, possessive 's) + noun — a two-day journey = two days' journey.
topics.key_idea: These are two equally correct ways of saying the exact same thing, built from opposite grammar — the compound-adjective version keeps the time word singular and hyphenated before the noun, while the possessive version pluralizes the time word and adds the possessive apostrophe after it.
examples: a six-month contract = six months' contract
a fifteen-minute break = fifteen minutes' break
a two-year lease = two years' lease
common_mistakes: Mixing the two patterns together: 'a four-hours journey' (wrongly pluralizing the hyphenated form) or 'four hour's journey' (wrongly keeping the time word singular in the possessive form) — each pattern has its own internally consistent singular/plural rule.

topics.formula: Hyphenate a compound adjective before a noun. After be or a sensory verb, the words are often written separately instead — though some very common compound adjectives stay hyphenated everywhere. Hyphen placement can also change meaning entirely. In number-based compound adjectives, spell the number out (two-minute, not 2-minute) unless it's very large.
topics.key_idea: The hyphen's main job is to show which words belong together as one descriptive unit before a noun, and it can genuinely change what's being described depending on exactly where it sits — moving it shifts which word the adjective actually modifies.
examples: He is a well-respected doctor. / This doctor is well respected in the field.
She is a small-business owner.
I had a five-minute call.
common_mistakes: Placing or omitting the hyphen carelessly in an ambiguous phrase: 'old book collector' without a hyphen could describe an elderly collector or a collector of old books, depending on which reading was intended — the hyphen resolves this.
Writing the number as a digit instead of spelling it out: 'a 2-minute break' instead of 'a two-minute break.'

topics.formula: noun + a specific, fixed preposition (e.g. interest in, contact with, room for, cause of, threat to) — often, though not always, matching the preposition used with a related adjective or verb form of the same word. Some nouns take different prepositions with genuinely different meanings; others accept more than one preposition with the same meaning.
topics.key_idea: Like verbs and adjectives, nouns often have one particular preposition permanently attached to them, and there's a useful shortcut for guessing an unfamiliar one — checking whether a related adjective or verb form of the same word is already known, since the preposition is often (not always) shared across all three word forms. A few nouns genuinely shift meaning depending on which preposition follows, while others simply allow more than one preposition interchangeably.
examples: I have great respect for her work.
There's been a rise in demand for this product.
What is the connection between these two events?
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition with a noun, or assuming the related verb/adjective's preposition always transfers exactly — this strategy is a helpful starting guess, not a guaranteed rule; the actual noun-preposition pairing still needs to be learned and double-checked case by case.

topics.formula: quite / much / a lot / far / way / a good deal + comparative adjective, for a big difference. nowhere near / not nearly / not at all + as + adjective + as, for the negative version of a big difference. by far + superlative, to emphasize the biggest gap within a group.
topics.key_idea: These words all dial the comparison up to emphasize a substantial gap between two things, whether phrased as a direct comparative or as a strongly negated as...as structure. By far does a similar intensifying job, but specifically with superlatives, to stress just how far ahead something is compared to everything else.
examples: This route is far shorter than the other one.
The new phone is way more expensive.
This test is nowhere near as difficult as the last one.
This is by far the funniest show I've seen.
common_mistakes: Using by far with a comparative instead of a superlative — it's specifically reserved for superlatives, emphasizing the gap between the top item and everything else.

topics.formula: a bit / a little / slightly / not much + comparative adjective, for a small difference. The same words also work before more/less + noun.
topics.key_idea: These soften a comparison down to a small, modest gap rather than a dramatic one, and they work the same way whether attached to a comparative adjective or to more/less in front of a noun.
examples: This bag is slightly heavier than mine.
The second option is a bit cheaper.
She has a little more experience than him.
common_mistakes: Confusing these small-difference modifiers with the big-difference ones like much or far: 'It's much warmer' implies a substantial gap, quite different from the modest gap 'It's slightly warmer' describes.

topics.formula: almost / nearly / not quite / roughly / more or less / just / exactly + as + adjective + as, or + the same as, to describe an almost non-existent (or exact) difference.
topics.key_idea: These modifiers describe two things as being very close to equal, ranging from just short of matching (almost, nearly, not quite) to a rough estimate (roughly, more or less) to a precise match (just, exactly).
examples: He's almost as tall as his father.
The two designs are more or less identical.
This restaurant is just as good as the one downtown.
common_mistakes: Using not quite and exactly interchangeably — not quite signals a small remaining gap, while exactly signals a perfect match, describing opposite ends of this near-equal range.

topics.formula: After certain verbs, adjectives, or nouns that don't strictly need a complement, the whole infinitive — including to — can be dropped entirely, going one step further than just reducing to 'to.'
topics.key_idea: Beyond shrinking a repeated infinitive phrase down to just to, some contexts allow dropping the infinitive completely, when the word before it doesn't grammatically require anything to follow it at all.
examples: We can leave whenever you're ready (to).
You don't have to help, but there's no harm (to).
common_mistakes: Dropping to after a verb, adjective, or noun that actually requires it to make sense — not every context that allows a reduced 'to' also allows dropping it completely.

topics.formula: Keep to after verbs needing a complement (afford, be able, choose, decide, plan, pretend), after would like/love/hate/prefer, want, and choose, and always with negative infinitives (not to). Also keep the full 'to be' rather than reducing further.
topics.key_idea: Not every verb, adjective, or noun allows to to be dropped — a specific group genuinely needs it to sound complete, and the negative form not to is never shortened any further. Similarly, when the omitted verb is be specifically, the full to be is kept rather than reduced to just to.
examples: 'Are you going to apply?' 'I'm planning to.'
'Would you like some cake?' 'Yes, I'd love to.'
We agreed not to mention it again.
common_mistakes: Dropping to after these specific verbs: 'I'm planning' or 'We can't afford' sound incomplete compared to 'I'm planning to' / 'We can't afford to.'

topics.formula: want and like normally keep to in a reduced infinitive, but to is often dropped after want, and always dropped after like, when they follow a conjunction like if, when, what, or as.
topics.key_idea: This is a specific exception to the usual want/like-keep-to rule — right after certain conjunctions, the to drops away, with like dropping it more consistently than want.
examples: Stay as long as you want (to).
Feel free to call whenever you like.
common_mistakes: Keeping to after like following a conjunction: 'You can come over when you like to' instead of 'You can come over when you like' — like always drops to in this specific position.

topics.formula: present simple or present continuous instead of past tenses, to make a story, joke, or anecdote sound more vivid and immediate — called the narrative present.
topics.key_idea: Switching a story into present tense pulls the listener into the action as if it's happening right now, which is why it's such a common trick for jokes and anecdotes, even though the events actually happened in the past.
examples: So, I open the door, and there's a cat sitting on my bed!
He picks up the phone and just hangs up on me.
common_mistakes: Mixing the narrative present with past tense mid-story inconsistently, rather than committing to present tense throughout for the vivid effect.

topics.formula: present simple, in sports commentary, demonstrations, and live broadcasts, to describe actions as they happen in real time.
topics.key_idea: This gives a fast, exciting, blow-by-blow feel to a description of something unfolding right now, common in commentary and step-by-step demonstrations.
examples: Diaz crosses the ball, and it's a goal!
Next, you whisk the eggs and fold in the flour.
common_mistakes: Using present continuous instead in this context, which sounds slower and less immediate than the rapid-fire present simple commentators and demonstrators typically use.

topics.formula: present simple + a performative verb (promise, apologise, admit, advise, agree, deny, guarantee, invite, recommend, refuse, suggest, thank, warn), where saying the sentence itself carries out the action. Some of these (apologise, deny, guarantee, promise, suggest) can also appear in the negative present continuous with essentially the same meaning.
topics.key_idea: These verbs are unusual because the act of speaking them out loud IS the action — saying 'I promise' doesn't describe a promise, it makes one. A handful of them can also show up in the negative continuous form without shifting the meaning at all.
examples: I apologise for the confusion.
I recommend the seafood pasta.
We warn you that the road ahead is closed.
common_mistakes: Treating performative verbs as ordinary descriptive statements rather than recognizing that the utterance itself performs the action.

topics.formula: present simple, in newspaper headlines and summaries, to make information sound immediate and factual, even for events already completed.
topics.key_idea: Headlines strip time markers and tense complexity down to the bare present simple, giving news a punchy, urgent, factual tone.
examples: Company announces record profits.
Researchers discover new species in rainforest.
common_mistakes: Expecting headline present simple to always mean an ongoing or repeated action — in headlines, it often just reports a single completed event.

topics.formula: present simple + communication verbs (say, tell, hear), to report what people are currently saying or information just received.
topics.key_idea: These verbs describe an ongoing flow of information reaching the speaker right now, even though the actual telling might technically be an ongoing or recent process.
examples: I hear you've moved to a new apartment.
They say the bridge will reopen next month.
common_mistakes: Using present continuous instead for this reporting sense: 'I'm hearing you're starting a new job' sounds unnatural compared to the standard 'I hear...'

topics.formula: present continuous with normally-stative verbs (be, like, look, love, sound), to emphasize that a state or behavior is temporary or currently true, rather than a fixed, permanent trait. A handful of stative verbs (believe, consist of, doubt, own, belong, possess) are rarely or never used this way.
topics.key_idea: Pushing an ordinarily stative verb into the continuous adds a layer of 'just for now' to an otherwise permanent-sounding state — loving something 'these days' rather than as a lasting fact, or being patient right now rather than as a personality trait.
examples: I'm loving this new playlist.
You're being unusually quiet today.
common_mistakes: Using this continuous form with verbs that never take it, like believe or own — these verbs stay firmly in the simple tense no matter how temporary the situation feels.

topics.formula: taste, measure, appear, expect, feel, fit, have, imagine, see, think, weigh — verbs with both a state meaning (present simple) and an action meaning (present continuous).
topics.key_idea: This adds more members to the family of verbs that shift between stative and dynamic depending on meaning — describing an inherent quality stays in present simple, while an active process the subject is doing takes the continuous.
examples: This fabric feels soft. / She's feeling the fabric to check the texture.
The box weighs five kilos. / We're weighing the luggage before the flight.
common_mistakes: Using the continuous form for the inherent-quality meaning: 'This soup is tasting wonderful' sounds wrong, since that meaning of taste is a fixed quality, not an action.

topics.formula: present continuous with mental-state verbs (find, think, realise, regret), to show that a feeling or opinion has recently started or is currently changing. A few mental-state verbs (agree, believe, know, prefer) are almost never used this way.
topics.key_idea: This continuous use captures a feeling in the process of forming or shifting, rather than one that's already fully settled — regretting something more and more, or gradually realising something, rather than simply holding that view as a fixed fact.
examples: I'm starting to find this whole situation quite frustrating.
I'm beginning to think he was right all along.
common_mistakes: Using the continuous with verbs that resist it, like prefer: 'I'm preferring to go to bed earlier' sounds wrong — prefer stays in the simple form even for a recently-formed preference.

topics.formula: present continuous, to make a request, opinion, or comment sound softer, more tentative, and more polite.
topics.key_idea: Framing something as currently in progress — 'I'm wondering,' 'we're hoping' — feels less direct and demanding than the plain present simple equivalent, which is why it's a common politeness strategy.
examples: I'm hoping you could look over this draft.
We're wondering if you'd be free to meet next week.
common_mistakes: Using the blunter present simple ('I wonder if you could...') in a context that calls for extra tact — the continuous version softens the request noticeably.

topics.formula: present continuous + always / constantly / continually / forever, to describe a repeated behavior seen as characteristic of a person or situation — often expressing irritation, surprise, or emphasis.
topics.key_idea: This combination breaks the usual continuous-means-right-now rule on purpose, using it instead to spotlight a recurring pattern the speaker finds notable, whether that's mild annoyance, admiration, or amusement.
examples: He's always losing his keys!
She's constantly checking her phone.
common_mistakes: Missing the added emotional color this pattern carries — it's not neutral like a present simple habit, it usually signals the speaker has a reaction to how often something happens.

topics.formula: present continuous + a frequency adverb (usually, normally), to describe something regularly in progress at a specific time — part of a predictable routine.
topics.key_idea: This pairs the continuous's 'in progress' meaning with a frequency adverb to describe a snapshot of a routine — what's typically happening at a particular moment, rather than the habit as a whole.
examples: At six, I'm usually cooking dinner, so text me later.
We're usually watching the news around eight.
common_mistakes: Using plain present simple instead when the point is specifically about being mid-action at that time: 'I usually drive to work' states the habit generally, while 'I'm usually driving to work' pictures the specific moment of being on the road.

topics.formula: past simple, to soften a statement or make it sound less direct — common in professional or delicate situations.
topics.key_idea: Using past tense for something that's actually still true right now creates a bit of distance, making a request or comment feel gentler and less confrontational than stating it plainly in the present.
examples: I wondered if you had a moment to talk.
I thought we had already discussed this.
common_mistakes: Using present tense in a context that calls for this softening effect: 'I want to ask you something' sounds more abrupt than the past-tense version, even though the want is happening right now.

topics.formula: as if / as though + past simple (for the present) or past perfect (for the past), to signal that the comparison is clearly hypothetical or untrue — the same past-for-unreal logic used with wish, would rather, and it's time.
topics.key_idea: Past tense inside an as if/as though clause specifically marks the comparison as not actually true, following the same underlying pattern that makes wish, would rather, and it's time all reach for a past-tense verb even when talking about the present.
examples: He talks as if he owned the place.
She acted as though she had never heard the story before.
common_mistakes: Using present tense in an as if clause when the intended meaning is clearly hypothetical: 'You sound as if you are the boss' reads more neutrally, losing the implication that it isn't actually true.

topics.formula: past continuous + always / constantly / forever, to describe a repeated behavior that was annoying or characteristic in the past — the past-tense version of the same pattern used with present continuous.
topics.key_idea: Just like its present-tense counterpart, this combination breaks the normal 'in progress at one moment' rule of the continuous on purpose, using repetition words to frame a pattern of past behavior as notably irritating or characteristic.
examples: He was constantly checking his phone during dinner.
She was always criticizing everyone's ideas.
common_mistakes: Missing the emotional coloring this combination carries — it's not a neutral description of repeated past actions, it usually signals disapproval or irritation.

topics.formula: past continuous, for repeated actions that happened during a limited, temporary period in the past — without the negative, annoyed tone the always/constantly pattern usually carries.
topics.key_idea: This use of past continuous for repetition isn't about irritation at all — it's simply highlighting that the repeated actions belonged to a specific, bounded stretch of time, rather than being a permanent past habit.
examples: While she was recovering, her sister was cooking for her every day.
During the renovation, we were sleeping at my parents' house.
common_mistakes: Assuming any past continuous describing repetition must carry an annoyed tone — without always/constantly/forever, this use is neutral, simply marking a temporary period.

topics.formula: past continuous, to soften a request, question, or suggestion — often sounding even more tentative than the present continuous equivalent.
topics.key_idea: This takes the present continuous's politeness effect one step further into the past, creating extra distance and tact, which is why it often feels gentler than 'I'm wondering' or 'we're hoping.'
examples: I was hoping you could give me some advice.
We were wondering if you'd join us for dinner.
common_mistakes: Assuming past continuous here refers to an actual past moment — it doesn't describe when the wondering or hoping happened; it's purely a politeness device about a present request.

topics.formula: Past perfect is typically used only once at the start of a sequence to establish the earlier event — once the order is clear, the narrative continues in past simple. After after, before, or by the time, past simple is often used instead of past perfect entirely, since these words already make the sequence obvious.
topics.key_idea: Past perfect isn't required every single time an earlier action is mentioned — once it's done its job of establishing which event came first, plain past simple can safely take over, and certain time words make the sequence so clear on their own that past perfect becomes unnecessary from the start.
examples: She had packed her bags, and then she called a taxi.
Before he left the office, he checked his email one last time.
common_mistakes: Overusing past perfect throughout a whole sequence once the time order has already been established — it's often only needed once, at the point where the earlier action first needs marking.

topics.formula: had + hoped/expected/wanted, etc. + past participle or clause, to express disappointment or an expectation that wasn't fulfilled.
topics.key_idea: This pattern signals that something was anticipated or wished for, and the rest of the sentence (stated or implied) makes clear that reality didn't match up.
examples: I had hoped the interview would go better.
They had expected the flight to be on time.
common_mistakes: Using present perfect or past simple instead, losing the specific 'expectation that didn't come true' nuance that had hoped/expected carries.

topics.formula: past perfect (simple or continuous), used on its own — without a modal like must — to imply a confident deduction about something that happened before a past moment, based on evidence described nearby.
topics.key_idea: Sometimes past perfect alone carries the weight of a deduction, letting the surrounding evidence do the work that a modal like must have would normally do explicitly.
examples: He had clearly rehearsed his answer.
She had been laughing; there were tears on her cheeks.
They had been cooking; the kitchen smelled amazing when I walked in.
common_mistakes: Assuming a deduction always needs an explicit modal like must have — plain past perfect, especially with a word like obviously or paired with clear supporting evidence, can carry that same inferential meaning.

topics.formula: had been + -ing, to explain the cause behind a physical or emotional state — the state itself is usually expressed with past simple.
topics.key_idea: This pairs a past simple description of how someone felt or seemed with a past perfect continuous explanation of what led to that state, creating a natural cause-and-effect narrative structure.
examples: He was starving; he had been hiking all day without eating.
Her hands were shaking because she had been carrying heavy boxes.
common_mistakes: Reversing the tenses — using past perfect continuous for the state and past simple for the cause would break the natural cause-then-effect logic this pattern relies on.

topics.formula: will, for characteristic behavior/habits (often with frequency adverbs), or things that are always true — not used for one specific occasion, except in the negative.
topics.key_idea: This use of will steps outside the future entirely, describing what someone typically does or what's generally, reliably true, the way a rule or trait would be. It resists being used for a single occasion in the positive, though the negative won't works fine that way (the car won't start).
examples: Every year, my aunt will send us the same holiday card.
Metal will expand when heated.
This printer won't work no matter what I try.
common_mistakes: Using will for a single positive occasion instead of a habit or general truth — this specific use needs either repeated/characteristic behavior or a negative statement about one occasion.

topics.formula: will, to criticize someone's annoying or characteristic habits. if you will (formal, less common), to express criticism or disapproval of someone's choice.
topics.key_idea: Will can carry real judgment, framing a behavior as so typical it's become an irritation, and the formal if you will structure does something similar, pointing out that a choice someone insists on making comes with a consequence they shouldn't complain about.
examples: He will always show up late and blame the traffic.
'I'm broke.' 'Well, if you will spend all your money on gadgets, you can't complain.'
common_mistakes: Missing the critical, judgmental tone this use of will carries — it's not neutral like the future-tense will.

topics.formula: will, to make a confident guess or assumption about the present.
topics.key_idea: This lets a speaker guess at something happening right now based on what's likely or expected, similar in spirit to must for deduction but a touch less certain.
examples: That'll be the delivery driver. Can you get the door?
Don't disturb her now. She'll be finishing her workout.
common_mistakes: Confusing this present-assumption use with will's usual future meaning — context makes clear this is a guess about now, not a prediction about later.

topics.formula: will have + past participle, to make a deduction about the past — a belief about what probably happened, similar to must have but slightly softer.
topics.key_idea: This extends will's assumption-making into the past, letting a speaker express a confident but not absolute belief about something that already happened.
examples: He will have received the invitation by now.
She'll have finished her shift already.
common_mistakes: Assuming must have is the only way to express a past deduction — will have works too, generally with a slightly less certain tone.

topics.formula: would, for repeated past actions, only works with dynamic verbs and only when the time reference is already clear from context — used to remains the only option for stative verbs, or when there's no established time frame.
topics.key_idea: This sharpens the would-versus-used-to distinction further: would isn't just blocked from describing states, it also needs the surrounding context to already establish when the habit took place, since would alone doesn't clearly anchor a time period the way used to naturally does.
examples: As a teenager, I used to be quite reserved.
I used to take the bus to school.
During our years in Madrid, we would (or used to) picnic in the park every Sunday.
common_mistakes: Using would for a habit without first establishing a clear time frame in the sentence or surrounding context — used to doesn't have this requirement, which is why it's the safer default.

topics.formula: would, for something that was always true or reliably the case in the past, given a clear past time reference.
topics.key_idea: This is the past-tense sibling of will's 'always true' use, describing a dependable pattern or fact from a specific earlier period rather than one true right now.
examples: Back in those days, families would gather every Sunday for lunch.
In her youth, the lake would freeze solid every January.
common_mistakes: Using this pattern without a clear past time reference — the surrounding context (back then, in those days) is what makes this reading of would work.

topics.formula: wouldn't, to describe refusal or unwillingness in the past.
topics.key_idea: This is the negative, past-tense version of will's refusal sense (the car won't start) — describing something or someone that stubbornly resisted doing what was expected or wanted.
examples: The engine wouldn't start no matter what we tried.
I asked her to reconsider, but she wouldn't budge.
common_mistakes: Using didn't instead of wouldn't when the meaning is specifically about resistance or refusal, not just a simple negative past action.

topics.formula: would, to criticize someone's past annoying habits or behavior — the past-tense counterpart to will's criticism use.
topics.key_idea: This carries the same judgmental tone as will's criticism use, just shifted into the past, framing a repeated past behavior as something that grated on the speaker.
examples: He would always cancel plans at the last minute.
She would criticize everyone's cooking, even at other people's dinner parties.
common_mistakes: Reading this would as a neutral description of a past habit rather than picking up on the critical tone it usually carries in this context.

topics.formula: would have + past participle, standing on its own (often with but) rather than inside a full third conditional if-clause, to describe something that could have happened but didn't.
topics.key_idea: This same grammar from third conditional can appear without an explicit if-clause at all, with the unrealized condition simply implied by context or stated with but instead.
examples: I would have joined you, but I had a prior commitment.
They would have won the game if the referee hadn't made that call.
common_mistakes: Assuming would have + past participle always needs a formal if-clause attached — it works perfectly well as a standalone statement about an unrealized past possibility too.

topics.formula: would, to soften an opinion or make it sound more tentative and tactful, often in fixed phrases like I'd say, I'd have to agree, I would have thought.
topics.key_idea: This use of would takes the edge off a direct opinion, presenting it as a careful, considered judgment rather than a blunt assertion.
examples: I'd say we should wait for more information.
I would have thought she'd call by now.
common_mistakes: Using a blunter present-tense equivalent where the tactful, hedged tone of would is actually wanted.

topics.formula: should, in a that-clause after verbs like suggest, propose, or advise, or after adjectives expressing importance or emotion (essential, surprised, etc.) — a formal structure especially common in British English.
topics.key_idea: This formal should doesn't carry its usual advice or expectation meaning — it's simply a grammatical marker required by this specific structure, appearing after certain recommending verbs and certain evaluative adjectives.
examples: The board proposed that the budget should be increased.
It's crucial that the report should be accurate.
common_mistakes: Dropping should without recognizing this is a distinct formal pattern — some varieties of English (especially American) prefer the bare subjunctive here instead, but the should version is the standard formal British pattern.

topics.formula: if + subject + should + infinitive, a more tentative, formal version of a first-conditional if-clause — can also invert to Should + subject + infinitive, dropping if entirely. so that / in case + subject + should, in formal purpose clauses.
topics.key_idea: Adding should into an if-clause makes the possibility feel a bit more remote or formal than a plain present-tense if-clause, and the same word shows up in formal purpose clauses after so that or in case, again adding a note of formality to an otherwise everyday structure.
examples: If you should hear anything, let us know immediately.
Should the weather turn bad, we'll reschedule.
Keep this number in case you should need assistance.
common_mistakes: Treating if + should as informal or interchangeable with a plain if-clause in casual speech — this is specifically a formal register choice.

topics.formula: can, generally preferred over be able to for ability happening right now, before a passive structure, or when describing a skill or competence.
topics.key_idea: Though be able to can technically substitute for can almost anywhere, native usage leans toward can specifically in these three situations — immediate ability, passive constructions, and describing what someone knows how to do.
examples: Look, I can juggle five balls at once!
This document can be downloaded from our website.
He can read Latin fluently.
common_mistakes: Defaulting to be able to in these specific contexts when can is the more natural, idiomatic choice.

topics.formula: couldn't, generally more natural than wasn't/weren't able to, for a negative specific past action.
topics.key_idea: While affirmative specific past ability strictly requires was/were able to (not could), the negative side of that same rule relaxes — couldn't is actually the more idiomatic choice even for one specific occasion.
examples: We couldn't get a table at the restaurant last night.
common_mistakes: Using wasn't/weren't able to in the negative when couldn't would sound more natural — this asymmetry between positive and negative specific-occasion ability is easy to overlook.

topics.formula: can, for a general or characteristic possibility (something that can happen in general). could (not can), for a specific possibility in one particular situation. could also joins might/may for positive future predictions.
topics.key_idea: Can and could split possibility along the same general-versus-specific line that separates habits from single events elsewhere in English — can states a broad tendency, while could zooms in on one particular case, including guessing at a specific future outcome.
examples: Long commutes can affect your mental health.
Careful, that could be dangerous.
It could be sunny by the weekend.
common_mistakes: Using can for a specific, one-off possibility instead of could: 'It can be your ex' sounds off compared to the correct 'It could be your ex.'

topics.formula: may, more common in formal or academic writing, often describing general characteristics or behavior. might, more common in spoken English, especially for future plans.
topics.key_idea: Even though may and might are largely interchangeable for possibility, they lean toward different registers — may fits written, formal contexts describing tendencies, while might feels more natural in everyday speech about personal plans.
examples: Extreme heat may impair concentration.
I might visit my parents this weekend.
common_mistakes: Using may in casual spoken contexts where might would sound more natural, or vice versa in formal academic writing.

topics.formula: may well / might well + infinitive, to suggest a stronger, more likely possibility than may/might alone.
topics.key_idea: Adding well nudges the possibility further toward likely, without going all the way to the certainty of must.
examples: This may well be our best option.
He might well change his mind after hearing the offer.
common_mistakes: Treating may/might well as equivalent in strength to plain may/might — well adds real emphasis, pushing the likelihood higher.

topics.formula: may as well / might as well + infinitive, to make an unenthusiastic suggestion, typically when there's no better option available.
topics.key_idea: This fixed idiom suggests doing something not out of enthusiasm but simply because there's nothing better to do — a resigned, practical kind of suggestion.
examples: We might as well order pizza; nobody feels like cooking.
common_mistakes: Using this pattern for an enthusiastic recommendation — its tone is specifically resigned or practical, not eager.

topics.formula: may is not used to ask about possibility — could or expressions like be likely to are used instead. May is reserved for formal requests and offers.
topics.key_idea: Even though may expresses possibility in statements, that use doesn't carry over into questions — asking about possibility needs could or a be likely to structure, while may in a question is understood as a formal request, not a question about likelihood.
examples: Could this be the missing document?
Is it likely to snow tonight?
May I ask you something?
common_mistakes: Using may to ask about possibility: 'May this be the right solution?' sounds like an odd, oddly formal request rather than the intended question about likelihood.

topics.formula: might have + past participle, to criticize someone's past behavior — similar in function to should have.
topics.key_idea: This offers another way to express 'you really should have done that,' framing the criticism through a missed possibility rather than a direct obligation.
examples: You might have mentioned that the road was closed.
common_mistakes: Assuming should have is the only way to express this kind of past criticism — might have carries a very similar critical meaning.

topics.formula: may + clause + but + contrasting clause, a formal way to acknowledge a point before presenting an opposing one — similar in function to although.
topics.key_idea: This structure concedes something is true before pivoting to a different or opposing point, giving the sentence a formal, balanced, almost argumentative feel.
examples: The idea may sound unusual, but it could work.
She may have been rude, but she meant well.
common_mistakes: Missing that this may doesn't express uncertainty here — it's conceding a point as true, functioning more like although than like a genuine possibility.

topics.formula: bare infinitive (base form of the verb, no -s, and be for all persons), in a that-clause after certain verbs (advise, ask, demand, insist, order, propose, recommend, request, suggest) or adjectives (essential, important, crucial, necessary, vital, etc.) expressing a demand, suggestion, or necessity. Negative: not + base form. More common in American English; British English often uses should + infinitive or plain present simple instead.
topics.key_idea: This formal structure keeps the verb in its most basic, unmarked form no matter who the subject is, since it isn't really describing a fact — it's naming something being demanded, suggested, or considered necessary, not something that's actually happening. It's the American-English-favored counterpart to the British should + infinitive pattern covering the same territory.
examples: The manager insisted that the invoice be paid immediately.
It is vital that the data remain confidential.
common_mistakes: Adding -s for he/she/it, or using is instead of be: 'It is essential that every member is present' is the informal British alternative, but the strict subjunctive form keeps be and leave (not leaves), regardless of subject.

topics.formula: A handful of fixed, idiomatic expressions preserve the present subjunctive form even in everyday use: Be that as it may, Come what may, Suffice it to say, God save the King/Queen, etc.
topics.key_idea: These phrases are frozen relics of the subjunctive, used as complete set expressions rather than productive grammar — they're memorized as whole chunks rather than built from a rule a learner would apply elsewhere.
examples: Be that as it may, we should proceed with caution.
Come what may, we'll finish this project together.
common_mistakes: Trying to modify or conjugate these fixed expressions as if they followed regular grammar rules — they're memorized as complete, unchanging phrases.

topics.formula: It's / This is / That is the + ordinal (first, second, only, etc.) + time + present perfect, a fixed pattern for describing how many times something has happened up to now.
topics.key_idea: This is a specific, very common fixed structure for framing an experience in terms of its place in a sequence — the first time, the third time, the only time — always paired with present perfect, since it's inherently about the whole span of experience up to this moment.
examples: This is the second time I've tried this recipe.
common_mistakes: Using past simple instead of present perfect in this pattern: 'This is the third time I tried this dish' breaks the fixed pattern, which specifically requires present perfect.

topics.formula: since + present perfect (instead of since + past simple), when the situation introduced by since is itself still ongoing or continuing to be true.
topics.key_idea: The clause after since doesn't always need past simple — when the state or relationship being referred to is itself unfinished and continuing, present perfect can appear there too, doubling up the 'still going on' meaning in both halves of the sentence.
examples: Since I've lived here, I've made so many good friends.
common_mistakes: Assuming since is always followed by past simple — it switches to present perfect specifically when the since-clause itself describes something still ongoing.

topics.formula: Across present, past, and future perfect alike: the simple form focuses on result, completion, or quantity, while the continuous form focuses on the activity, duration, or ongoing nature of the action. Certain stative verbs (know, believe, understand, own, belong, like, love, hate, want) essentially never appear in any perfect continuous form. With verbs like live, work, teach, study, perfect simple suggests something long-term or permanent, while perfect continuous suggests something more temporary.
topics.key_idea: This result-versus-activity contrast isn't unique to present perfect — it runs consistently through past and future perfect too, always asking the same underlying question: is the point of the sentence what got finished, or how the time was actually spent doing it? A handful of stative verbs sidestep this choice entirely, staying in the simple form no matter what, and a few verbs about long-term situations use the same simple/continuous choice to hint at whether the situation feels permanent or temporary.
examples: I've fixed the leak. / I've been fixing the leak all afternoon.
By March, she'll have completed her thesis. / By March, she'll have been researching this topic for a year.
common_mistakes: Using perfect continuous with a firmly stative verb: 'I've been knowing her for years' instead of 'I've known her for years' — some verbs simply never take the continuous form, regardless of tense.

topics.formula: noun/pronoun + participle (its own subject, different from the main clause), in formal writing — an exception to the usual same-subject rule for participle clauses.
topics.key_idea: This is the formal escape hatch from the ordinary participle clause rule that both clauses must share a subject — an absolute clause supplies its own subject up front, letting it describe a separate but related circumstance, reason, or condition.
examples: The rain having stopped, we decided to go for a walk.
Weather permitting, the ceremony will be held outdoors.
common_mistakes: Assuming participle clauses always need the same subject as the main clause — this formal structure is the specific, deliberate exception, mainly reserved for written English.

topics.formula: There being + noun (absolute clause), for the existence or absence of something, corresponding to 'because/as there is/was.' There having been, when the existence described happened before the main clause's action.
topics.key_idea: This extends the absolute clause pattern to there itself, letting an entire 'there is/was' statement become a compact opening clause explaining a reason or circumstance.
examples: There being nothing left to discuss, the meeting ended early.
There having been no reply, they assumed the offer was declined.
common_mistakes: Using there being when the existence being described actually happened earlier than the main clause — that calls for there having been instead.

topics.formula: with + noun + participle (-ing for active/in-progress, past participle for passive/resulting state, or having + past participle for something completed earlier), describing a circumstance accompanying the main clause's action. The noun after with is the subject of that participle.
topics.key_idea: This construction packages an entire accompanying situation into a compact phrase built around with, and the participle form chosen tells you exactly how that situation relates in time and voice to the main action — ongoing, already finished, passively affecting something, or completed before the main clause.
examples: With the deadline approaching, the team worked through the weekend.
With the windows closed, the room felt stuffy.
With the guests having left, we finally cleaned up.
common_mistakes: Choosing the wrong participle form for the intended relationship — using the plain -ing form when the situation is actually already completed loses the 'already finished' meaning that having + past participle specifically signals.

topics.formula: Fixed participle expressions (generally speaking, judging by, considering, etc.) that comment on an entire sentence rather than describing an action performed by the main subject — these don't need to match the main clause's subject.
topics.key_idea: These phrases step outside the normal participle-clause rules entirely, functioning more like a fixed introductory comment on the whole statement that follows, which is exactly why the usual same-subject requirement doesn't apply to them.
examples: Roughly speaking, the project is halfway done.
Judging by the reviews, the restaurant is excellent.
Considering the budget, the results were impressive.
common_mistakes: Trying to apply the same-subject rule to these fixed expressions — they're set phrases commenting on the whole sentence, not participle clauses describing what the main subject is doing.

topics.formula: main clause + -ing participle clause, placed after the main clause to describe a direct consequence or result of what's just been stated.
topics.key_idea: Unlike the time/reason/cause uses that typically come before or alongside the main clause, this result use always trails after it, spelling out what naturally followed from the situation just described.
examples: The strike halted production, leaving thousands of orders unfulfilled.
The bridge collapsed, cutting off the only route to the village.
common_mistakes: Placing this result-expressing participle clause before the main clause instead of after — its position specifically after the main clause reflects that it describes a consequence, not a preceding cause or circumstance.
